Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD deception datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Claim: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on a single source dataset, Roleplaying deception scenarios, and evaluated on 3 held-out OOD target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Main framing: probes strong in-distribution can learn spurious correlations and fail OOD; authors work in the source-domain PCA basis rather than raw activations to select subspaces that generalize.

Key claimed findings: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained/oracle probe. (2) Source-side and target-side PC rankings fail: ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not transfer better than the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover transferable PCs without target data by interpreting most/least activating examples and selecting PCs encoding transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns. Abstract quantified LLM-judge result: probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Broad conclusion to track: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Claimed interpretation: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on single source dataset Roleplaying and evaluated OOD on Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Framing: strong in-distribution probes can learn spurious correlations and fail OOD; authors select subspaces in source-domain PCA basis.

Setup details: use 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al.; labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 assigned by GPT-4o, with ambiguous removed. Activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer 15 residual stream, chosen following Ying et al. (2026) as highest cross-domain AUROC; activations extracted by passing prompt through model and averaging token activations over assistant response. Standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance, apply same source stats to targets. Run PCA on scaled source activations, retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression probes with lambda=10. For PC subset S, project activations onto S before training/eval; baseline probes train directly on full standardized activations (not PC subset). Justification for top 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align better with SAE decoder features and are more interpretable; not claiming low-index PCs generalize better. Section 4.1 is said to confirm 100-PC subspace retains enough information for separation on every target.

Key claimed findings to check later: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components nearly matching target-trained/oracle; source/target probe-weight PC rankings fail vs full baseline; LLM judge partially recovers transferable PCs without target data. Abstract: LLM-judge highest-scoring PCs close baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Uses Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on source Roleplaying and OOD targets Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed. Activations: layer 15 residual stream, averaged over assistant response. Source standardization applied to targets. PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression lambda=10. For PC subset, project then train/eval; full baseline trains on full standardized reps. Low-index PCs justified by interpretability/SAE alignment, not claimed to generalize better.

4.1 baseline: full source-trained AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) get Report/Confirm/Sandbagging = 0.936/0.950/0.869, confirming 100-PC subspace contains enough info; difficulty is source-trained direction not generalizing.

4.2 greedy oracle PC selection: start empty, search top 100 source PCs, add candidate improving target AUROC most; train weights only on source projections. Uses 5-fold CV over target: select on non-held-out target folds, evaluate selected source-trained probe on held-out fold. Stop if no AUROC improvement >0.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. This is upper bound, not unbiased OOD, because subset selection uses target labels. Compare top-k PCs by variance with k matched to greedy. Greedy close to target-trained for Report and Sandbagging, improves baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC; variance control only matches greedy for Confirm and lags on Report/Sandbagging. Choice of PCs matters; variance explained not predictive.

4.3 begins testing hypotheses: transferable PCs might separate target classes individually, or be high-weight source-probe PCs. Rankings use standardized coefficient = |probe coefficient| * SD of PC after training on source-PCA-basis activations.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes, source Roleplaying, targets Insider Trading Report/Confirm and Sandbagging. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed. Activations layer 15 residual stream averaged over assistant response. Source standardization applied to targets. PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression lambda=10. Full source-trained baseline target AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained 100-source-PC probes CV: Report 0.936, Confirm 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869.

Greedy oracle PC selection (target-label-aided upper bound): iteratively add top-100 source PC that maximizes target AUROC with source-trained weights; 5-fold target CV selection/eval. Avg selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves Report/Sandbagging by ~0.22/0.23 AUROC; variance-matched top-k only matches for Confirm.

4.3 tests whether transferable PCs are (i) high source-probe-weight PCs or (ii) target-class-separating PCs. Rankings use standardized coefficient = |coef|*SD in source-PCA basis. For k set by greedy on full target (not CV): Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 14. Source-PCA ranking transfers about like full baseline. Target-PCA ranking good on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, below random on Sandbagging.

4.4 interpret PCs: for each top-100 source PC, use 8 most/least source examples; LLM describes poles/direction and rates OOD generalizability 1–10. No PC scored above 6, so 6 max observed; PCs scoring 6 in both runs = 19. Of 5 PCs appearing in greedy selections for >1 target, 3 got max OOD score; only 1 of top 5 source-PCA PCs did.

4.5 interp-selected subspace: use 19 max-score PCs; controls full baseline, top-19 variance PCs, and remaining 81 PCs after ablation; Figure 5 AUROCs with 95% CIs.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Activations are standardized using source statistics; PCA is applied to scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression parameter lambda set to 10.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic-regression classifiers) on one source dataset and evaluates 3 held-out target datasets. Main question: whether selecting principal components (PCs), directions in a source activation basis, improves OOD deception detection. A target-supervised greedy search adding PCs by target performance finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Probes are logistic regression classifiers on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations; token activations are averaged over assistant response. Source domain is Roleplaying; PCA basis is built from standardized source activations (source mean/unit variance, applied to targets). Targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Main metric AUROC; target evaluation uses 5-fold CV. Full representation baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe = trained directly on target data. Greedy oracle = target-supervised selection of subset S of retained 100 source PCs, repeatedly adding PC maximizing target AUROC; found 8–15 PCs nearly matching target-trained probes. Variance control selects top k source PCs by variance. Source-PCA/target-PCA probe coefficients use standardized coefficient = abs coefficient × PC std to rank PCs; summary says these rankings do not recover transferable subspace. LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) interprets PC positive/negative poles from token<TAB>activation examples normalized -10 to +10 and rates OOD deception usefulness 1–10. Maximum observed score is 6; interp-selected PCs are 19 PCs scoring 6 in both runs; interp-ablated control is remaining 81 PCs. Summary claims interp-selection improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of full-baseline-to-greedy gap on two targets. No causal validation/inference-time ablation was done. Appendix C compares PCs to SAE decoder features from andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct, reports Spearman rho for PC index vs decoder alignment. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD deception datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Claim: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on a single source dataset, Roleplaying deception scenarios, and evaluated on 3 held-out OOD target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Main framing: probes strong in-distribution can learn spurious correlations and fail OOD; authors work in the source-domain PCA basis rather than raw activations to select subspaces that generalize.

Key claimed findings: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained/oracle probe. (2) Source-side and target-side PC rankings fail: ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not transfer better than the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover transferable PCs without target data by interpreting most/least activating examples and selecting PCs encoding transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns. Abstract quantified LLM-judge result: probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Broad conclusion to track: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Claimed interpretation: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions.

4.2 greedy oracle PC selection: start empty, search top 100 source PCs, add candidate improving target AUROC most; train weights only on source projections. Uses 5-fold CV over target: select on non-held-out target folds, evaluate selected source-trained probe on held-out fold. Stop if no AUROC improvement >0.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. This is upper bound, not unbiased OOD, because subset selection uses target labels. Compare top-k PCs by variance with k matched to greedy. Greedy close to target-trained for Report and Sandbagging, improves baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC; variance control only matches greedy for Confirm and lags on Report/Sandbagging. Choice of PCs matters; variance explained not predictive.

4.3 begins testing hypotheses: transferable PCs might separate target classes individually, or be high-weight source-probe PCs. Rankings use standardized coefficient = |probe coefficient| * SD of PC after training on source-PCA-basis activations.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Activations are standardized using source statistics; PCA is applied to scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression parameter lambda set to 10.

Main claims from abstract/summary: train linear probes on source and evaluate on 3 held-out targets. Target-supervised greedy oracle repeatedly adds source PC maximizing target AUROC; finds 8–15 PCs nearly matching target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source-probe or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. Standardized coefficient = abs(probe coefficient) * PC std. Variance control = top k source PCs.

LLM interpretability: GPT-5-mini judge describes PC positive/negative poles from examples and scores OOD deception usefulness 1–10; activation magnitudes normalized -10 to +10 in prompt. Max observed OOD score = 6. Interp-selected PCs = 19 PCs receiving score 6 in both scoring runs; interp-ablated/control = remaining 81 PCs. This selection improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of gap between full baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. No causal/inference-time ablation validation performed. Appendix C uses andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct SAE decoder alignment; Spearman rho, Jaccard overlap appear later.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Setup confirmed in Sec 3: 4 deception datasets (Roleplaying source; Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging targets/test transfer), GPT-4o labels honest=0/ambiguous=-1/deceptive=1 and ambiguous removed. final_notes:
Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual stream averaged over assistant response; source Roleplaying; targets Insider Trading Report/Confirm and Sandbagging. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed. Dataset totals/label counts (-1/0/1): Roleplaying 371=140/59/172; Report 473=218/194/61; Confirm 151=29/38/84; Sandbagging 1000=379/375/246.

Source standardization applied to targets. PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression lambda=10. Full source-trained baseline target AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained 100-source-PC probes CV: Report 0.936, Confirm 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869.

Greedy oracle PC selection: target-label-aided upper bound; 5-fold target CV. Avg selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy oracle reported Report 0.929, Sandbagging 0.832; improves Report/Sandbagging by ~0.22/0.23 AUROC. §4.3 k by full-target greedy: Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 14.

§4.4/Appendix B/E: GPT-5-mini PC interpretation; no PC >6; 19 PCs scored 6 in both runs. Interp-selected 19 max-score PCs outperform baseline/top-19 variance/remaining-81 ablated on all targets. Report gap inconsistency noted earlier: 68% vs limitations 78% to 0.881. Sandbagging 0.606→0.662 closes 25% to greedy 0.832. Appendix E Table 3 says “selected for likely transferability” but includes PC9 and PC81 with score 3 and explanations saying brittle/domain-specific.

Appendix C: lower PCs stronger decoder alignment; Spearman rho -0.857 best SAE feature, -0.917 top-10 mean. Appendix D table lists PC sets; internal conflicts: stated Jaccards don’t match table; Sandbagging greedy table has 15 PCs vs earlier k=14.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD deception datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Claim: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on a single source dataset, Roleplaying deception scenarios, and evaluated on 3 held-out OOD target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Main framing: probes strong in-distribution can learn spurious correlations and fail OOD; authors work in the source-domain PCA basis rather than raw activations to select subspaces that generalize.

Key claimed findings: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained/oracle probe. (2) Source-side and target-side PC rankings fail: ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not transfer better than the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover transferable PCs without target data by interpreting most/least activating examples and selecting PCs encoding transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns. Abstract quantified LLM-judge result: probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Broad conclusion to track: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Claimed interpretation: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Paper summary claims: asks whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD deception detection. Compares probes (classifiers for a property) in full representations vs selected directions. Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Reported high-level results: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. Scope/caveats: uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Source dataset V8 Roleplaying; targets C2R Insider Trading Report, W6 Insider Trading Confirm, J9 Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses: -1 ambiguous removed, 0 honest, 1 deceptive. All classifiers logistic regression with lambda=10; metric AUROC with 95% CIs.

H2 greedy oracle = target-guided direction selection via 5-fold CV: uses non-held-out target folds for selection, held-out fold for evaluation, but fits probe weights only on source; treated as transfer upper bound not unbiased OOD estimate. T6 source-PCA probe and M9 target-PCA probe provide coefficient rankings; standardized coefficient X4 = abs coefficient × PC SD. LLM judge C7 rates direction OOD usefulness (R5) from natural-language interpretations; P2 GPT-5-mini interprets directions using high positive/negative activation examples. L2 interp-selected PC probe uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs; A7 uses complement.
Earlier high-level claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; source weights/target separation/variance don’t recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full baseline on all targets but recovery varies sharply. Decoder alignment with SAE decoder features (`andyrdt/...`) assessed; leading PCs have stronger alignment; Spearman rho reported. Jaccard overlap compares selected sets. Caveats: one model/source, interpretations descriptive not causal.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD deception datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Claim: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on a single source dataset, Roleplaying deception scenarios, and evaluated on 3 held-out OOD target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Main framing: probes strong in-distribution can learn spurious correlations and fail OOD; authors work in the source-domain PCA basis rather than raw activations to select subspaces that generalize.

Key claimed findings: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained/oracle probe. (2) Source-side and target-side PC rankings fail: ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not transfer better than the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover transferable PCs without target data by interpreting most/least activating examples and selecting PCs encoding transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns. Abstract quantified LLM-judge result: probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Broad conclusion to track: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Claimed interpretation: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions.

4.1 baseline: full source-trained AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) get Report/Confirm/Sandbagging = 0.936/0.950/0.869, confirming 100-PC subspace contains enough info; difficulty is source-trained direction not generalizing.

4.2 greedy oracle PC selection: start empty, search top 100 source PCs, add candidate improving target AUROC most; train weights only on source projections. Uses 5-fold CV over target: select on non-held-out target folds, evaluate selected source-trained probe on held-out fold. Stop if no AUROC improvement >0.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. This is upper bound, not unbiased OOD, because subset selection uses target labels. Compare top-k PCs by variance with k matched to greedy. Greedy close to target-trained for Report and Sandbagging, improves baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC; variance control only matches greedy for Confirm and lags on Report/Sandbagging. Choice of PCs matters; variance explained not predictive.

4.3 begins testing hypotheses: transferable PCs might separate target classes individually, or be high-weight source-probe PCs. Rankings use standardized coefficient = |probe coefficient| * SD of PC after training on source-PCA-basis activations.

Avg selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves Report/Sandbagging by ~0.22/0.23 AUROC; variance-matched top-k only matches for Confirm.

4.3 tests whether transferable PCs are (i) high source-probe-weight PCs or (ii) target-class-separating PCs. Rankings use standardized coefficient = |coef|*SD in source-PCA basis. For k set by greedy on full target (not CV): Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 14. Source-PCA ranking transfers about like full baseline. Target-PCA ranking good on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, below random on Sandbagging.

4.4 interpret PCs: for each top-100 source PC, use 8 most/least source examples; LLM describes poles/direction and rates OOD generalizability 1–10. No PC scored above 6, so 6 max observed; PCs scoring 6 in both runs = 19. Of 5 PCs appearing in greedy selections for >1 target, 3 got max OOD score; only 1 of top 5 source-PCA PCs did.

4.5 interp-selected subspace: use 19 max-score PCs; controls full baseline, top-19 variance PCs, and remaining 81 PCs after ablation; Figure 5 AUROCs with 95% CIs.

Setup specifics: Model is Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Uses layer 15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens only, justified by Ying et al. (2026) as highest cross-domain discrimination. Datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025): one source Roleplaying (V8) and three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9); no other source dataset. Labels by GPT-4o (K8): honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed.

Preprocessing/training: source activations standardized to zero mean/unit variance; same source stats standardize targets. PCA transformation N4D retains leading 100 principal components, called PCs/Q7. Subset S projection precedes training/evaluation. Logistic regression with lambda=10 for classifiers. Comparator/full-representation baseline B8Q trains directly on all standardized activations. Retaining 100 PCs is for interpretability comparability, not because low-index PCs generalize better; alignment with U9/Bricken et al. decreases with PC index, so lower indices are more natural-language interpretable. Error bars are 95% CIs.

Earlier possible terminology issue now clarified: Figure 1’s “source N4D basis” appears to be PCA basis; “Q7 directions/coordinates” are principal components.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Activations are standardized using source statistics; PCA is applied to scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression parameter lambda set to 10.

Main claims from abstract/summary: train linear probes on source and evaluate on 3 held-out targets. Target-supervised greedy oracle repeatedly adds source PC maximizing target AUROC; finds 8–15 PCs nearly matching target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source-probe or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. Standardized coefficient = abs(probe coefficient) * PC std. Variance control = top k source PCs.

LLM interpretability: GPT-5-mini judge describes PC positive/negative poles from examples and scores OOD deception usefulness 1–10; activation magnitudes normalized -10 to +10 in prompt. Max observed OOD score = 6. Interp-selected PCs = 19 PCs receiving score 6 in both scoring runs; interp-ablated/control = remaining 81 PCs. This selection improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of gap between full baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. No causal/inference-time ablation validation performed. Appendix C uses andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct SAE decoder alignment; Spearman rho, Jaccard overlap appear later.

Activations standardized using source stats; PCA on scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression lambda=10.

Intro states research question: which source-domain PC subset supports generalizable deception-probe training and how identify it. Contributions: (1) target-supervised greedy search adds source PCs by target performance and finds 8–15 PCs on which source-trained probe nearly matches target-trained probe (Sec 4.2/Fig 3); (2) source- and target-probe weight rankings fail to recover transferable subspace / do not transfer better than full-representation baseline (Sec 4.3/Fig 4); (3) LLM judge partially recovers subspace without target data (Sec 4.5/Fig 5), selecting 19 PCs, with 78% and 25% gap recovery on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging.

Earlier abstract/claims: greedy oracle averages 15 / 8 / 14 PCs across three targets. Standardized coefficient = abs(probe coefficient) * PC std. Variance control = top k source PCs. LLM interpretability: GPT-5-mini judge describes PC poles from examples and scores OOD deception usefulness 1–10; activation magnitudes normalized -10 to +10 in prompt. Max observed OOD score=6; interp-selected PCs = 19 PCs receiving score 6 in both scoring runs; control/ablated = remaining 81 PCs. Selection improves transfer on all 3 targets. No causal/inference-time ablation validation. Appendix C uses andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct SAE decoder alignment; Spearman rho, Jaccard overlap later.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Setup confirmed in Sec 3: 4 deception datasets (Roleplaying source; Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging targets/test transfer), GPT-4o labels honest=0/ambiguous=-1/deceptive=1 and ambiguous removed. Sec 4.1: Figure 2 compares source-trained full reps (blue), source-trained top-100 PCs (orange), target-trained top-100 source PCs (green). Paper summary claims: asks whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD deception detection. Compares probes (classifiers for a property) in full representations vs selected directions. Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Reported high-level results: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. Scope/caveats: uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Paper studies whether selected subspaces of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6) layer-15 residual-stream activations improve OOD deception detection. Activations averaged over assistant-response tokens, standardized with source stats, PCA keeps leading 100 source PCs (Q7/N4D). Source dataset V8 Roleplaying; targets C2R Insider Trading Report, W6 Insider Trading Confirm, J9 Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses: -1 ambiguous removed, 0 honest, 1 deceptive. All classifiers logistic regression with lambda=10; metric AUROC with 95% CIs.
Key terms/methods: B8Q full-representation baseline = source-trained on all standardized activations. Y4 variance control = source-trained on top-k PCs by explained variance. H2 greedy oracle = target-guided direction selection via 5-fold CV: uses non-held-out target folds for selection, held-out fold for evaluation, but fits probe weights only on source; treated as transfer upper bound not unbiased OOD estimate. T6 source-PCA probe and M9 target-PCA probe provide coefficient rankings; standardized coefficient X4 = abs coefficient × PC SD. LLM judge C7 rates direction OOD usefulness (R5) from natural-language interpretations; P2 GPT-5-mini interprets directions using high positive/negative activation examples. L2 interp-selected PC probe uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs; A7 uses complement.
Earlier high-level claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; source weights/target separation/variance don’t recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full baseline on all targets but recovery varies sharply. Decoder alignment with SAE decoder features (`andyrdt/...`) assessed; leading PCs have stronger alignment; Spearman rho reported. Jaccard overlap compares selected sets. Caveats: one model/source, interpretations descriptive not causal.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD deception datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Claim: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on a single source dataset, Roleplaying deception scenarios, and evaluated on 3 held-out OOD target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Main framing: probes strong in-distribution can learn spurious correlations and fail OOD; authors work in the source-domain PCA basis rather than raw activations to select subspaces that generalize.

Key claimed findings: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained/oracle probe. (2) Source-side and target-side PC rankings fail: ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not transfer better than the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover transferable PCs without target data by interpreting most/least activating examples and selecting PCs encoding transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns. Abstract quantified LLM-judge result: probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Broad conclusion to track: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Claimed interpretation: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Activations are standardized using source statistics; PCA is applied to scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression parameter lambda set to 10.

Main claims from abstract/summary: train linear probes on source and evaluate on 3 held-out targets. Target-supervised greedy oracle repeatedly adds source PC maximizing target AUROC; finds 8–15 PCs nearly matching target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source-probe or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. Standardized coefficient = abs(probe coefficient) * PC std. Variance control = top k source PCs.

LLM interpretability: GPT-5-mini judge describes PC positive/negative poles from examples and scores OOD deception usefulness 1–10; activation magnitudes normalized -10 to +10 in prompt. Max observed OOD score = 6. Interp-selected PCs = 19 PCs receiving score 6 in both scoring runs; interp-ablated/control = remaining 81 PCs. This selection improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of gap between full baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. No causal/inference-time ablation validation performed. Appendix C uses andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct SAE decoder alignment; Spearman rho, Jaccard overlap appear later.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Setup confirmed in Sec 3: 4 deception datasets (Roleplaying source; Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging targets/test transfer), GPT-4o labels honest=0/ambiguous=-1/deceptive=1 and ambiguous removed. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant response tokens only. Source activations standardized to zero mean/unit variance; same source stats applied to targets. PCA fit on scaled source activations; retain top 100 source PCs, PC index/order by source variance. PC-subset probes project activations to subset S before train/eval. Baseline probes train on full standardized activations (“full representation”). Logistic regression classifiers throughout, lambda=10. AUROC metric; earlier notes say 5 target folds/CV and 95% CI error bars.

Motivation for retaining top 100 PCs: SAE decoder alignment decreases with PC index (Appendix C), making lower-index PCs more interpretable/comparable to interpretability-driven selection; explicitly not a claim that low-index PCs generalize better. Paper summary claims: asks whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD deception detection. Compares probes (classifiers for a property) in full representations vs selected directions. Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Reported high-level results: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Authors Daniel Yoo, Adrians Skapars.

Abstract claims: Linear probes can detect behaviors/concepts in LM activations but may fail OOD. Study uses Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct probes over 3 held-out deception detection datasets totaling 1,216 non-ambiguous responses. Main result: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training distribution of activations enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). Further: PC interpretations can identify a subset of transferable PCs. Method: use an LLM judge to score each PC by whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction, then probe on highest-scoring PCs. Reported gap closure: 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging (baseline-to-oracle gap). Interpretation claim: source probe’s heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features; directions that transfer encode same contrast more abstractly, capturable by natural language descriptions. Overall claim: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Intro: Motivation is linear probes can learn spurious correlations despite concepts being linearly represented. They work in source-domain PCA basis, not raw activations, to study which PCs support generalizable probe training. Testbed: deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, trained on single source dataset “Roleplaying deception scenarios,” evaluated on 3 held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Contributions claimed: (1) small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components where source-trained probe nearly matches target-trained probe (Sec 4.2); (2) source-side and target-side rankings fail: ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not transfer better than full-representation baseline (Sec 4.3); (3) LLM judge partially recovers subspace without target data, selecting PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns (Sec 4.5). Figure 1 overview: project activations to source PCA basis, filter candidate PC directions, train probes on selected low-dimensional subspace.

Abstract/Intro claims: Linear probes may fail OOD; using source-domain PCA basis/subspace selection improves transfer for deception probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Setup: Uses 4 Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) datasets: Roleplaying source; Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging targets. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed. Model activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer 15 residual stream, chosen following Ying et al. (2026) as highest cross-domain AUROC; average token activations over assistant response. Standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance and apply same stats to targets. PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Probes: logistic regression classifiers (λ=10). Subset experiments project activations onto selected PCs before training/evaluation; baseline probes train directly on full standardized activations. Justification for top 100: lower-index PCs align better with SAE decoder features and are more interpretable; not claiming low-index PCs generalize better. Sec 4.1 is said to confirm 100-PC subspace retains enough info to separate deceptive/honest on every target.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Paper summary claims: asks whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD deception detection. Compares probes (classifiers for a property) in full representations vs selected directions. Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Reported high-level results: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims study of linear probes for deception detection in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct over 3 held-out deception detection datasets. Main finding: projecting inputs onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution of activations enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). Also claims PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: using an LLM judge to score PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction, then probing on highest-scoring PCs, closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation: source-probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural-language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract: linear probes for deception detection in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct over 3 held-out datasets; projecting onto small subset of source-training PCs enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching oracle target-trained probes. LLM judge scores PCs from most/least activating examples for transferable deception direction; selecting high-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Intro: trains on single source dataset “Roleplaying deception scenarios,” evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2025). Uses Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Works in source-domain PCA basis instead of raw activations; studies which PC subsets support generalizable probes and how to identify them. Contributions: (1) target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds small transferable subspace of 8–15 components where source-trained probe nearly matches target-trained oracle (Sec 4.2); (2) source-side and target-side PC rankings by source/target probe weights fail to recover subspace and do not transfer better than full-representation baseline (Sec 4.3); (3) LLM judge partially recovers subspace without target data by interpreting/selecting PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns (Sec 4.5). Figure 1: pipeline projects activations onto source-domain PCA basis, filters candidate PC directions, trains probes on selected low-dimensional subspace.

Retaining 100 PCs is for interpretability comparability, not because low-index PCs generalize better; alignment with U9/Bricken et al. decreases with PC index, so lower indices are more natural-language interpretable. Title/setup: 4 deception datasets: Roleplaying source; Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging targets. GPT-4o labels honest=0/ambiguous=-1/deceptive=1; ambiguous removed. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual activations averaged over assistant tokens. Source standardized; same stats to targets. PCA fit on scaled source; top 100 PCs. Sec 4.1: full-rep source transfer AUROC Report 0.706, Confirm 0.874, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained top-100 source PCs: 0.936/0.950/0.869.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Activations are standardized using source statistics; PCA is applied to scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression parameter lambda set to 10.

Main claims from abstract/summary: train linear probes on source and evaluate on 3 held-out targets. Target-supervised greedy oracle repeatedly adds source PC maximizing target AUROC; finds 8–15 PCs nearly matching target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source-probe or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. Standardized coefficient = abs(probe coefficient) * PC std. Variance control = top k source PCs.

LLM interpretability: GPT-5-mini judge describes PC positive/negative poles from examples and scores OOD deception usefulness 1–10; activation magnitudes normalized -10 to +10 in prompt. Max observed OOD score = 6. Interp-selected PCs = 19 PCs receiving score 6 in both scoring runs; interp-ablated/control = remaining 81 PCs. This selection improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of gap between full baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. No causal/inference-time ablation validation performed. Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Reported high-level results: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD deception datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Uses Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on source Roleplaying and OOD targets Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed. Activations: layer 15 residual stream, averaged over assistant response. Source standardization applied to targets. PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression lambda=10. For PC subset, project then train/eval; full baseline trains on full standardized reps. Low-index PCs justified by interpretability/SAE alignment, not claimed to generalize better.

4.1 baseline: full source-trained AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) get Report/Confirm/Sandbagging = 0.936/0.950/0.869, confirming 100-PC subspace contains enough info; difficulty is source-trained direction not generalizing.

4.2 greedy oracle PC selection: start empty, search top 100 source PCs, add candidate improving target AUROC most; train weights only on source projections. Uses 5-fold CV over target: select on non-held-out target folds, evaluate selected source-trained probe on held-out fold. Stop if no AUROC improvement >0.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. This is upper bound, not unbiased OOD, because subset selection uses target labels. Compare top-k PCs by variance with k matched to greedy. Greedy close to target-trained for Report and Sandbagging, improves baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC; variance control only matches greedy for Confirm and lags on Report/Sandbagging. Choice of PCs matters; variance explained not predictive.

4.3 begins testing hypotheses: transferable PCs might separate target classes individually, or be high-weight source-probe PCs. Rankings use standardized coefficient = |probe coefficient| * SD of PC after training on source-PCA-basis activations.

Avg selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves Report/Sandbagging by ~0.22/0.23 AUROC; variance-matched top-k only matches for Confirm.

For k set by greedy on full target (not CV): Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 14. Source-PCA ranking transfers about like full baseline. Target-PCA ranking good on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, below random on Sandbagging.

4.4 interpret PCs: for each top-100 source PC, use 8 most/least source examples; LLM describes poles/direction and rates OOD generalizability 1–10. Activations standardized using source stats; PCA on scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression lambda=10.

Intro states research question: which source-domain PC subset supports generalizable deception-probe training and how identify it. Contributions: (1) target-supervised greedy search adds source PCs by target performance and finds 8–15 PCs on which source-trained probe nearly matches target-trained probe (Sec 4.2/Fig 3); (2) source- and target-probe weight rankings fail to recover transferable subspace / do not transfer better than full-representation baseline (Sec 4.3/Fig 4); (3) LLM judge partially recovers subspace without target data (Sec 4.5/Fig 5), selecting 19 PCs, with 78% and 25% gap recovery on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging.

Earlier abstract/claims: greedy oracle averages 15 / 8 / 14 PCs across three targets. Standardized coefficient = abs(probe coefficient) * PC std. Variance control = top k source PCs. LLM interpretability: GPT-5-mini judge describes PC poles from examples and scores OOD deception usefulness 1–10; activation magnitudes normalized -10 to +10 in prompt. Max observed OOD score=6; interp-selected PCs = 19 PCs receiving score 6 in both scoring runs; control/ablated = remaining 81 PCs. Selection improves transfer on all 3 targets. No causal/inference-time ablation validation. Appendix C uses andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct SAE decoder alignment; Spearman rho, Jaccard overlap later.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Setup confirmed in Sec 3: 4 deception datasets (Roleplaying source; Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging targets/test transfer), GPT-4o labels honest=0/ambiguous=-1/deceptive=1 and ambiguous removed. Sec 4.1: Figure 2 compares source-trained full reps (blue), source-trained top-100 PCs (orange), target-trained top-100 source PCs (green). Full-rep source transfer AUROC: Report 0.706, Confirm 0.874, Sandbagging 0.606. Sec 4.2: Greedy oracle PC selection starts empty; searches top 100 PCs; adds PC that most improves target AUROC; source logistic probe trained for each subset; subset selection uses non-held-out target folds in 5-fold CV, evaluated on held-out fold; stops if no candidate improves AUROC by >0.001. Mean selected sizes: 15 Report, 8 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging. Control: top-k PCs by variance with k matched to greedy. Greedy improves baseline by 0.22 Report and 0.23 Sandbagging, nearly target-trained; variance control only matches on Confirm, worse on Report/Sandbagging. Paper summary claims: asks whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD deception detection. Compares probes (classifiers for a property) in full representations vs selected directions. Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Reported high-level results: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. Scope/caveats: uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD deception datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD deception datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Claim: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Methods: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual stream, assistant response token average. Source activations standardized, stats applied to targets. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Activations are standardized using source statistics; PCA is applied to scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression parameter lambda set to 10.

Main claims from abstract/summary: train linear probes on source and evaluate on 3 held-out targets. Target-supervised greedy oracle repeatedly adds source PC maximizing target AUROC; finds 8–15 PCs nearly matching target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source-probe or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. Standardized coefficient = abs(probe coefficient) * PC std. Variance control = top k source PCs.

LLM interpretability: GPT-5-mini judge describes PC positive/negative poles from examples and scores OOD deception usefulness 1–10; activation magnitudes normalized -10 to +10 in prompt. Max observed OOD score = 6. Interp-selected PCs = 19 PCs receiving score 6 in both scoring runs; interp-ablated/control = remaining 81 PCs. This selection improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of gap between full baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. No causal/inference-time ablation validation performed. Appendix C uses andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct SAE decoder alignment; Spearman rho, Jaccard overlap appear later.

Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD deception datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Claim: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on a single source dataset, Roleplaying deception scenarios, and evaluated on 3 held-out OOD target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Main framing: probes strong in-distribution can learn spurious correlations and fail OOD; authors work in the source-domain PCA basis rather than raw activations to select subspaces that generalize.

Key claimed findings: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained/oracle probe. 4.1 baseline: full source-trained AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) get Report/Confirm/Sandbagging = 0.936/0.950/0.869, confirming 100-PC subspace contains enough info; difficulty is source-trained direction not generalizing.

4.2 greedy oracle PC selection: start empty, search top 100 source PCs, add candidate improving target AUROC most; train weights only on source projections. Uses 5-fold CV over target: select on non-held-out target folds, evaluate selected source-trained probe on held-out fold. Stop if no AUROC improvement >0.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. This is upper bound, not unbiased OOD, because subset selection uses target labels. Compare top-k PCs by variance with k matched to greedy. Greedy close to target-trained for Report and Sandbagging, improves baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC; variance control only matches greedy for Confirm and lags on Report/Sandbagging. Choice of PCs matters; variance explained not predictive.

4.3 begins testing hypotheses: transferable PCs might separate target classes individually, or be high-weight source-probe PCs. Rankings use standardized coefficient = |probe coefficient| * SD of PC after training on source-PCA-basis activations.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Activations are standardized using source statistics; PCA is applied to scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression parameter lambda set to 10.

Main claims from abstract/summary: train linear probes on source and evaluate on 3 held-out targets. Target-supervised greedy oracle repeatedly adds source PC maximizing target AUROC; finds 8–15 PCs nearly matching target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source-probe or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. Standardized coefficient = abs(probe coefficient) * PC std. Variance control = top k source PCs.

LLM interpretability: GPT-5-mini judge describes PC positive/negative poles from examples and scores OOD deception usefulness 1–10; activation magnitudes normalized -10 to +10 in prompt. Max observed OOD score = 6. Interp-selected PCs = 19 PCs receiving score 6 in both scoring runs; interp-ablated/control = remaining 81 PCs. This selection improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of gap between full baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. No causal/inference-time ablation validation performed. Appendix C uses andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct SAE decoder alignment; Spearman rho, Jaccard overlap appear later.

Paper summary claims: asks whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD deception detection. Compares probes (classifiers for a property) in full representations vs selected directions. Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Reported high-level results: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. Scope/caveats: uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.
