grade.reason: The first reported error directly flags the claim about transfer to every LLM family as contradicted by the paper's one-model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) experimental setup.

errors.claim: “the source probe’s favored directions causally increase the model’s deception on target responses”
errors.evidence: The experimental setup in this part only describes training and evaluating logistic-regression probes on fixed activations: “we also train a probe directly on target data within this subspace using 5-fold cross-validation” and Figure 2 reports “Probe AUROC.” Earlier notes likewise say activations are extracted from model responses and probes are classifiers trained/evaluated on representations.
errors.explanation: Nothing in the described experiment intervenes on the model or changes its responses; the probes are evaluated as detectors on already-generated activations. Thus the causal claim that probe directions increase deception conflicts with the paper’s own described classification-only setup.

errors.claim: “The ‘target-PCA probe’ ranks PCs by the weights learned by a probe trained on target data.”
errors.evidence: Immediately after: “In both cases, the probes are trained on source data that has been projected onto the top k PCs, selected based to their respective rankings.”
errors.explanation: The target-PCA probe is described as using weights from a target-trained probe, but then the text says both probes are trained on source data. Unless these are two distinct probes, the description is internally inconsistent.

errors.claim: “These are descriptive claims, not causal ones.” / “No causal validation.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “authors say source probe’s favored directions ‘causally increase’ deception despite classifier-only experiments.”
errors.explanation: The limitations section says the paper is not making causal claims about PCs/representations, but an earlier section reportedly described source-probe-favored directions as causally increasing deception. Those two characterizations conflict internally.

errors.claim: “Jaccard overlap between the PC sets of 2 methods (greedy and target-pca) is 0.182 for Insider Trading Report, 0.077 for Insider Trading Confirm, and 0.167 for Sandbagging.”
errors.evidence: Table 2 lists Greedy Report = {PC6, PC89, PC62, PC66, PC26, PC14, PC57, PC25, PC93, PC9, PC70, PC97, PC78} and Target Report = 15 PCs including PC5, PC6, PC89, PC18, PC79, PC46, PC87, PC4, PC14, PC34, PC29, PC1, PC66, PC67, PC19. Their intersection is 4 PCs and union is 24, giving 4/24 = 0.167, not 0.182. For Confirm, table intersection is 2 and union is 20, giving 0.100, not 0.077. For Sandbagging, table intersection is 5 and union is 25, giving 0.200, not 0.167.
errors.explanation: The Jaccard values stated in the text do not match the PC sets shown in the table in the same appendix.

errors.claim: “The 2 methods agree on less than a fifth of their selections.”
errors.evidence: Using the PC sets listed in Table 2 for Sandbagging, the overlap is 5 PCs out of a union of 25 PCs, i.e. 5/25 = 0.200.
errors.explanation: For Sandbagging, the table implies agreement of exactly one fifth, not less than one fifth.

errors.claim: Table 2 presents “Selected PCs” for “Target separability ranking” and lists 15 PCs for Insider Trading Report and 15 PCs for Insider Trading Confirm.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Section 4.3: “k chosen on full target: Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 14.”
errors.explanation: If these are the selected target separability PCs, the table’s 15 PCs for Report and Confirm conflict with the earlier stated selected k values of 13 and 7.

errors.claim: “Table 3: Principal components selected for likely transferability, based on interpretation with an LLM judge” includes PC9 with OOD Score 3 and PC81 with OOD Score 3.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Section 4.4: LLM interprets top 100 PCs; no PC >6 OOD score; retain 19 PCs scoring 6 both runs.”
errors.explanation: If PCs were selected for likely transferability by the LLM-judge criterion described earlier, they should be among the retained PCs scoring 6 in both runs. This table labels PC9 and PC81 as selected for likely transferability despite giving them low OOD scores of 3.

final_notes:
Section 4.1 baseline: source-trained full-representation probes on targets: Confirm 0.874 AUROC, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes within top-100 source-PC subspace: Report/Confirm/Sandbagging 0.936/0.950/0.869. Possible contradiction: source probe directions said to “causally increase” deception, but Section 5 says no causal validation/descriptive only.

4.2 greedy oracle PC selection upper bound: avg subset sizes Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves Report/Sandbagging by 0.22/0.23; variance-matched control only matches Confirm.

4.3 standardized coefficient ranking = abs(coef)*SD. Possible inconsistency: describes source-PCA/target-PCA ranks by source/target-trained probes, then says both probes trained on source data. k chosen on full target: Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 14.

4.4/4.5/5: LLM interprets top 100 PCs; no PC >6 OOD score; retain 19 PCs scoring 6 both runs. Interp-selected 19 PCs use no target data and improve all three: Report 0.706→0.881, Confirm baseline 0.874 near ceiling, Sandbagging 0.606→0.662. Limitations: single model/source/layer, linear pipeline, no causal validation/inference ablation.

Appendix A counts: Roleplaying 371, Report 473, Confirm 151, Sandbagging 1000. Appendix C: lower PCs align more with SAE decoder. Appendix D: Jaccards conflict with table sets; target lists 15 PCs despite earlier k values.

Appendix E: Table 3 says PCs selected for likely transferability: PC62 score6, PC57 score6, PC9 score3, PC81 score3, PC86 score6. This conflicts with earlier criterion retaining only score-6 PCs. Table 4 examples: PC7 3, PC8 4, PC11 3, PC12 3, PC4 6.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD deception datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Claim: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on a single source dataset, Roleplaying deception scenarios, and evaluated on 3 held-out OOD target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Main framing: probes strong in-distribution can learn spurious correlations and fail OOD; authors work in the source-domain PCA basis rather than raw activations to select subspaces that generalize.

Key claimed findings: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained/oracle probe. (2) Source-side and target-side PC rankings fail: ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not transfer better than the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover transferable PCs without target data by interpreting most/least activating examples and selecting PCs encoding transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns. Abstract quantified LLM-judge result: probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Broad conclusion to track: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Claimed interpretation: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on single source dataset Roleplaying and evaluated OOD on Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Framing: strong in-distribution probes can learn spurious correlations and fail OOD; authors select subspaces in source-domain PCA basis.

Setup details: use 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al.; labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 assigned by GPT-4o, with ambiguous removed. Activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer 15 residual stream, chosen following Ying et al. (2026) as highest cross-domain AUROC; activations extracted by passing prompt through model and averaging token activations over assistant response. Standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance, apply same source stats to targets. Run PCA on scaled source activations, retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression probes with lambda=10. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Paper summary claims: asks whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD deception detection. Compares probes (classifiers for a property) in full representations vs selected directions. Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Reported high-level results: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. Scope/caveats: uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

final_notes:
Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Source Roleplaying; targets Report, Confirm, Sandbagging; labels honest=0/deceptive=1/ambiguous=-1, ambiguous removed for probing. Counts incl ambiguous: Roleplaying 371=140/-1,59/0,172/1; Report 473=218/-1,194/0,61/1; Confirm 151=29/-1,38/0,84/1; Sandbagging 1000=379/-1,375/0,246/1. Model Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual, response-token avg. Source-standardize; PCA on source; top 100 PCs; logistic λ=10.

Baseline source-trained full target AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained within top-100 source-PC subspace CV: 0.936/0.950/0.869 apparently Report/Confirm/Sandbagging.

Greedy target-supervised PC selection: avg sizes Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14; full-target k noted earlier: Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves Report +0.22, Sandbagging +0.23; close to target-trained. Source-probe PC ranking transfers like baseline; target-probe ranking good Report, worse Confirm, below random Sandbagging.

Interp PCs: GPT-5-mini rates bipolar PC directions; scores 6 both runs = 19 PCs. Interp-selected 19 beats baseline/variance/remaining-81 on all: Report 0.706→0.881, closes 78% to greedy 0.929; Sandbagging 0.606→0.662, closes 25% to greedy 0.832. Confirm baseline 0.874 near ceiling. Limitations: single model/source/layer, Sandbagging margins small, linear/descriptive, no ablation.

Appendix C: lower PCs have stronger decoder alignment with SAE features, Spearman -0.857 best match, -0.917 top-10 mean. Appendix D table lists PC sets; stated Jaccards and Sandbagging greedy count conflict with table/earlier k. Appendix E Table 3 selected-for-transfer PCs lists PC62/57/86 score6 but also PC9/81 score3, conflicting with earlier selection criterion.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims study of linear probes for deception detection in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct over 3 held-out deception detection datasets. Main finding: projecting inputs onto a small subset of PCs from the training distribution of activations enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). Also claims PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: using an LLM judge to score PCs based on whether their most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction, then probing on highest-scoring PCs, closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation: source-probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural-language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract: linear probes for deception detection in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct over 3 held-out datasets; projecting onto small subset of source-training PCs enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching oracle target-trained probes. LLM judge scores PCs from most/least activating examples for transferable deception direction; selecting high-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation: source-probe weights often encode source-specific surface features, transferable PCs encode abstract contrast describable in natural language; OOD robustness determined by subspace selection.

Intro: trains on single source dataset “Roleplaying deception scenarios,” evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2025). Uses Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Works in source-domain PCA basis instead of raw activations; studies which PC subsets support generalizable probes and how to identify them. Contributions: (1) target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds small transferable subspace of 8–15 components where source-trained probe nearly matches target-trained oracle (Sec 4.2); (2) source-side and target-side PC rankings by source/target probe weights fail to recover subspace and do not transfer better than full-representation baseline (Sec 4.3); (3) LLM judge partially recovers subspace without target data by interpreting/selecting PCs likely to encode transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns (Sec 4.5). Figure 1: pipeline projects activations onto source-domain PCA basis, filters candidate PC directions, trains probes on selected low-dimensional subspace.

Title/setup: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Datasets: Roleplaying source; Insider Trading Report/Confirm, Sandbagging targets. Labels honest=0/ambiguous=-1/deceptive=1, ambiguous removed. Counts (-1/0/1): Roleplaying 371=140/59/172; Report 473=218/194/61; Confirm 151=29/38/84; Sandbagging 1000=379/375/246. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual activations averaged over assistant tokens. Source standardized; same stats to targets. PCA on scaled source; top 100 PCs retained. Logistic regression lambda=10; AUROC; target 5-fold CV CIs.

Key results: source full-representation transfer AUROC Report 0.706, Confirm 0.874, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained within top-100 source-PC subspace: 0.936/0.950/0.869. Greedy oracle selects PC subsets using target AUROC; target-CV version uses train folds; stops >0.001; mean sizes 15/8/14; not unbiased OOD. Greedy improves Report/Sandbagging ~0.22/0.23 and nearly matches target-trained with 8–15 components.

4.3: coefficient rankings use abs probe coeff*PC std. Full-target greedy k previously noted 13/7/14. Source ranking ≈ full baseline. Target ranking good on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, below random on Sandbagging. Greedy vs target-ranked Jaccards reported 0.182/0.077/0.167. Appendix D inconsistencies: calls comparison “target-pca” though table defines target separability ranking based on target-probe weights; table rows’ full listed sets do not yield reported Jaccards; Sandbagging greedy row lists 15 PCs, conflicting with earlier k=14.

Interpretability: GPT-5-mini PC interpretation, max score 6; 19 PCs score 6 in both runs. Interp-selected 19 PCs: Report 0.881, Confirm little headroom, Sandbagging 0.662. Appendix E: repeatedly greedy-selected PCs scored: PC62/57/86 get 6; PC9/81 get 3. Leading source-probe PCs: only PC4 gets 6; PC7/8/11/12 get 3/4/3/3. Limitations: descriptive not causal; no inference-time PC ablations. Appendix C SAE decoder alignment stronger for lower-index PCs; Spearman rho -0.857 best feature, -0.917 mean top-10.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Activations are standardized using source statistics; PCA is applied to scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression parameter lambda set to 10.

Paper summary claims: asks whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD deception detection. Compares probes (classifiers for a property) in full representations vs selected directions. Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Reported high-level results: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. Scope/caveats: uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Paper studies whether selected subspaces of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6) layer-15 residual-stream activations improve OOD deception detection. Activations averaged over assistant-response tokens, standardized with source stats, PCA keeps leading 100 source PCs (Q7/N4D). Source dataset V8 Roleplaying; targets C2R Insider Trading Report, W6 Insider Trading Confirm, J9 Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses: -1 ambiguous removed, 0 honest, 1 deceptive. errors.claim: “Retaining H2-selected Q7 causally makes E6 more honest, independently of explained variance.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: the paper’s methods/results so far concern logistic-regression deception probes on projected residual-stream activations; H2 is defined as “target-guided direction selection” for source-trained probes, and the caveat says “interpretations descriptive not causal.” This part itself describes H2 as projecting activations and fitting/evaluating source logistic-regression probes, not intervening on the model: “For each candidate addition, it projects source activations onto that subset and fits source logistic-regression weights… evaluates the selected source-trained probe.”
errors.explanation: The claim that retaining H2-selected directions causally makes the model more honest is not supported by, and conflicts with, the described experiment, which only evaluates classifier performance on subspaces. No causal model intervention or honesty-change measurement is described here or in the prior notes.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD deception datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Claim: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on a single source dataset, Roleplaying deception scenarios, and evaluated on 3 held-out OOD target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Main framing: probes strong in-distribution can learn spurious correlations and fail OOD; authors work in the source-domain PCA basis rather than raw activations to select subspaces that generalize.

Key claimed findings: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained/oracle probe. Setup details: use 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al.; labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 assigned by GPT-4o, with ambiguous removed. Activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer 15 residual stream, chosen following Ying et al. (2026) as highest cross-domain AUROC; activations extracted by passing prompt through model and averaging token activations over assistant response. Standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance, apply same source stats to targets. Run PCA on scaled source activations, retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression probes with lambda=10. For PC subset S, project activations onto S before training/eval; baseline probes train directly on full standardized activations (not PC subset). Justification for top 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align better with SAE decoder features and are more interpretable; not claiming low-index PCs generalize better. Section 4.1 is said to confirm 100-PC subspace retains enough information for separation on every target.

Key claimed findings to check later: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components nearly matching target-trained/oracle; source/target probe-weight PC rankings fail vs full baseline; LLM judge partially recovers transferable PCs without target data. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Uses Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on source Roleplaying and OOD targets Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed. Activations: layer 15 residual stream, averaged over assistant response. Source standardization applied to targets. PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression lambda=10. For PC subset, project then train/eval; full baseline trains on full standardized reps. Low-index PCs justified by interpretability/SAE alignment, not claimed to generalize better.

4.1 baseline: full source-trained AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) get Report/Confirm/Sandbagging = 0.936/0.950/0.869, confirming 100-PC subspace contains enough info; difficulty is source-trained direction not generalizing.

4.2 greedy oracle PC selection: start empty, search top 100 source PCs, add candidate improving target AUROC most; train weights only on source projections. Uses 5-fold CV over target: select on non-held-out target folds, evaluate selected source-trained probe on held-out fold. Stop if no AUROC improvement >0.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. This is upper bound, not unbiased OOD, because subset selection uses target labels. Compare top-k PCs by variance with k matched to greedy. Greedy close to target-trained for Report and Sandbagging, improves baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC; variance control only matches greedy for Confirm and lags on Report/Sandbagging. Choice of PCs matters; variance explained not predictive.

4.3 begins testing hypotheses: transferable PCs might separate target classes individually, or be high-weight source-probe PCs. Rankings use standardized coefficient = |probe coefficient| * SD of PC after training on source-PCA-basis activations.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes, source Roleplaying, targets Insider Trading Report/Confirm and Sandbagging. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed. Activations layer 15 residual stream averaged over assistant response. Source standardization applied to targets. PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression lambda=10. Full source-trained baseline target AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained 100-source-PC probes CV: Report 0.936, Confirm 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869.

Greedy oracle PC selection (target-label-aided upper bound): iteratively add top-100 source PC that maximizes target AUROC with source-trained weights; 5-fold target CV selection/eval. Avg selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves Report/Sandbagging by ~0.22/0.23 AUROC; variance-matched top-k only matches for Confirm.

4.3 tests whether transferable PCs are (i) high source-probe-weight PCs or (ii) target-class-separating PCs. Rankings use standardized coefficient = |coef|*SD in source-PCA basis. For k set by greedy on full target (not CV): Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 14. Source-PCA ranking transfers about like full baseline. Target-PCA ranking good on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, below random on Sandbagging.

4.4 interpret PCs: for each top-100 source PC, use 8 most/least source examples; LLM describes poles/direction and rates OOD generalizability 1–10. No PC scored above 6, so 6 max observed; PCs scoring 6 in both runs = 19. Of 5 PCs appearing in greedy selections for >1 target, 3 got max OOD score; only 1 of top 5 source-PCA PCs did.

4.5 interp-selected subspace: use 19 max-score PCs; controls full baseline, top-19 variance PCs, and remaining 81 PCs after ablation; Figure 5 AUROCs with 95% CIs.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Activations are standardized using source statistics; PCA is applied to scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression parameter lambda set to 10.

Main claims from abstract/summary: train linear probes on source and evaluate on 3 held-out targets. Target-supervised greedy oracle repeatedly adds source PC maximizing target AUROC; finds 8–15 PCs nearly matching target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source-probe or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. Standardized coefficient = abs(probe coefficient) * PC std. Variance control = top k source PCs.

LLM interpretability: GPT-5-mini judge describes PC positive/negative poles from examples and scores OOD deception usefulness 1–10; activation magnitudes normalized -10 to +10 in prompt. Max observed OOD score = 6. Interp-selected PCs = 19 PCs receiving score 6 in both scoring runs; interp-ablated/control = remaining 81 PCs. Paper summary claims: asks whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD deception detection. Compares probes (classifiers for a property) in full representations vs selected directions. Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Reported high-level results: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. Scope/caveats: uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Paper studies whether selected subspaces of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6) layer-15 residual-stream activations improve OOD deception detection. Activations averaged over assistant-response tokens, standardized with source stats, PCA keeps leading 100 source PCs (Q7/N4D). Source dataset V8 Roleplaying; targets C2R Insider Trading Report, W6 Insider Trading Confirm, J9 Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses: -1 ambiguous removed, 0 honest, 1 deceptive. All classifiers logistic regression with lambda=10; metric AUROC with 95% CIs.
Key terms/methods: B8Q full-representation baseline = source-trained on all standardized activations. Y4 variance control = source-trained on top-k PCs by explained variance. H2 greedy oracle = target-guided direction selection via 5-fold CV: uses non-held-out target folds for selection, held-out fold for evaluation, but fits probe weights only on source; treated as transfer upper bound not unbiased OOD estimate. T6 source-PCA probe and M9 target-PCA probe provide coefficient rankings; standardized coefficient X4 = abs coefficient × PC SD. LLM judge C7 rates direction OOD usefulness (R5) from natural-language interpretations; P2 GPT-5-mini interprets directions using high positive/negative activation examples. L2 interp-selected PC probe uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs; A7 uses complement.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Study Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes over 3 held-out deception detection datasets. Main finding: projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training distribution of activations enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on test distribution (“oracle”). PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: use an LLM judge to score each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction, then probe on highest-scoring PCs. Reported gap closure: 78% of baseline-to-oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source probe heavily weighted directions cause deceptive responses via source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes over 3 held-out datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of source-domain PCs enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching target-trained/oracle probes. PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores PCs from most/least activating examples for transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes 78% of baseline-to-oracle gap on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Interpretation claim: source probe heavily weighted directions reflect source-specific surface features causing deceptive responses, while transferable directions encode same contrast more abstractly and can be described in natural language. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness largely determined by subspace selection.

Introduction: Motivation is that linear probes can detect concepts but learn spurious correlations OOD. Method works in source-domain PCA basis instead of raw activations. Testbed: train on single source dataset “Roleplaying deception scenarios”; evaluate on 3 held-out target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Research question: which subset of source PCs supports generalizable probe training and how to identify it. Contributions claimed: (1) small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components where source-trained probe nearly matches target-trained probe (Sec 4.2). (2) Source-side and target-side rankings by source/target probe weights fail to recover subspace and do not transfer better than full-representation baseline (Sec 4.3). (3) LLM judge partially recovers subspace without target data by selecting PCs likely encoding transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns (Sec 4.5). Figure 1 overview: project activations into source PCA basis, filter PC directions, train probes on selected low-dimensional subspace.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Activations are standardized using source statistics; PCA is applied to scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression parameter lambda set to 10.

Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD deception datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Claim: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on a single source dataset, Roleplaying deception scenarios, and evaluated on 3 held-out OOD target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Main framing: probes strong in-distribution can learn spurious correlations and fail OOD; authors work in the source-domain PCA basis rather than raw activations to select subspaces that generalize.

Key claimed findings: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained/oracle probe. (2) Source-side and target-side PC rankings fail: ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not transfer better than the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover transferable PCs without target data by interpreting most/least activating examples and selecting PCs encoding transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns. Abstract quantified LLM-judge result: probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Broad conclusion to track: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Claimed interpretation: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on single source dataset Roleplaying and evaluated OOD on Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Framing: strong in-distribution probes can learn spurious correlations and fail OOD; authors select subspaces in source-domain PCA basis.

Setup details: use 4 deception datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al.; labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 assigned by GPT-4o, with ambiguous removed. Activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer 15 residual stream, chosen following Ying et al. (2026) as highest cross-domain AUROC; activations extracted by passing prompt through model and averaging token activations over assistant response. Standardize source activations to zero mean/unit variance, apply same source stats to targets. Run PCA on scaled source activations, retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression probes with lambda=10. For PC subset S, project activations onto S before training/eval; baseline probes train directly on full standardized activations (not PC subset). Justification for top 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align better with SAE decoder features and are more interpretable; not claiming low-index PCs generalize better. Section 4.1 is said to confirm 100-PC subspace retains enough information for separation on every target.

Key claimed findings to check later: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components nearly matching target-trained/oracle; source/target probe-weight PC rankings fail vs full baseline; LLM judge partially recovers transferable PCs without target data. Abstract: LLM-judge highest-scoring PCs close baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Uses Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on source Roleplaying and OOD targets Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed. Activations: layer 15 residual stream, averaged over assistant response. Source standardization applied to targets. PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression lambda=10. For PC subset, project then train/eval; full baseline trains on full standardized reps. Low-index PCs justified by interpretability/SAE alignment, not claimed to generalize better.

4.1 baseline: full source-trained AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) get Report/Confirm/Sandbagging = 0.936/0.950/0.869, confirming 100-PC subspace contains enough info; difficulty is source-trained direction not generalizing.

4.2 greedy oracle PC selection: start empty, search top 100 source PCs, add candidate improving target AUROC most; train weights only on source projections. Uses 5-fold CV over target: select on non-held-out target folds, evaluate selected source-trained probe on held-out fold. Stop if no AUROC improvement >0.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. This is upper bound, not unbiased OOD, because subset selection uses target labels. Compare top-k PCs by variance with k matched to greedy. Greedy close to target-trained for Report and Sandbagging, improves baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC; variance control only matches greedy for Confirm and lags on Report/Sandbagging. Choice of PCs matters; variance explained not predictive.

4.3 begins testing hypotheses: transferable PCs might separate target classes individually, or be high-weight source-probe PCs. Rankings use standardized coefficient = |probe coefficient| * SD of PC after training on source-PCA-basis activations.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes, source Roleplaying, targets Insider Trading Report/Confirm and Sandbagging. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed. Activations layer 15 residual stream averaged over assistant response. Source standardization applied to targets. PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression lambda=10. Full source-trained baseline target AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained 100-source-PC probes CV: Report 0.936, Confirm 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869.

Greedy oracle PC selection (target-label-aided upper bound): iteratively add top-100 source PC that maximizes target AUROC with source-trained weights; 5-fold target CV selection/eval. Avg selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves Report/Sandbagging by ~0.22/0.23 AUROC; variance-matched top-k only matches for Confirm.

4.3 tests whether transferable PCs are (i) high source-probe-weight PCs or (ii) target-class-separating PCs. Rankings use standardized coefficient = |coef|*SD in source-PCA basis. For k set by greedy on full target (not CV): Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 14. Source-PCA ranking transfers about like full baseline. Target-PCA ranking good on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, below random on Sandbagging.

4.4 interpret PCs: for each top-100 source PC, use 8 most/least source examples; LLM describes poles/direction and rates OOD generalizability 1–10. No PC scored above 6, so 6 max observed; PCs scoring 6 in both runs = 19. Of 5 PCs appearing in greedy selections for >1 target, 3 got max OOD score; only 1 of top 5 source-PCA PCs did.

4.5 interp-selected subspace: use 19 max-score PCs; controls full baseline, top-19 variance PCs, and remaining 81 PCs after ablation; Figure 5 AUROCs with 95% CIs.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Activations are standardized using source statistics; PCA is applied to scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression parameter lambda set to 10.

Main claims from abstract/summary: train linear probes on source and evaluate on 3 held-out targets. Target-supervised greedy oracle repeatedly adds source PC maximizing target AUROC; finds 8–15 PCs nearly matching target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source-probe or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. Standardized coefficient = abs(probe coefficient) * PC std. Variance control = top k source PCs.

LLM interpretability: GPT-5-mini judge describes PC positive/negative poles from examples and scores OOD deception usefulness 1–10; activation magnitudes normalized -10 to +10 in prompt. Max observed OOD score = 6. Interp-selected PCs = 19 PCs receiving score 6 in both scoring runs; interp-ablated/control = remaining 81 PCs. Compares probes (classifiers for a property) in full representations vs selected directions. Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Reported high-level results: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. Scope/caveats: uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

final_notes:
Paper: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual stream. Datasets: Roleplaying source 371 labels -1/0/1=140/59/172; ambiguous removed ->311. Targets: Report 473, Confirm 151, Sandbagging 1000; GPT-4o labels; ambiguous removed. Activations averaged over assistant tokens. Source standardization applied to targets. PCA on scaled source activations; top 100 PCs; logistic regression λ=10.

4.1 baseline target AUROCs: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes within top-100 source-PC subspace, 5-fold CV, achieve 0.936/0.950/0.869 across targets.

4.2 greedy target-supervised PC selection: held-out target AUROC; source probe weights trained on source; subset chosen using non-held-out target folds; stop ≤0.001. Avg selected PCs: 15 Report, 8 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging. Greedy improves baseline by ~0.22 Report and ~0.23 Sandbagging; near target-trained. Variance control only matches greedy for Confirm.

4.3 k using full-target greedy: 13 Report, 7 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging. Source-PCA ≈ full baseline; target-PCA good Report, worse Confirm, below random Sandbagging.

4.4–4.5 interpretability: GPT-5-mini selects 19 PCs scoring max 6 in both runs. Interp-selected probe: Report 0.706→0.881, Confirm near ceiling, Sandbagging 0.606→0.662.

Appendix C: lower PCs have stronger decoder alignment with SAE features: Spearman -0.857 best match, -0.917 mean top 10. Appendix D Table 2 lists source probe PC ranking and greedy/target PC sets; its Jaccards appear inconsistent with listed sets; Sandbagging greedy listed as 15 PCs despite earlier 14. Appendix E Table 3 labels PCs as selected for likely transferability but includes PC9 and PC81 with OOD score 3 and explanations saying domain/surface brittle.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD deception datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Claim: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on a single source dataset, Roleplaying deception scenarios, and evaluated on 3 held-out OOD target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Main framing: probes strong in-distribution can learn spurious correlations and fail OOD; authors work in the source-domain PCA basis rather than raw activations to select subspaces that generalize.

Key claimed findings: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained/oracle probe. (2) Source-side and target-side PC rankings fail: ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not transfer better than the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover transferable PCs without target data by interpreting most/least activating examples and selecting PCs encoding transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns. Abstract quantified LLM-judge result: probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Broad conclusion to track: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Claimed interpretation: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions.

Experiments: W6 transfer easy/high baseline; C2R moderate robust improvement; J9 poorest/OOD partial improvement. Target-trained probes within retained source 100-PC subspace separate all targets, so info exists but source-trained direction fails.

Fig2: B8Q full-rep source-trained baseline; source-trained leading 100 PCs/Q7; target-trained leading 100 source PCs with 5-fold CV.

H2 greedy oracle: starts empty over leading 100 source PCs; fits logistic weights on source for candidate subset and adds PC maximizing target F3. Target CV uses non-held-out target folds for selection, evaluates source-trained probe on held-out fold; stop improvement >0.001. Target labels guide selection only, not weights; transfer upper bound. Fig3: small source-trained H2 subspaces nearly match target-trained esp C2R/J9; variance selection only matches H2 on W6 and fails C2R/J9.

Title/setup: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Datasets: Roleplaying source, targets Insider Trading Report/Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1 removed, deceptive=1. Earlier source retained stated 311, but Appendix A Roleplaying counts -1/0/1=140/59/172 imply retained 231 (conflict). Other counts: Report 255; Confirm 122; Sandbagging 621. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual stream averaged over assistant tokens. Standardize with source mean/std; PCA on scaled source; retain top 100 source PCs. Logistic regression lambda=10; AUROC; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI bars.

4.1 full-rep source transfer AUROC: Report 0.706, Confirm 0.874, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes within top-100 source PCs: 0.936/0.950/0.869. 4.2 greedy oracle uses target labels/CV, stop improvement ≤0.001; mean subset sizes 15/8/14; improves Report/Sandbagging, near target-trained. 4.3 ranking k=13/7/14; source ranking ≈ baseline/fails; target ranking good Report, worse than greedy Confirm, below random Sandbagging; Jaccards 0.182/0.077/0.167. 4.4 no interp OOD scores >6; 19 PCs score 6 retained. 4.5 interp-selected 19 PCs beats baseline all 3; Report 0.881, Sandbagging 0.662; greedy 0.929/0.832.

Appendix B: judge GPT-5-mini. Appendix C: lower-index PCs align more strongly with SAE decoder features; rho -0.857 best-match, -0.917 mean top-10. Appendix D Table 2 lists source weights 15 PCs; greedy sets Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 15; target ranking rows 15 PCs each. Its reported Jaccards do not match listed sets.

Appendix E: repeatedly greedy-selected PCs Table3 scores: PC62/57/86 score 6; PC9/81 score 3. Leading source-probe PCs Table4: PC4 score 6; PC7/8/11/12 score 3/4/3/3. High-score explanations still caveat lexical/surface/noisy/brittle false positives.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Activations are standardized using source statistics; PCA is applied to scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression parameter lambda set to 10.

Target-supervised greedy oracle repeatedly adds source PC maximizing target AUROC; finds 8–15 PCs nearly matching target-trained probes. Variance control = top k source PCs.

LLM interpretability: GPT-5-mini judge describes PC positive/negative poles from examples and scores OOD deception usefulness 1–10; activation magnitudes normalized -10 to +10 in prompt. Paper summary claims: asks whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD deception detection. Compares probes (classifiers for a property) in full representations vs selected directions. Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Reported high-level results: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. Scope/caveats: uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Paper studies whether selected subspaces of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6) layer-15 residual-stream activations improve OOD deception detection. Activations averaged over assistant-response tokens, standardized with source stats, PCA keeps leading 100 source PCs (Q7/N4D). Source dataset V8 Roleplaying; targets C2R Insider Trading Report, W6 Insider Trading Confirm, J9 Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses: -1 ambiguous removed, 0 honest, 1 deceptive. All classifiers logistic regression with lambda=10; metric AUROC with 95% CIs.
Key terms/methods: B8Q full-representation baseline = source-trained on all standardized activations. Y4 variance control = source-trained on top-k PCs by explained variance. H2 greedy oracle = target-guided direction selection via 5-fold CV: uses non-held-out target folds for selection, held-out fold for evaluation, but fits probe weights only on source; treated as transfer upper bound not unbiased OOD estimate. T6 source-PCA probe and M9 target-PCA probe provide coefficient rankings; standardized coefficient X4 = abs coefficient × PC SD. LLM judge C7 rates direction OOD usefulness (R5) from natural-language interpretations; P2 GPT-5-mini interprets directions using high positive/negative activation examples. L2 interp-selected PC probe uses directions reaching max R5 in both scoring runs; A7 uses complement.
Earlier high-level claims: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; source weights/target separation/variance don’t recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full baseline on all targets but recovery varies sharply. Decoder alignment with SAE decoder features (`andyrdt/...`) assessed; leading PCs have stronger alignment; Spearman rho reported. Jaccard overlap compares selected sets. Caveats: one model/source, interpretations descriptive not causal.

Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Activations are standardized using source statistics; PCA is applied to scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression parameter lambda set to 10.

Main claims from abstract/summary: train linear probes on source and evaluate on 3 held-out targets. Target-supervised greedy oracle repeatedly adds source PC maximizing target AUROC; finds 8–15 PCs nearly matching target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source-probe or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. Standardized coefficient = abs(probe coefficient) * PC std. Variance control = top k source PCs.

LLM interpretability: GPT-5-mini judge describes PC positive/negative poles from examples and scores OOD deception usefulness 1–10; activation magnitudes normalized -10 to +10 in prompt. Max observed OOD score = 6. Interp-selected PCs = 19 PCs receiving score 6 in both scoring runs; interp-ablated/control = remaining 81 PCs. This selection improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of gap between full baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. No causal/inference-time ablation validation performed. Appendix C uses andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct SAE decoder alignment; Spearman rho, Jaccard overlap appear later.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: Studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes for deception detection across 3 held-out OOD deception datasets. Main finding: projecting activations onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training activation distribution enables cross-domain transfer nearly matching probes trained directly on the test distribution (“oracle”). PC interpretations can identify transferable PCs: an LLM judge scores each PC based on whether its most/least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction; probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging. Claim: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions. Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/introduction: studies Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on a single source dataset, Roleplaying deception scenarios, and evaluated on 3 held-out OOD target datasets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, and Sandbagging (Goldowsky-Dill et al., 2025). Main framing: probes strong in-distribution can learn spurious correlations and fail OOD; authors work in the source-domain PCA basis rather than raw activations to select subspaces that generalize.

Key claimed findings: (1) A small transferable subspace exists: target-supervised greedy search over source PCs finds 8–15 components on which a source-trained probe nearly matches a target-trained/oracle probe. (2) Source-side and target-side PC rankings fail: ranking PCs by source or target probe weights does not transfer better than the full-representation baseline. (3) An LLM judge can partially recover transferable PCs without target data by interpreting most/least activating examples and selecting PCs encoding transferable behavioral contrast rather than surface patterns. Abstract quantified LLM-judge result: probing on highest-scoring PCs closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Broad conclusion to track: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection. Claimed interpretation: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features, while transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions.

Activations: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer 15 residual stream, chosen following Ying et al. Justification for top 100 PCs: lower-index PCs align better with SAE decoder features and are more interpretable; not claiming low-index PCs generalize better. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Uses Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear deception probes trained on source Roleplaying and OOD targets Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed. Activations: layer 15 residual stream, averaged over assistant response. Source standardization applied to targets. PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression lambda=10. For PC subset, project then train/eval; full baseline trains on full standardized reps. Low-index PCs justified by interpretability/SAE alignment, not claimed to generalize better.

4.1 baseline: full source-trained AUROC on targets: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in top-100 source-PC subspace (5-fold CV) get Report/Confirm/Sandbagging = 0.936/0.950/0.869, confirming 100-PC subspace contains enough info; difficulty is source-trained direction not generalizing.

4.2 greedy oracle PC selection: start empty, search top 100 source PCs, add candidate improving target AUROC most; train weights only on source projections. Uses 5-fold CV over target: select on non-held-out target folds, evaluate selected source-trained probe on held-out fold. Stop if no AUROC improvement >0.001. Average selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. This is upper bound, not unbiased OOD, because subset selection uses target labels. Compare top-k PCs by variance with k matched to greedy. Greedy close to target-trained for Report and Sandbagging, improves baseline by 0.22 and 0.23 AUROC; variance control only matches greedy for Confirm and lags on Report/Sandbagging. Choice of PCs matters; variance explained not predictive.

4.3 begins testing hypotheses: transferable PCs might separate target classes individually, or be high-weight source-probe PCs. Rankings use standardized coefficient = |probe coefficient| * SD of PC after training on source-PCA-basis activations.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct linear probes, source Roleplaying, targets Insider Trading Report/Confirm and Sandbagging. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed. Activations layer 15 residual stream averaged over assistant response. Source standardization applied to targets. Target-trained 100-source-PC probes CV: Report 0.936, Confirm 0.950, Sandbagging 0.869.

Greedy oracle PC selection (target-label-aided upper bound): iteratively add top-100 source PC that maximizes target AUROC with source-trained weights; 5-fold target CV selection/eval. Avg selected PCs: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves Report/Sandbagging by ~0.22/0.23 AUROC; variance-matched top-k only matches for Confirm.

4.3 tests whether transferable PCs are (i) high source-probe-weight PCs or (ii) target-class-separating PCs. Rankings use standardized coefficient = |coef|*SD in source-PCA basis. For k set by greedy on full target (not CV): Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 14. Source-PCA ranking transfers about like full baseline. Target-PCA ranking good on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, below random on Sandbagging.

4.4 interpret PCs: for each top-100 source PC, use 8 most/least source examples; LLM describes poles/direction and rates OOD generalizability 1–10. No PC scored above 6, so 6 max observed; PCs scoring 6 in both runs = 19. Of 5 PCs appearing in greedy selections for >1 target, 3 got max OOD score; only 1 of top 5 source-PCA PCs did.

4.5 interp-selected subspace: use 19 max-score PCs; controls full baseline, top-19 variance PCs, and remaining 81 PCs after ablation; Figure 5 AUROCs with 95% CIs.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Summary claims: trains linear probes (logistic regression) on one source dataset and evaluates on 3 held-out target datasets. Investigates selecting principal components (PCs), defined as directions in a source activation basis, for OOD deception detection. Target-supervised greedy search adds PCs according to target performance and finds 8–15 PCs that nearly match probes trained on target data. Ranking PCs by source- or target-probe weights does not recover this transferable subspace. An LLM judge scores natural-language PC descriptions without target data. Selecting 19 PCs that receive the maximum observed score in both runs improves transfer on all 3 targets, and closes 78% and 25% of the gap between the full-representation baseline and greedy oracle on two targets.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core setup: all probes are logistic regression on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, token activations averaged over assistant response. Source domain = Roleplaying; targets = Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. GPT-4o labels responses honest=0, ambiguous=-1 (removed), deceptive=1. Activations are standardized using source statistics; PCA is applied to scaled source activations. Experiments use retained 100 source PCs; PC index/order by source variance. Baseline = source-trained probe on full standardized activations. Target-trained probe fit on target data. AUROC metric; 5 target folds/CV; 95% CI error bars. Logistic-regression parameter lambda set to 10.

Main claims from abstract/summary: train linear probes on source and evaluate on 3 held-out targets. Target-supervised greedy oracle repeatedly adds source PC maximizing target AUROC; finds 8–15 PCs nearly matching target-trained probes. Ranking PCs by source-probe or target-probe standardized coefficients does not recover the transferable subspace. Standardized coefficient = abs(probe coefficient) * PC std. Variance control = top k source PCs.

LLM interpretability: GPT-5-mini judge describes PC positive/negative poles from examples and scores OOD deception usefulness 1–10; activation magnitudes normalized -10 to +10 in prompt. Max observed OOD score = 6. Interp-selected PCs = 19 PCs receiving score 6 in both scoring runs; interp-ablated/control = remaining 81 PCs. This selection improves transfer on all 3 targets and closes 78% and 25% of gap between full baseline and greedy oracle on two targets. No causal/inference-time ablation validation performed. Appendix C uses andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct SAE decoder alignment; Spearman rho, Jaccard overlap appear later.

Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Setup confirmed in Sec 3: 4 deception datasets (Roleplaying source; Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging targets/test transfer), GPT-4o labels honest=0/ambiguous=-1/deceptive=1 and ambiguous removed. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant response tokens only. Source activations standardized to zero mean/unit variance; same source stats applied to targets. PCA fit on scaled source activations; retain top 100 source PCs, PC index/order by source variance. PC-subset probes project activations to subset S before train/eval. Baseline probes train on full standardized activations (“full representation”). Logistic regression classifiers throughout, lambda=10. AUROC metric; earlier notes say 5 target folds/CV and 95% CI error bars.

Motivation for retaining top 100 PCs: SAE decoder alignment decreases with PC index (Appendix C), making lower-index PCs more interpretable/comparable to interpretability-driven selection; explicitly not a claim that low-index PCs generalize better. Sec 4.1 will check 100-PC subspace retains enough information to distinguish honest/deceptive on every target.

Intro/abstract claims to check later: target-supervised greedy oracle adds source PCs by target performance and finds near target-trained performance with avg 15/8/14 PCs across targets (also described as 8–15 PCs). Source/target probe weight rankings fail to recover transferable subspace / not better than full baseline. LLM interpretability method: GPT-5-mini describes PC poles from examples and scores OOD usefulness 1–10 using activation magnitudes normalized -10 to +10; max OOD score observed=6; selects 19 PCs scoring 6 in both scoring runs, control/ablated=remaining 81 PCs. It improves transfer on all 3 targets, with reported 78% and 25% gap recovery on Insider Trading Report and Sandbagging. No causal inference-time ablation validation. Appendix C: andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct SAE decoder alignment; Spearman rho/Jaccard overlap later.

Paper summary claims: asks whether selecting subspaces of LM representations improves OOD deception detection. Compares probes (classifiers for a property) in full representations vs selected directions. Selection methods: (1) target-guided uses target labels but does not fit probe weights on them; (2) interpretation-based uses natural-language interpretations without target data. Reported high-level results: small target-guided subspaces nearly match target-trained probes; selecting directions by source weights, target-class separation, or explained variance does not recover same transferable subspaces; interpretation-based selection improves over full-representation baseline on all targets, but recovery varies sharply. Scope/caveats: uses one model and one source dataset; interpretations are descriptive, not causal.

Paper: Dropout JMLR 2014. Dropout trains sampled thinned nets; retain prob p; test uses full net with outgoing weights scaled by p. Inverted dropout: scale retained activations by 1/p during training, no test scaling. Hidden p often .5; input p closer to 1 / real-valued typical .8.
