Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Abstract/main claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping units/connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Training samples an exponential number of “thinned” networks. At test time, approximate averaging predictions of all thinned nets using one unthinned network with smaller weights. Claims significant reductions in overfitting and improvements over other regularization methods on vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks.

Intro: Deep nets expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing regularization: early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Bayesian gold standard would average over parameter settings weighted by posterior; dropout aims to approximate this with less computation by using an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Model combination helps but separately training/testing many large nets is expensive; diverse nets require different architectures or data subsets.

Dropout definition: “dropping out” hidden or visible units means temporarily removing the unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Units are randomly retained independently with probability p. p chosen by validation or often 0.5, near optimal for many networks/tasks; input-unit retention probability usually closer to 1. Figure 1 shows standard vs dropout network. Figure 2: at training a unit present with probability p and weights w to next layer; at test unit always present and outgoing weights multiplied by p, so test output equals expected training output.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims/definition: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameters remain O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net, so training can be viewed as training 2^n shared-weight nets, each rarely trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. This approximate averaging is claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Broader scope: Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. graphical models/Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine and compares to standard RBMs; claims dropout RBMs are better in certain respects.

Paper structure: Sec2 motivation; Sec3 previous work; Sec4 formal dropout model; Sec5 training algorithm; Sec6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec7 effects on network properties and hyperparameters; Sec8 Dropout RBM; Sec9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide/hyperparameter considerations.

This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Motivation section: Dropout is motivated by sexual reproduction/evolution: genes must work with random subsets of other genes, discouraging complex co-adaptations and promoting robust, independently useful features. Also motivated by “conspiracies”: many small co-adaptations generalize better under changing/non-stationary conditions than one large fragile co-adaptation. Notes that hidden units will still learn different things; simply duplicating units would be a poor solution, like replica codes for noisy channels.

Broader scope/structure: Applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. dropout RBMs (claimed better in some respects). Sections: 3 related work; 4 formal model; 5 training; 6 experiments; 7 effects/hyperparameters; 8 Dropout RBM; 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A guide. Sec3 begins: dropout can be interpreted as regularizing a neural net by adding noise to hidden units; relates to Denoising Autoencoders adding noise to unit states.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava et al.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible/input units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Dropping out 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units often optimal. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test; Sec4 states W_test^(l)=p W^(l). This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Resulting net used without dropout.

Related work/motivation: Related to denoising autoencoders, which add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically use ~5% noise; dropout’s weight scaling permits much higher noise. Deterministic counterpart can be obtained by marginalizing dropout noise in simple cases; related to van der Maaten et al. “blankout noise” (inputs only/no hidden layers), Wang & Manning speeding up dropout by marginalizing noise, Chen et al. marginalizing DAEs. Adversarial dropping work fixes max units dropped but no hidden units.

Sec4 formalism: Standard layer: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), ỹ^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then next layer uses ỹ. Backprop derivatives through sampled sub-network.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014). Dropout: randomly drop hidden or visible/input units and connections during training; retained independently with probability p (often hidden p=0.5; inputs closer to 1; common optimal: 20% input, 50% hidden dropped). Each training case samples a thinned net; n units imply 2^n thinned nets with shared weights.

Test-time approximation: use one unthinned net without dropout, with trained outgoing weights multiplied by p: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), so expected training-time unit output equals test-time output.

Sec4 formalism: standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses ỹ^(l)=r*y; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Related work: dropout compared to denoising autoencoders, blankout/marginalized noise, adversarial dropping; dropout extends noise to hidden layers/supervised/model averaging/various architectures and allows high noise via weight scaling.

Sec5 training: SGD as usual except each training case in mini-batch uses sampled thinned net; parameters unused by a case get zero gradient; gradients averaged over mini-batch. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weights to hidden unit ||w||2≤c, projecting to ball radius c; c tuned on validation; helps even without dropout. Dropout + max-norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives boost.

Pretraining: can finetune pretrained nets with dropout; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. Smaller finetuning LRs preserve pretrained information; improves final generalization vs finetuning without dropout.

Experiments intro: classification across MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Claim: dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout nets; details in Appendix B.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), but test-time uses no removals and scaled weights \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). It also says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*y)+b)]\) is not generally equal to \(f(p\mathbf w y+b)\). The equations only make the expected preactivation/input contribution match, not the hidden unit’s expected output.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier model equations in notes: with dropout, gates are applied before the next affine transform, then activation: “\(\tilde y^{(l)}=r^{(l)}*y^{(l)}\), then \(z_i=w_i\tilde y+b_i\), \(y_i=f(z_i)\).” Notes also record the caveat that equality under scaling is supported for expected preactivation/input contribution, not generally for nonlinear output.
errors.explanation: Multiplying weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation contribution match the pretrained preactivation, but with a nonlinear activation \(f\), it does not in general make the expected unit output match the pretrained output. This repeats/conflicts with the earlier equations unless “output” is meant imprecisely as input/preactivation.

errors.claim: “K9D (ILSVRC-2012) | Vision | 65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: The same cell describes the dimensionality as both “65536” and “256 × 256 color.” A 256 × 256 color image has 256×256×3 = 196608 values, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the parenthetical description if “color” means three channels, as it does elsewhere in the same table for 32×32 color images listed as 3072.

errors.claim: “Prose comparison | Pre-QX2 error | 8-layer net | 20.5%”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-QX2 error belongs to a 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained NN, which is 20.7%.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right)”
errors.evidence: The same section defines the ordinary U2L exponent as “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\)”, where \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the model definition, hidden conditionals should use hidden bias \(a_j\), and visible conditionals should use visible bias \(b_i\). The displayed conditionals swap \(a\) and \(b\), which also creates an index/dimension mismatch.

final_notes:
Paper: Dropout/QX2 thins units during training; test uses unthinned net with weights scaled by p, preserving expected preactivation contributions, not nonlinear activations. Typical p hidden≈0.5 (appendix says 0.5–0.8, default 0.5), input≈0.8, input optimum closer to 1. Uses high momentum, decaying LR, max-norm/V9C; appendix: QX2 LR often 10–100x standard, momentum 0.95–0.99, V9C c 3–4, QX2 layer at least n/p units if standard optimum n. Pretraining finetuning multiplies by 1/p before dropout. Claim dropout improves vs non-dropout NNs on every tested dataset; SOTA on five vision collections. Training typically 2–3x standard; stochastic gradients not gradients of final inference architecture.

Key results/errors noted: H4Z/MNIST dropout logistic 1.35, ReLU 1.25, +max-norm ReLU 0.95, maxout 0.94, DBN+dropout 0.92, DBM+dropout 0.79. Table 9 shared F3N: Y5F 1.62; Y5F+O3U 1.60; +KL 1.55; V9C 1.35; QX2+Y5F 1.25; QX2+V9C 1.05. SVHN: conv max-pool 3.95; +dropout FC 3.02; +dropout all 2.55; +maxout 2.47. Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958; submitted 11/13, published 6/14. Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov; U Toronto. Abstract: dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned nets; at test time single unthinned net with reduced/scaled weights approximates averaged predictions. Claims reduced overfitting, improvements vs other regularizers, SOTA on many benchmarks in vision, speech, docs, biology. Intro claims: with unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is best regularization; dropout cheaply approximates equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned parameter-sharing models. An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets but only O(n^2) or fewer parameters; a new thinned net sampled for each training case presentation, so each particular member trained rarely/never. Regularization alternatives: early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1/L2 penalties (not model averaging). Model combination helps but training/evaluating many large nets is expensive/infeasible; diversity needs different architectures/data. Practical inference: weight scaling uses one unthinned net instead of explicit exponential averaging; Monte Carlo model averaging is more expensive. §2 motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction: recombination breaks large co-adapted gene sets yet may favor genes that work with random partners, robustness, and reduced barriers to spread of useful genes. Dropout-trained hidden units likewise face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful robust features instead of relying on other units to fix mistakes; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes in noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies more robust than one large conspiracy under changing/non-stationary conditions; complex co-adaptations may fit training data but fail on test data more readily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), but test-time uses no removals and scaled weights \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). It also says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*y)+b)]\) is not generally equal to \(f(p\mathbf w y+b)\). The equations only make the expected preactivation/input contribution match, not the hidden unit’s expected output.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The later equations define training as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with Bernoulli gates, and testing as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), with nonlinear activations allowed such as \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). Figure 2 also says testing scales outgoing weights to \(pw\).
errors.explanation: The equations and Figure 2 imply the reduced-weight test network matches the expected incoming contribution/preactivation from a dropped unit, not in general the expected post-nonlinearity output of every hidden unit. For nonlinear \(f\), \(E[f(w(r*y)+b)]\) is generally not equal to \(f(pwy+b)\).

errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and separately lists “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5.”

errors.claim: P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined as exp( v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v ), so a is the hidden-unit bias and b is the visible-unit bias. The visible conditional is then also given as P(v_i=1\mid h)=sigma(a_i+sum_j W_ij h_j).
errors.explanation: Given the stated energy, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias a_j, while the visible conditional should use the visible bias b_i. This part swaps a and b in both conditional distributions.

errors.claim: P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).
errors.evidence: The model definition uses exp( v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v ), where b is the visible bias term.
errors.explanation: The visible conditional conflicts with the earlier parameterization in the same section: it should depend on b_i, not a_i.

Intro details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is best regularization; dropout is less expensive and approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned parameter-sharing models’ predictions. An n-unit network represents 2^n thinned networks while retaining O(n^2) or fewer parameters; each training presentation samples a new thinned network, so any particular member is rarely/never trained. Overfitting arises from sampling noise; responses include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 (O3U) and L2 (Y5F) penalties. Model combination helps but separately training/evaluating many large nets is computationally costly; diversity may require different architectures/data, and joint inference can be infeasible.

Current intro says practical inference rule T6R = weight scaling: use one unthinned network instead of explicitly evaluating exponentially many members; alternative X9M = Monte Carlo model averaging averages sampled members’ predictions. §2 Motivation: Biological analogy: sexual reproduction may favor genes that mix well with random partners rather than only maximizing individual fitness; dropout-trained hidden units likewise must work with randomly selected partner units, encouraging robust, independently useful features instead of complex co-adaptations. Units in a layer still learn different functions; simple replication of units is not a good solution. Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies are more robust under non-stationarity than one large conspiracy requiring many coordinated participants. Complex co-adaptations may fit training data but fail on novel test data more easily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

errors.claim: ImageNet dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has three color channels, so its raw dimensionality would be 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608, whereas 65536 corresponds only to 256 × 256 grayscale/single-channel.
errors.explanation: The table’s numeric dimensionality conflicts with its own parenthetical description of the input as 256 × 256 color.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” as 20.7%, while 20.5% is listed for “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The prose attributes the 20.5% baseline to the 8-layer DBN-pretrained network, but the table gives that model 20.7% and assigns 20.5% to a different 5-layer mcRBM-DBN model.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)=… \sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_j W_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same model definition: “\(\exp\!\left(v^\top Wh+a^\top h+b^\top v\right)\). The parameters are \(\theta=\{W,a,b\}\).” Thus \(a\) is the hidden-unit bias vector and \(b\) is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional probabilities swap the roles of the visible and hidden biases. Given the stated joint distribution, hidden conditionals should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), and visible conditionals should use the visible bias \(b_i\), not vice versa.

errors.claim: “Dropout RBMs show different features and greater sparsity: Figures 12–13, qualitative evidence.”
errors.evidence: Notes from earlier parts record these properties under Sec7 autoencoders: “autoencoders dropout p=0.5 similar reconstruction, more stroke-like features; mean activation 2.0 no dropout vs 0.7 dropout.”
errors.explanation: This part attributes the reported feature/sparsity evidence to Dropout RBMs, but the earlier recorded evidence was for autoencoders, not RBMs.

Paper summary: Dropout reduces overfitting in large neural nets without training/using many separate networks. During training, dropout randomly removes units and connections, effectively sampling many smaller weight-sharing networks. At test time, a single full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble prediction. Claimed improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural nets. Examines learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging. Dropout RBMs reportedly learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout with multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation: dropout networks typically take 2–3 times longer to train than standard networks with same architecture.

Model: L hidden layers; y^(0)=x; standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^(l)+b_i, y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples independent r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), masks outputs \tilde y=r*y, computes/backprops through sampled sub-network.

Related: DAEs work best with ~5% noise; dropout can use higher noise due to test-time scaling; often optimal drop 20% inputs/50% hidden. Extends noise to supervised/hidden/BMs. Deterministic marginalization in simple cases; related to blankout/marginalized DAEs; not adversarial feature removal.

Learning: SGD mini-batches; per case sample thinned net; gradients averaged, unused parameters get zero. Momentum, annealed LR, L2 help. Max-norm bounds each hidden unit incoming vector ||w||≤c, project to ball surface; validation picks c. Dropout+max-norm+large decaying LR+high momentum gives further boost; explanation speculative. Pretraining via RBMs/autoencoders/DBMs; dropout can finetune pretrained nets by first multiplying pretrained weights by 1/p so expected unit output under dropout equals pretraining output. Large finetuning LR can erase pretrained info; smaller LR retains it; no numerical table for that observation.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=...\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=...\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same model definition, the RBM exponent is “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+ \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\)”, so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden-bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible-bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional distributions swap the biases: hidden-unit probabilities should use the hidden bias indexed by j, while visible-unit probabilities should use the visible bias indexed by i. As written, the equations use \(b_j\) for hidden units and \(a_i\) for visible units, contradicting the preceding definition of the joint distribution.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under training-time deletion equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: This part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation during dropout as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), allows nonlinear activations such as the logistic function, and says test weights are \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(\mathbf r*\mathbf y)+b)] \ne f(p\mathbf w\mathbf y+b)\). The equality holds for the expected gated output/contribution \(E[r y]=p y\), not for every hidden unit’s post-activation output as stated.

errors.claim: "K9D (ILSVRC-2012) | Vision | 65536 (256 × 256 color)"
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has three color channels, so the dimensionality implied by "256 × 256 color" is 256×256×3 = 196608, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The table’s numeric dimensionality matches 256×256 grayscale, but the parenthetical says color, creating an internal inconsistency within the same entry.

errors.claim: For the 8-layer net, the prose comparison lists the pre-QX2 error as 20.5%.
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” as 20.7, while 20.5 belongs to “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The prose comparison appears to use the 5-layer mcRBM-G6W baseline value for the 8-layer G6W-pretrained network, contradicting Table 7.

errors.claim: “QX2 improves the reported neural-net comparisons… Evidence includes Table 2, 1.60 versus 1.35”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “H4Z regularizers same F3N: Y5F 1.62; Y5F+O3U 1.60; +KL 1.55; V9C 1.35; QX2+Y5F 1.25; QX2+V9C 1.05.”
errors.explanation: The cited Table 2 comparison 1.60 versus 1.35 is between L2+L1 and max-norm, not between a non-dropout model and a QX2 model. The QX2 results in the same table are 1.25 and 1.05, so this evidence is misstated.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=…\sigma(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_j W_{ij}h_j)”
errors.evidence: The ordinary RBM energy/probability just above is defined with exponent “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\)”, so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the paper’s own definition, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), and the visible conditional should use the visible bias \(b_i\). The displayed conditionals swap these biases, and even use indices inconsistent with the earlier dimensions.

Summary claims: Paper studies preventing overfitting in large neural nets via dropout. Dropout randomly removes selected units and connections during training, effectively training many parameter-sharing smaller networks. At test time, uses one complete network with reduced weights to approximate averaged predictions. Claims dropout improves generalization over no-dropout networks on every tested dataset. Experiments include images, speech, documents, and gene-splicing prediction. Reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, Restricted Boltzmann Machines, noise marginalization, and Gaussian corruption. Training with dropout typically takes 2–3x as long as training a standard network of same architecture.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer net the error reduces from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” as 20.7%, while 20.5% is listed for “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The text attributes the 20.5% baseline to an 8-layer net, but the table shows the 8-layer DBN-pretrained baseline is 20.7%; 20.5% belongs to a different 5-layer model.

errors.claim: “Adding dropout reduced the error to 29.62%. We found that this was a 14.3% relative reduction…”
errors.evidence: The preceding sentence says the no-dropout error was 31.05%, so the reduction is 31.05 − 29.62 = 1.43 percentage points, which is about 4.6% relative to 31.05%, not 14.3%.
errors.explanation: The reported relative reduction is arithmetically inconsistent with the two error rates given in the same paragraph.

errors.claim: “dropout ... outperforms all other methods.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 lists “Neural Network with dropout” at 567 Code Quality, but “Bayesian Neural Network” at 623, and the text also says “Bayesian neural nets perform better than dropout.”

errors.claim: Dropout improves generalization on all datasets.
errors.evidence: This part says: “for extremely small data sets (100, 500) dropout does not give any improvements.”
errors.explanation: The earlier broad claim that dropout improves generalization on all datasets is contradicted by the MNIST subset experiment reported here, where dropout gives no improvement for datasets of size 100 and 500.

errors.claim: “P(hj = 1 | rj, v) = 1(rj = 1) σ(bj + Σi Wij vi)” and “P(vi = 1 | h) = σ(ai + Σj Wij hj)”

errors.explanation: The conditional probabilities swap the biases: hidden-unit probabilities should use the hidden bias a_j, while visible-unit probabilities should use the visible bias b_i. This conflicts with the model definition in the same section.

errors.claim: “Dropout considerably improved the performance of standard neural nets on other data sets as well.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Intro claimed dropout improves generalization on all datasets, but Sec 7.4 says MNIST subsets 100 and 500 get no dropout improvement.”
errors.explanation: This concluding summary again broadly says dropout considerably improved standard neural nets on other datasets, but the paper previously reported at least two datasets/subsets where dropout gave no improvement.

final_notes:
Paper: Dropout JMLR 2014. Dropout trains sampled thinned nets; retain prob p; test full net with outgoing weights scaled by p. Inverted dropout: retained activations scaled by 1/p at train time, no test scaling. Max-norm incoming hidden weights ||w||≤c. Pretrained weights scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetune. Appendix guide: good dropout net should have at least n/p units if n is optimal standard layer size; dropout LR typically 10–100× standard net; momentum 0.95–0.99; max-norm c typical 3–4; hidden p typical 0.5–0.8, input p for real-valued data ~0.8. Conclusion says training time 2–3×; marginalizing noise gives linear-regression regularizer modified L2.

Known internal conflicts: Table 1 ImageNet 65536 conflicts with 256×256 color=196608. TIMIT Table7 DBN 4+dropout and DBN 8+dropout both 19.7; text misstates 8-layer baseline as 20.5. Reuters no-dropout 31.05, dropout 29.62; text says 14.3% relative reduction but arithmetic ~4.6%. Alt Splicing: dropout NN 567, Bayesian NN 623; text says BNN better but also says dropout outperforms all other methods. Intro/conclusion claim dropout improves on all/other datasets, but Sec 7.4 MNIST subsets 100 and 500 get no improvement.

Sec 7: p variation: fixed architecture p=.4-.8 flat; with pn fixed p≈.6 best. MC averaging k~50 matches weight scaling; MC slightly better within 1 SD. Sec 8 RBM conditionals earlier swapped a/b. Sec 9 linear dropout coeff (1-p)/p. Sec 10 Gaussian variance σ²=(1-p)/p; Table 10 Gaussian slightly better.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Abstract/main claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping units/connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Training samples an exponential number of “thinned” networks. Intro: Deep nets expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing regularization: early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Bayesian gold standard would average over parameter settings weighted by posterior; dropout aims to approximate this with less computation by using an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Model combination helps but separately training/testing many large nets is expensive; diverse nets require different architectures or data subsets.

Dropout definition: “dropping out” hidden or visible units means temporarily removing the unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Units are randomly retained independently with probability p. p chosen by validation or often 0.5, near optimal for many networks/tasks; input-unit retention probability usually closer to 1. Figure 1 shows standard vs dropout network. Figure 2: at training a unit present with probability p and weights w to next layer; at test unit always present and outgoing weights multiplied by p, so test output equals expected training output.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims/definition: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameters remain O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net, so training can be viewed as training 2^n shared-weight nets, each rarely trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. This approximate averaging is claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Broader scope: Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. graphical models/Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine and compares to standard RBMs; claims dropout RBMs are better in certain respects.

Paper structure: Sec2 motivation; Sec3 previous work; Sec4 formal dropout model; Sec5 training algorithm; Sec6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec7 effects on network properties and hyperparameters; Sec8 Dropout RBM; Sec9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide/hyperparameter considerations.

This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Motivation section: Dropout is motivated by sexual reproduction/evolution: genes must work with random subsets of other genes, discouraging complex co-adaptations and promoting robust, independently useful features. Also motivated by “conspiracies”: many small co-adaptations generalize better under changing/non-stationary conditions than one large fragile co-adaptation. Notes that hidden units will still learn different things; simply duplicating units would be a poor solution, like replica codes for noisy channels.

Broader scope/structure: Applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. dropout RBMs (claimed better in some respects). Sections: 3 related work; 4 formal model; 5 training; 6 experiments; 7 effects/hyperparameters; 8 Dropout RBM; 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A guide. Sec3 begins: dropout can be interpreted as regularizing a neural net by adding noise to hidden units; relates to Denoising Autoencoders adding noise to unit states.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava et al.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible/input units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Dropping out 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units often optimal. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test; Sec4 states W_test^(l)=p W^(l). This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Resulting net used without dropout.

Related work/motivation: Related to denoising autoencoders, which add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically use ~5% noise; dropout’s weight scaling permits much higher noise. Deterministic counterpart can be obtained by marginalizing dropout noise in simple cases; related to van der Maaten et al. “blankout noise” (inputs only/no hidden layers), Wang & Manning speeding up dropout by marginalizing noise, Chen et al. marginalizing DAEs. Adversarial dropping work fixes max units dropped but no hidden units.

Sec4 formalism: Standard layer: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), ỹ^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then next layer uses ỹ. Backprop derivatives through sampled sub-network.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014). Dropout: randomly drop hidden or visible/input units and connections during training; retained independently with probability p (often hidden p=0.5; inputs closer to 1; common optimal: 20% input, 50% hidden dropped). Each training case samples a thinned net; n units imply 2^n thinned nets with shared weights.

Test-time approximation: use one unthinned net without dropout, with trained outgoing weights multiplied by p: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), so expected training-time unit output equals test-time output.

Sec4 formalism: standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses ỹ^(l)=r*y; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Related work: dropout compared to denoising autoencoders, blankout/marginalized noise, adversarial dropping; dropout extends noise to hidden layers/supervised/model averaging/various architectures and allows high noise via weight scaling.

Sec5 training: SGD as usual except each training case in mini-batch uses sampled thinned net; parameters unused by a case get zero gradient; gradients averaged over mini-batch. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weights to hidden unit ||w||2≤c, projecting to ball radius c; c tuned on validation; helps even without dropout. Dropout + max-norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives boost.

Pretraining: can finetune pretrained nets with dropout; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. Smaller finetuning LRs preserve pretrained information; improves final generalization vs finetuning without dropout.

Experiments intro: classification across MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Claim: dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout nets; details in Appendix B.

Dropout-trained hidden units likewise face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful robust features instead of relying on other units to fix mistakes; units in a layer still learn different functions. errors.explanation: The 2.55% all-layer dropout result was recorded as following the stochastic-pooling convolutional net, not the max-pooling network. This part characterizes it as a max-pooling-network result, conflicting with the earlier Table 3 notes.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) + dropout | 19.7”. The 20.5% value belongs to “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers)”.
errors.explanation: The prose uses 20.5% as the non-dropout 8-layer baseline, but the table gives 20.7% for that model; 20.5% is a different 5-layer mcRBM-DBN model.

errors.claim: “Our best neural network without dropout gives 31.05% error. Dropout reduces it to 29.62%. This is a 14.3% relative reduction.”
errors.evidence: The reported errors are 31.05% and 29.62%, whose relative reduction is (31.05 − 29.62) / 31.05 ≈ 4.6%, not 14.3%.
errors.explanation: The stated relative reduction does not follow from the paper’s own numbers. The absolute reduction is 1.43 percentage points, not a 14.3% relative reduction.

errors.claim: “dropout ... outperforms every other method listed.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 lists “Neural Network with dropout” = 567 bits and “Bayesian Neural Network” = 623 bits; the same paragraph says “Bayesian networks perform better than dropout.”
errors.explanation: If higher code quality in bits is better, as the paragraph states, dropout does not outperform every other listed method because the Bayesian neural network is listed and scores higher.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)= 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j+∑_i W_{ij}v_i)” and “P(v_i=1\mid h)= σ(a_i+∑_j W_{ij}h_j)”

errors.explanation: The conditional probabilities swap the biases: hidden-unit conditionals should use hidden bias a_j, while visible-unit conditionals should use visible bias b_i, given the model definition in the same subsection.

errors.claim: “This form essentially scales the cost on weight \(w_i\) by the standard deviation of data dimension \(i\).”
errors.evidence: The penalty is defined using \(\Gamma=(\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X))^{1/2}\), so the factor for dimension \(i\) is \(\sqrt{\sum_n X_{ni}^2}\), not the standard deviation unless additional centering/normalization assumptions are made, which are not stated.
errors.explanation: The displayed definition of \(\Gamma\) gives an uncentered column norm, whereas standard deviation would require centering and division by the number of observations. The prose description therefore does not match the formula as written.

final_notes: Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. QX2/dropout gates units during training; usual test scales weights by retention p. Claims QX2 improves over no-dropout on every tested dataset, but §7.4 says two smallest H4Z training sets show no QX2 improvement; gain rises then falls with more data. Usually 2–3× training time. Definitions: O3U=L1, Y5F=L2, U2L=RBM, B8T=Dropout RBM, E5Q/DBM; F3N=ReLU; L8J=maxout; G6W=DBN/stacked RBM init; V9C=max-norm. §10: P7V=Bernoulli dropout; D4K=Gaussian dropout; σ²=(1-p)/p, no test-time scaling. Known internal errors: Table 1 K9D row says 65536 is “256×256 color” though color would be ×3; TIMIT prose says 8-layer pre-QX2 baseline 20.5 but Table 7 says 20.7; docs says 31.05→29.62 is 14.3% relative reduction, actually ≈4.6%; §6 cites “Table 2, 1.60 versus 1.35” as QX2 evidence, but those are Table 9 non-QX2 regularizer results; conclusion A2F 2.47/SOTA attributed to QX2 though notes say QX2 all 2.55. Key results: H4Z best E5Q+QX2 0.79; D4K 0.95 vs P7V 1.08. A2F best maxout 2.47, QX2 all 2.55. J3V/W6R QX2 all 12.61/37.20, maxout 11.68/38.57. ImageNet 2010 ConvNet+QX2 37.5/17.0. TIMIT Table7: NN6 23.4, QX2 NN6 21.8; G6W8 20.7; G6W+QX2 19.7. M5X: Reuters subset 402,738 docs, 2000 vocab, 50 disjoint classes, single-label, equal train/test. Z7P: 3665 exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue softmaxes each with inc/exc/nc; 2×1024 QX2, p hidden .5/input .7, same 5 folds as Xiong; Table 8 QX2 567 bits, early-stopped NN 440, Bayesian NN 623; QX2 uses 1000s hidden units vs Bayesian few tens.

Summary claims: paper studies dropout to prevent overfitting in large neural nets. Dropout randomly removes selected units and connections during training, effectively training many smaller parameter-sharing networks; at test time uses one complete network with reduced weights to approximate averaged predictions. Claims dropout improves generalization over no-dropout networks on every tested dataset. Experiments span images, speech, documents, gene-splicing prediction. Reports state-of-the-art on several benchmarks. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, RBMs, noise marginalization, Gaussian corruption. Training with dropout typically takes 2–3× as long as standard network of same architecture.

Summary claims: paper studies dropout to prevent overfitting in large neural nets. Dropout randomly removes units and their connections during training, training many shared-parameter thinned networks; test uses one complete unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability to approximate equally weighted/geometric-mean model averaging. Claims dropout improves generalization over no-dropout networks on every tested dataset. Experiments span images, speech, documents, gene-splicing prediction; reports state-of-the-art on several benchmarks. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, RBMs/dropout RBMs, noise marginalization, Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout/corruption. Training with dropout typically takes 2–3× as long as standard network of same architecture. Key terms: retention probability p; thinned network/submodel; unthinned network; max-norm regularization bounds each hidden unit’s incoming-weight-vector norm; L1/lasso and L2/Tikhonov are comparison regularizers; KL-sparsity compared in some experiments; maxout and ReLUs are activation classes compared with logistic units; dropout described as reducing co-adaptation. Dropout extends to RBMs/DBMs/DBNs/pretraining; CD-1 used for RBM/dropout RBM. Image experiments include conv nets, pooling variants, padding/data augmentation, permutation-invariant comparisons. Other comparisons include SVMs, PCA, linear/logistic/ridge regression, bag-of-words documents, denoising autoencoders, Bayesian/model averaging, Monte Carlo dropout/model averaging, marginalization, blankout noise, Gaussian noise with matched moments/entropy.

Paper studies dropout for preventing overfitting in large neural nets. Dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, training many shared-parameter thinned networks; test uses complete unthinned network with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p to approximate model averaging/geometric mean. Claims dropout improves generalization over no-dropout on every tested dataset; reports SOTA on several benchmarks. Training with dropout typically takes 2–3× as long as standard same-architecture network. Max-norm regularization bounds each hidden unit’s incoming-weight-vector norm. Comparisons include L1/lasso, L2/Tikhonov, KL-sparsity, maxout/ReLU/logistic units, SVMs, PCA, linear/logistic/ridge regression, denoising autoencoders, Bayesian/model averaging, MC dropout, marginalization, blankout/Gaussian noise.
Datasets/metrics: MNIST handwritten digits; SVHN centered digit Street View; CIFAR-10/100 tiny natural images; ImageNet/ILSVRC (annual competition begun 2010 using ImageNet subset; began as part of Pascal VOC); TIMIT phone recognition using phone error rate; Reuters-RCV1 documents; Alternative Splicing dataset uses RNA features to predict probabilities over three states inc/exc/nc with softmax units; Code Quality score is negative KL divergence in bits, higher better, predictions should match wet-lab-observed distribution; cassette exon count reported in App. B. Image metrics include top-1 and top-5 error; Table 6 uses val/test labels. Baselines/features include WDCH Binary Features, HOG, KMeans, SIFT/Dense SIFT/CSIFT/LBP/GIST, Fisher Vectors/FVs, Sparse Coding. Preprocessing/implementation: SVHN RGB normalized; global contrast normalization subtracts each image/color-channel mean; local contrast normalization gave no noticeable improvement; ZCA whitening mean-centers, rotates to PCs, normalizes, rotates back. TIMIT uses Kaldi log-filter banks; monophone forced alignment labels. GPU/CUDA implementations use cudamat and cuda-convnet. Abbreviations: NA, K/M, dim/conv/Avg/NN, %/bits. Funding: OGS, NSERC, Early Researcher Award.

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958, submitted 11/13 published 6/14. Studies dropout to prevent overfitting: during training retain units/inputs with probability p, giving 2^n thinned networks from n units with shared O(n^2) parameters; at test use full network with weights W_test=pW (outgoing weights scaled by p) approximating model averaging/geometric mean. Claims dropout improves generalization over no-dropout on every tested dataset; SOTA on several; usually 2–3× training time. Max-norm regularization bounds each hidden unit’s incoming-weight norm by c. Practical width heuristic noted as n/p to keep expected retained width pn.
Datasets/metrics: MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet/ILSVRC, TIMIT phone error rate, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. ImageNet/ILSVRC competition began 2010 as part of Pascal VOC. Alternative Splicing predicts probabilities over inc/exc/nc states by tissue; score is negative KL divergence in bits (higher better), comparing q_t^s(r_i) to wet-lab p_{i,t}^s; average baseline uses pbar^s. Image metrics top-1/top-5; Table 6 uses val/test labels.
Methods/baselines include L1/L2, KL-sparsity, maxout/ReLU/logistic, SVMs, PCA, linear/logistic/ridge regression, denoising autoencoders, Bayesian/model averaging, MC dropout, marginalization, blankout/Gaussian noise. Regression dropout notation: X,N,D,y,w,R Bernoulli input mask; marginalized penalty coefficient (1-p)/p with Gamma=(diag(X^T X))^1/2; rescaled weights w~ = pw. Multiplicative Gaussian noise uses N(1,sigma^2); Bernoulli/Gaussian multipliers matched by variance.
Preprocessing/implementation: SVHN RGB normalized; global contrast normalization subtracts each image/channel mean; local contrast normalization no noticeable improvement; ZCA whitening mean-centers, rotates to PCs, normalizes, rotates back. TIMIT: Kaldi log-filter banks, monophone forced alignment. GPU uses cudamat/cuda-convnet.

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958, submitted 11/13 published 6/14. Authors Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov; editor Yoshua Bengio. Dropout/QX2 randomly removes units/inputs during training, sampling thinned shared-parameter subnetworks; a net with n units represents 2^n thinned nets with O(n^2) or fewer params. Each training case samples a member, so individual members trained rarely. Test-time T6R/weight scaling uses full network with outgoing weights scaled by p, approximating equally weighted geometric mean/model averaging; X9M/MC model averaging samples k thinned nets/test case and is more expensive (later §7.5 says ~k=50 before as good as T6R). Claims T6R/QX2 lowers generalization error vs other regularizers across varied classification problems and improves over no-dropout on every tested dataset; usually 2–3× training time. Table 9 evidence noted in intro: rows Y5F/L2, V9C, QX2+Y5F, QX2+V9C = 1.62, 1.35, 1.25, 1.05.
Definitions: O3U=L1, Y5F=L2, U2L=RBM, B8T=Dropout RBM. Max-norm bounds each hidden unit incoming-weight norm by c. Width heuristic n/p for expected retained width pn.
Datasets/metrics: MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet/ILSVRC, TIMIT phone error rate, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Image metrics top-1/top-5. Alternative Splicing score negative KL divergence in bits (higher better), baseline pbar^s.
Preprocessing/other: SVHN RGB normalized; GCN subtracts image/channel mean; LCN no noticeable improvement; ZCA mean-centers/rotates/normalizes/rotates back. TIMIT uses Kaldi log-filter banks, monophone forced alignment. Regression dropout: Bernoulli input mask R; marginalized penalty coefficient (1-p)/p with Gamma=(diag(X^T X))^1/2; rescaled weights p w.

Related work §3: DAEs/S2H corrupt inputs and reconstruct; QX2 extends with hidden-layer corruption and model averaging, supervised/unsupervised/neuron architectures incl. Boltzmann Machines. Test-time T6R permits higher noise than S2H: S2H typical best 5%, QX2 input removal often 20%, hidden removal often 50%. Adversarial deletion work has no hidden units. Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958; Dropout/QX2 randomly gates unit outputs/inputs during training, sampling thinned shared-parameter subnetworks; n units => 2^n thinned nets. Test-time T6R/weight scaling uses full network, no units removed, with weights/outgoing connections scaled by retention probability p (part 4: W_test^(l)=pW^(l) in fixed-p construction; Fig. 2 outgoing weights pw), approximating geometric mean/model averaging. MC model averaging samples k thinned nets/test case, expensive (later §7.5 says ~k=50 before as good as T6R). Claims QX2 lowers generalization error vs other regularizers across varied classification problems and improves over no-dropout on every tested dataset; usually 2–3× training time. Definitions: O3U=L1, Y5F=L2, U2L=RBM, B8T=Dropout RBM. Max-norm bounds each hidden unit incoming-weight norm by c. Width heuristic n/p for expected retained width pn. Part 4 notation: L hidden layers; y^(0)=x; feedforward z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i, y=f(z); dropout gates r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), ytilde^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), backprop through sampled subnetwork; hidden and visible units can be removed. Default hidden retention near optimal; input retention usually closer to complete retention; p can be validation-selected.
Motivation: QX2 discourages co-adaptations; replication poor.
Datasets/metrics: MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet/ILSVRC top-1/top-5, TIMIT phone error, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing negative KL bits (higher better), baseline pbar^s.

Related: QX2 extends DAEs/S2H with hidden-layer corruption/model averaging; S2H typical best 5%, QX2 input removal often 20%, hidden 50%; blankout noise name in no-hidden exponential-family cases.

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. QX2/dropout randomly gates unit outputs/inputs during training, sampling thinned shared-parameter subnetworks; n units => 2^n nets. Test-time T6R/weight scaling uses full net with outgoing weights scaled by retention p (W_test^(l)=pW^(l)), approximating geometric mean/model averaging; MC averaging samples k thinned nets/test case and §7.5 later says ~50 samples before as good as T6R. Claims QX2 lowers generalization error vs other regularizers across varied classification problems and improves over no-dropout on every tested dataset; usually 2–3× training time. Table 9 comparison: Y5F/L2 1.62, V9C/max-norm 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, QX2+V9C 1.05.
Definitions: O3U=L1, Y5F=L2, U2L=RBM, B8T=Dropout RBM, E5Q/DBM mentioned as pretraining methods. Max-norm/V9C constrains each hidden unit incoming-weight vector norm ||w||2≤c; if outside radius-c ball, project to surface; c tuned by validation. Width heuristic n/p for expected retained width pn. Default hidden retention near optimal; input retention usually closer to complete retention; p validation-selected.
Training: backprop through sampled subnetworks; each case has its own sampled net; unused parameter contributes zero gradient. Momentum, annealed/large learning rates, Y5F useful. High LR/momentum and max-norm said to boost QX2; Appendix A.2: LR often 10–100× standard-net optimum, momentum ~0.95–0.99. Weight-space exploration account proposed, not numerically established here.
Pretraining: unchanged; QX2 finetuning with smaller LR preserves pretrained info. Before QX2 finetuning, multiply pretrained weights by 1/p to match expected output under random removal. Table 2 claims pretrained H4Z: G6W finetune 1.18 no QX2 vs 0.92 QX2; E5Q 0.96 vs 0.79. Appendix B.4: best QX2 G6W finetune LR ~0.01 vs high LR 0.1.

errors.claim: K9D dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image would have 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608 dimensions, not 65536. 65536 corresponds to 256 × 256 without color channels.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Abstract/main claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping units/connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Training samples an exponential number of “thinned” networks. Intro: Deep nets expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing regularization: early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Bayesian gold standard would average over parameter settings weighted by posterior; dropout aims to approximate this with less computation by using an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Model combination helps but separately training/testing many large nets is expensive; diverse nets require different architectures or data subsets.

Dropout definition: “dropping out” hidden or visible units means temporarily removing the unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Units are randomly retained independently with probability p. p chosen by validation or often 0.5, near optimal for many networks/tasks; input-unit retention probability usually closer to 1. Figure 1 shows standard vs dropout network. Figure 2: at training a unit present with probability p and weights w to next layer; at test unit always present and outgoing weights multiplied by p, so test output equals expected training output.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims/definition: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameters remain O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net, so training can be viewed as training 2^n shared-weight nets, each rarely trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. This approximate averaging is claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Broader scope: Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. graphical models/Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine and compares to standard RBMs; claims dropout RBMs are better in certain respects.

Paper structure: Sec2 motivation; Sec3 previous work; Sec4 formal dropout model; Sec5 training algorithm; Sec6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec7 effects on network properties and hyperparameters; Sec8 Dropout RBM; Sec9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide/hyperparameter considerations.

Motivation section: Dropout is motivated by sexual reproduction/evolution: genes must work with random subsets of other genes, discouraging complex co-adaptations and promoting robust, independently useful features. Also motivated by “conspiracies”: many small co-adaptations generalize better under changing/non-stationary conditions than one large fragile co-adaptation. Notes that hidden units will still learn different things; simply duplicating units would be a poor solution, like replica codes for noisy channels.

Broader scope/structure: Applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. dropout RBMs (claimed better in some respects). Sections: 3 related work; 4 formal model; 5 training; 6 experiments; 7 effects/hyperparameters; 8 Dropout RBM; 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A guide. Sec3 begins: dropout can be interpreted as regularizing a neural net by adding noise to hidden units; relates to Denoising Autoencoders adding noise to unit states.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava et al.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible/input units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Dropping out 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units often optimal. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test; Sec4 states W_test^(l)=p W^(l). This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Resulting net used without dropout.

Related work/motivation: Related to denoising autoencoders, which add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically use ~5% noise; dropout’s weight scaling permits much higher noise. Deterministic counterpart can be obtained by marginalizing dropout noise in simple cases; related to van der Maaten et al. “blankout noise” (inputs only/no hidden layers), Wang & Manning speeding up dropout by marginalizing noise, Chen et al. marginalizing DAEs. Adversarial dropping work fixes max units dropped but no hidden units.

Sec4 formalism: Standard layer: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), ỹ^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then next layer uses ỹ. Backprop derivatives through sampled sub-network.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014). Dropout: randomly drop hidden or visible/input units and connections during training; retained independently with probability p (often hidden p=0.5; inputs closer to 1; common optimal: 20% input, 50% hidden dropped). Each training case samples a thinned net; n units imply 2^n thinned nets with shared weights.

Test-time approximation: use one unthinned net without dropout, with trained outgoing weights multiplied by p: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), so expected training-time unit output equals test-time output.

Sec4 formalism: standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses ỹ^(l)=r*y; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Related work: dropout compared to denoising autoencoders, blankout/marginalized noise, adversarial dropping; dropout extends noise to hidden layers/supervised/model averaging/various architectures and allows high noise via weight scaling.

Sec5 training: SGD as usual except each training case in mini-batch uses sampled thinned net; parameters unused by a case get zero gradient; gradients averaged over mini-batch. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weights to hidden unit ||w||2≤c, projecting to ball radius c; c tuned on validation; helps even without dropout. Dropout + max-norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives boost.

Pretraining: can finetune pretrained nets with dropout; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. Smaller finetuning LRs preserve pretrained information; improves final generalization vs finetuning without dropout.

Experiments intro: classification across MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Claim: dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout nets; details in Appendix B.

§2 motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction: recombination breaks large co-adapted gene sets yet may favor genes that work with random partners, robustness, and reduced barriers to spread of useful genes. Dropout-trained hidden units likewise face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful robust features instead of relying on other units to fix mistakes; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes in noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies more robust than one large conspiracy under changing/non-stationary conditions; complex co-adaptations may fit training data but fail on test data more readily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Test-time weight scaling/approximation permits higher noise than typically best for DAEs. Table: DAE typical best noise 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; hidden-unit removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise minimizes expected loss; adversarial removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) choose removals subject to max number and have no hidden units. Exponential-family input-noise/“blankout noise” regularizers studied by van der Maaten et al. 2013, limited to no hidden layers; Chen et al. 2012 marginalized DAEs; Wang & Manning 2013 proposed marginalization to accelerate dropout.

grade.reason: None of the reviewer's reported errors mention the MNIST training/validation recombination or the incorrect 55,000 vs 60,000 image count, so the planted error was not identified.

errors.claim: ImageNet (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has three color channels, so the dimensionality implied by the parenthetical is 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the stated image size and color format in the same table cell.

errors.claim: “The best convolutional networks without dropout achieve 3.95% error.”
errors.location: this part, SVHN discussion after Table 3
errors.evidence: Table 3 lists “Conv Net + stochastic pooling (Zeiler and Fergus, 2013) | 2.80,” which is a convolutional network entry not described as using dropout, and has lower error than 3.95%.
errors.explanation: The text’s claim that the best convolutional networks without dropout achieve 3.95% conflicts with the table’s lower non-dropout convolutional result of 2.80%, unless the claim was meant only for the authors’ max-pooling architecture, which it does not say.

errors.claim: “Dropout improves the max-pooling network: Table 3, ‘Conv Net + max-pooling,’ 3.95%; dropout in fully connected layers, 3.02%; dropout in all layers, 2.55%.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes for Table 3: “Conv Net + max-pooling 3.95; +dropout FC 3.02; Conv Net + stochastic pooling 2.80; +dropout all layers 2.55; maxout 2.47.”
errors.explanation: The 2.55% all-layer dropout result was recorded as following the stochastic-pooling convolutional net, not the max-pooling network. This part characterizes it as a max-pooling-network result, conflicting with the earlier Table 3 notes.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” as 20.7%, and “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) + dropout” as 19.7%. The 20.5% value belongs to “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The prose assigns the 20.5% baseline to the 8-layer pretrained network, but the table assigns 20.7% to that model and 20.5% to a different 5-layer mcRBM-DBN model.

errors.claim: “dropout substantially improves standard neural networks and outperforms every other method listed.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says “Bayesian networks perform better than dropout,” and Table 8 shows Bayesian Neural Network = 623 bits versus Neural Network with dropout = 567 bits.
errors.explanation: Since higher Code Quality is better, dropout does not outperform the Bayesian Neural Network listed in the table. The claim is only true if “other” is meant to exclude the Bayesian method, but as written it conflicts with the table and preceding sentence.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)=1(r_j=1) σ(b_j+∑_i W_{ij}v_i)” and “P(v_i=1\mid h)=σ(a_i+∑_j W_{ij}h_j)”
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same subsection the RBM distribution is defined as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), so a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use hidden bias a_j and the visible conditional should use visible bias b_i. The displayed conditional equations swap a and b.

errors.claim: “We then reunited training and validation data and trained on all 55,000 images”
errors.evidence: The same subsection says: “MNIST has 60,000 training and 10,000 test cases” and “We randomly held out 10,000 training images for validation.” Reuniting the 50,000 remaining training images with the 10,000 validation images would give 60,000, not 55,000.
errors.explanation: The reported reunited training-set size contradicts the dataset size and validation split stated immediately before it.

final_notes:
Internal errors found: ImageNet claims 65536-dimensional “256×256 color” input, but 256×256×3 = 196608. SVHN prose says best no-dropout convnets 3.95 and calls 2.55 max-pooling; table has stochastic pooling 2.80, +dropout all layers 2.55, maxout 2.47. TIMIT prose says 20.5 but table has 8-layer +dropout 19.7. Reports state-of-the-art on several benchmarks. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, RBMs, noise marginalization, Gaussian corruption. Training with dropout typically takes 2–3× as long as standard network of same architecture.

Claims dropout improves generalization over no-dropout networks on every tested dataset. Experiments span images, speech, documents, gene-splicing prediction; reports state-of-the-art on several benchmarks. Also examines learned features, sparsity, retention rates, training-set size, RBMs/dropout RBMs, noise marginalization, Bernoulli vs Gaussian dropout/corruption. Training with dropout typically takes 2–3× as long as standard network of same architecture. Key terms: retention probability p; thinned network/submodel; unthinned network; max-norm regularization bounds each hidden unit’s incoming-weight-vector norm; L1/lasso and L2/Tikhonov are comparison regularizers; KL-sparsity compared in some experiments; maxout and ReLUs are activation classes compared with logistic units; dropout described as reducing co-adaptation. Dropout extends to RBMs/DBMs/DBNs/pretraining; CD-1 used for RBM/dropout RBM. Image experiments include conv nets, pooling variants, padding/data augmentation, permutation-invariant comparisons. Other comparisons include SVMs, PCA, linear/logistic/ridge regression, bag-of-words documents, denoising autoencoders, Bayesian/model averaging, Monte Carlo dropout/model averaging, marginalization, blankout noise, Gaussian noise with matched moments/entropy.

Claims QX2 lowers generalization error vs other regularizers across varied classification problems and improves over no-dropout on every tested dataset; usually 2–3× training time. Table 9 comparison: Y5F/L2 1.62, V9C/max-norm 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, QX2+V9C 1.05.
Definitions: O3U=L1, Y5F=L2, U2L=RBM, B8T=Dropout RBM, E5Q/DBM mentioned as pretraining methods. Max-norm/V9C constrains each hidden unit incoming-weight vector norm ||w||2≤c; if outside radius-c ball, project to surface; c tuned by validation. Width heuristic n/p for expected retained width pn. Default hidden retention near optimal; input retention usually closer to complete retention; p validation-selected.
Training: backprop through sampled subnetworks; each case has its own sampled net; unused parameter contributes zero gradient. Momentum, annealed/large learning rates, Y5F useful. High LR/momentum and max-norm said to boost QX2; Appendix A.2: LR often 10–100× standard-net optimum, momentum ~0.95–0.99. Weight-space exploration account proposed, not numerically established here.
Pretraining: unchanged; QX2 finetuning with smaller LR preserves pretrained info. Before QX2 finetuning, multiply pretrained weights by 1/p to match expected output under random removal. Table 2 claims pretrained H4Z: G6W finetune 1.18 no QX2 vs 0.92 QX2; E5Q 0.96 vs 0.79. Appendix B.4: best QX2 G6W finetune LR ~0.01 vs high LR 0.1.

grade.reason: None of the reported errors addresses the MNIST training/validation recombination count—each reported issue concerns unrelated table numbers, baseline values, or swapped biases.

errors.claim: “The weights obtained from pretraining should be scaled up by a factor of 1/(1-p). This makes sure that for each unit, the expected output from it under random dropout will be the same as the output during pretraining.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Units retained independently with probability p”; “Sec4 states W_test^(l)=p W^(l). This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output”; “Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p).”
errors.explanation: If p is the retention probability, dropout multiplies a unit’s output by a Bernoulli(p) mask, so scaling pretrained weights by 1/p—not 1/(1-p)—would preserve the expected output. The stated factor conflicts with the paper’s earlier definition of p as retention probability and with the expectation argument.

errors.claim: ImageNet dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image would have 256 × 256 × 3 = 196,608 dimensions, not 65,536; 65,536 corresponds to 256 × 256 grayscale.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the parenthetical description “color” in the same table.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer net the error reduces from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” as 20.7, while 20.5 is listed for “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The text attributes the 20.5% baseline to an 8-layer net, but the table shows the 8-layer baseline is 20.7%; 20.5% belongs to a different 5-layer mcRBM-DBN model.

errors.claim: “dropout ... outperforms all other methods”
errors.location: this part, Section 6.4 text after Table 8
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says “Bayesian neural nets perform better than dropout,” and Table 8 reports Bayesian Neural Network = 623 vs Neural Network with dropout = 567, with higher Code Quality better.
errors.explanation: Taken literally, dropout does not outperform all other methods in Table 8; it is below the Bayesian neural network. The statement is only true if “other methods” excludes Bayesian neural networks, which the text does not explicitly say.

errors.claim: “P(hj = 1|rj, v) = 1(rj = 1) σ(bj + Σi Wij vi)” and “P(vi = 1|h) = σ(ai + Σj Wij hj)”
errors.evidence: The RBM distribution is defined just above as “exp(vᵀWh + aᵀh + bᵀv)”, where a is multiplied by hidden units h and b by visible units v.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias a_j, and the visible conditional should use the visible bias b_i. The displayed conditionals swap a and b, contradicting the model definition in the same section.

errors.claim: “The CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 data sets consists of 50,000 training and 10,000 test images each.”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 1 recorded in notes: “CIFAR-10/100 3072 60K/10K.”
errors.explanation: The paper earlier listed CIFAR-10/100 as having 60,000 training examples, but this appendix says they have 50,000 training examples.

final_notes:
Dropout definition: p = retaining probability; typical hidden p=0.5 (appendix says 0.5–0.8), input ~0.8. Test-time full net scales outgoing weights by p; inverted dropout scales retained activations by 1/p at train time and no test scaling. Earlier pretraining said weights scaled up by 1/(1-p), conflicting with p retention.

Dataset Table 1: MNIST 784 60K/10K; SVHN 3072 600K/26K; CIFAR-10/100 3072 60K/10K, but Appendix B.3 says CIFAR has 50K train/10K test; ImageNet 65536 “256×256 color” (dimension inconsistency) 1.2M/150K; TIMIT 2520 1.1M/58K; Reuters 2000 200K/200K; Alt Splicing 1014 2932/733.

Key results: MNIST best DBM+dropout 0.79; DBN+dropout 0.92; maxout 0.94; large dropout nets 2×8192 0.95. SVHN: dropout all layers 2.55 vs FC only 3.02; maxout 2.47. CIFAR dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; FC only 14.32/41.26; maxout 11.68/38.57. ImageNet 2010 ConvNet+dropout 37.5/17.0; 2012 avg 5 ConvNets+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top-5 16.4. TIMIT text incorrectly says 8-layer reduces from 20.5 to 19.7 though table has both 4+dropout and 8+dropout 19.7. Reuters no dropout 31.05, dropout 29.62.

Alt Splicing Table 8: dropout NN 567, Bayesian NN 623; text says BNN better but also dropout “outperforms all other methods,” conflicting unless excluding BNN. Table 9: Dropout+Max-norm best 1.05. Sec 8.1 RBM conditionals swap a/b vs joint. Gaussian dropout: σ²=(1-p)/p; MNIST Gaussian better than Bernoulli. Conclusion claims SOTA on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST; training 2–3× longer.
