Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Abstract/main claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping units/connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Training samples an exponential number of “thinned” networks. At test time, approximate averaging predictions of all thinned nets using one unthinned network with smaller weights. Claims significant reductions in overfitting and improvements over other regularization methods on vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks.

Intro: Deep nets expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing regularization: early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Bayesian gold standard would average over parameter settings weighted by posterior; dropout aims to approximate this with less computation by using an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Model combination helps but separately training/testing many large nets is expensive; diverse nets require different architectures or data subsets.

Dropout definition: “dropping out” hidden or visible units means temporarily removing the unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Units are randomly retained independently with probability p. p chosen by validation or often 0.5, near optimal for many networks/tasks; input-unit retention probability usually closer to 1. Figure 1 shows standard vs dropout network. Figure 2: at training a unit present with probability p and weights w to next layer; at test unit always present and outgoing weights multiplied by p, so test output equals expected training output.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims/definition: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameters remain O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net, so training can be viewed as training 2^n shared-weight nets, each rarely trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. This approximate averaging is claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Broader scope: Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. graphical models/Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine and compares to standard RBMs; claims dropout RBMs are better in certain respects.

Paper structure: Sec2 motivation; Sec3 previous work; Sec4 formal dropout model; Sec5 training algorithm; Sec6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec7 effects on network properties and hyperparameters; Sec8 Dropout RBM; Sec9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide/hyperparameter considerations.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Motivation section: Dropout is motivated by sexual reproduction/evolution: genes must work with random subsets of other genes, discouraging complex co-adaptations and promoting robust, independently useful features. Also motivated by “conspiracies”: many small co-adaptations generalize better under changing/non-stationary conditions than one large fragile co-adaptation. Notes that hidden units will still learn different things; simply duplicating units would be a poor solution, like replica codes for noisy channels.

Broader scope/structure: Applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. dropout RBMs (claimed better in some respects). Sections: 3 related work; 4 formal model; 5 training; 6 experiments; 7 effects/hyperparameters; 8 Dropout RBM; 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A guide. Sec3 begins: dropout can be interpreted as regularizing a neural net by adding noise to hidden units; relates to Denoising Autoencoders adding noise to unit states.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava et al.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible/input units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Dropping out 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units often optimal. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test; Sec4 states W_test^(l)=p W^(l). This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Resulting net used without dropout.

Related work/motivation: Related to denoising autoencoders, which add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically use ~5% noise; dropout’s weight scaling permits much higher noise. Deterministic counterpart can be obtained by marginalizing dropout noise in simple cases; related to van der Maaten et al. “blankout noise” (inputs only/no hidden layers), Wang & Manning speeding up dropout by marginalizing noise, Chen et al. marginalizing DAEs. Adversarial dropping work fixes max units dropped but no hidden units.

Sec4 formalism: Standard layer: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), ỹ^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then next layer uses ỹ. Backprop derivatives through sampled sub-network.

errors.claim: “The weights obtained from pretraining should be scaled up by a factor of 1/(1-p). This makes sure that for each unit, the expected output from it under random dropout will be the same as the output during pretraining.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Units retained independently with probability p”; “Sec4 states W_test^(l)=p W^(l). This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output”; “Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p).”
errors.explanation: If p is the retention probability, dropout multiplies a unit’s output by a Bernoulli(p) mask, so scaling pretrained weights by 1/p—not 1/(1-p)—would preserve the expected output. The stated factor conflicts with the paper’s earlier definition of p as retention probability and with the expectation argument.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014). Dropout randomly drops visible/input or hidden units during training to prevent co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 hidden, closer to 1 input. Dropping 20% input and 50% hidden often optimal. Each case samples a thinned network; n units imply 2^n thinned nets with shared weights.

Test-time approximation: Use full network without dropout, scaling outgoing trained weights by p: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), so expected training-time output equals deterministic test output.

Training: SGD mini-batches; each case samples thinned net; unused parameters get zero gradient for that case; average gradients over mini-batch. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 decay useful. Max-norm regularization constrains incoming weights at each hidden unit ||w||2≤c by projection; c tuned on validation. Dropout plus max-norm, large decaying learning rates, high momentum improves over dropout alone.

Pretraining: Nets may be pretrained with RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs, then finetuned with dropout; pretraining unchanged. Current part claims pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/(1-p) to preserve expected outputs under dropout—this conflicts with earlier definition p=retention probability, since factor should be 1/p if preserving expectation.

Experiments intro: Dropout tested on classification datasets across domains: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Claims dropout improved generalization on all datasets versus non-dropout neural nets. Table 1 describes datasets; Appendix B has details.

§2 motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction: recombination breaks large co-adapted gene sets yet may favor genes that work with random partners, robustness, and reduced barriers to spread of useful genes. Dropout-trained hidden units likewise face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful robust features instead of relying on other units to fix mistakes; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes in noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies more robust than one large conspiracy under changing/non-stationary conditions; complex co-adaptations may fit training data but fail on test data more readily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

§3 related work: dropout as noise in hidden-unit states, extending denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) from input corruption/clean reconstruction to effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised+unsupervised use, and architectures like Boltzmann Machines. Test-time weight scaling/approximation permits higher noise than typically best for DAEs. Table: DAE typical best noise 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; hidden-unit removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise minimizes expected loss; adversarial removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) choose removals subject to max number and have no hidden units. Marginalizing dropout can yield deterministic regularizers in simple cases. Exponential-family input-noise/“blankout noise” regularizers studied by van der Maaten et al. 2013, limited to no hidden layers; Chen et al. 2012 marginalized DAEs; Wang & Manning 2013 proposed marginalization to accelerate dropout.

grade.reason: Review item 2 identifies the exact planted error, noting the paper's retention probability p implies scaling by 1/p (not 1/(1-p)), matching the planted-claim contradiction with earlier definitions.

errors.claim: “Pretrained weights should first be multiplied by \(1/(1-p)\). This makes each unit’s expected output under dropout equal its output during pretraining.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes define \(p\) as the retention probability and dropout as sampling masks \(r_j\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\), with test using full network weights scaled by \(p\). Under that definition, dropout reduces expected retained output by a factor \(p\), not \(1-p\).
errors.explanation: If \(p\) is the probability a unit is kept, compensating pretrained weights to preserve expected output would involve a factor tied to \(1/p\), not \(1/(1-p)\). The stated scaling treats \(1-p\) as the retention probability, contradicting the paper’s own definition of \(p\).

errors.claim: ImageNet (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality: “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has 256 × 256 × 3 = 196,608 dimensions, not 65,536. 65,536 equals 256 × 256 for a single-channel image.
errors.explanation: The table’s dimensionality conflicts with its own parenthetical description of the images as color.

errors.location: this part, SVHN discussion after Table 3
errors.evidence: Table 3 lists “Conv Net + stochastic pooling (Zeiler and Fergus, 2013) | 2.80,” which is a convolutional network result and is not described as using dropout.
errors.explanation: The text says the best convolutional networks without dropout get 3.95%, but the same table reports a lower-error convolutional network without dropout at 2.80%.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” as 20.7, and lists 20.5 for “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The prose attributes the 20.5% baseline to the 8-layer pretrained network, but the table gives the 8-layer baseline as 20.7%; 20.5% belongs to a different 5-layer mcRBM-DBN model.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)= 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j+∑_i W_{ij}v_i)” and “P(v_i=1\mid h)=σ(a_i+∑_j W_{ij}h_j)”
errors.evidence: The RBM distribution was defined as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), so a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated energy/probability form, hidden conditional probabilities should use hidden biases a_j, and visible conditionals should use visible biases b_i. The text swaps a and b in the conditional distributions.

errors.claim: “Pretrained weights should first be multiplied by \(1/(1-p)\). This makes each unit’s expected output under dropout equal its output during pretraining.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes define \(p\) as the retention probability and dropout as sampling masks \(r_j\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\), with test using full network weights scaled by \(p\). Under that definition, dropout reduces expected retained output by a factor \(p\), not \(1-p\).
errors.explanation: If \(p\) is the probability a unit is kept, compensating pretrained weights to preserve expected output would involve a factor tied to \(1/p\), not \(1/(1-p)\). The stated scaling treats \(1-p\) as the retention probability, contradicting the paper’s own definition of \(p\).

grade.reason: Review item 0 directly flags the incorrect scaling 1/(1-p), noting p is the retention probability so the correct compensating factor is 1/p (not 1/(1-p)).

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/(1-p). This matches each unit’s expected output under random removal to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes define p as the retention probability: “dropout gates r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p)” and “Test-time ... weights/outgoing connections scaled by retention probability p.” With retention probability p, random removal makes expected activation/input p times the undropped value.
errors.explanation: If p is the probability a unit is retained, matching the pretrained no-dropout expected output would require scaling weights by 1/p, not 1/(1-p). The stated factor treats p as if it were the drop probability, conflicting with the paper’s earlier notation.

errors.claim: “K9D (ILSVRC-2012) | Vision | 65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has three color channels, so its dimensionality would be 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608, not 65536. The value 65536 corresponds only to 256 × 256 grayscale/single-channel.
errors.explanation: The table’s stated dimensionality conflicts with its own parenthetical description of the image size and color format.

errors.claim: “Prose comparison | 8-layer net | Pre-QX2 error 20.5%” / “The prose comparison for the deeper pretrained network uses a pre-QX2 baseline different from the corresponding table baseline.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” while 20.5 belongs to “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The prose comparison appears to use 20.5% as the pre-dropout baseline for the 8-layer G6W-pretrained network, but the table’s 8-layer G6W baseline is 20.7%; 20.5% is a different 5-layer mcRBM-G6W model.

errors.claim: “The QX2 gain is absent for the smallest sets”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Claims QX2 lowers generalization error on all tested datasets” and §6 claims evidence of QX2 improvements across datasets.
errors.explanation: The paper’s earlier broad claim says QX2 improves generalization on all tested datasets, but this section states that for the smallest data sets the QX2 gain is absent. Unless these smallest sets are excluded from the earlier scope, the claims conflict.

errors.claim: QX2 lowers generalization error on all tested datasets
errors.evidence: This part states: “The two smallest tested training sets show no QX2 improvement.”
errors.explanation: The earlier broad claim says QX2 improves generalization error on all tested datasets, but this section reports tested H4Z training-set sizes where QX2 gives no improvement.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), so a is the hidden-bias vector and b is the visible-bias vector. The text also says θ={W,a,b}.
errors.explanation: Given the model definition, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias a_j, not b_j. This conflicts with the earlier equation in the same section.

errors.claim: “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), where b^T v is the visible-bias term.
errors.explanation: Given the model definition, the visible conditional should use the visible bias b_i, not a_i. This is the reverse of the bias roles established earlier in the same section.

errors.claim: “The stated benchmark successes include ... Table 6’s K9D top-5 test error 16.4”
errors.evidence: Notes record: “K9D ILSVRC-2010 QX2 37.5/17.0; ILSVRC-2012 avg 5 QX2 nets 38.1/16.4 val and 16.4 test.”
errors.explanation: The 16.4 top-5 test error belongs to the ILSVRC-2012 averaged 5-network result, while the recorded K9D/ILSVRC-2010 result is 17.0 top-5. This part appears to attribute the 16.4 result to K9D/Table 6, conflicting with the earlier recorded K9D result.

final_notes: Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958; QX2/dropout gates units with retention p; test full net with weights scaled by p. Broad claim: QX2 lowers generalization error on all tested datasets, but §7.4/Fig.10 says two smallest H4Z sampled training sets show no improvement. Terms: O3U=L1, Y5F=L2, U2L=RBM, B8T=Dropout RBM, V9C=max-norm, F3N=ReLU, L8J=maxout, G6W=DBN, E5Q=DBM. Internal issues found: pretraining says multiply weights by 1/(1-p), conflicting with p=retention; Table 1 K9D says 65536 (256×256 color), dimension inconsistency; N8Q prose uses 20.5 as 8-layer baseline though Table 7 gives 20.7; §8.1 RBM conditionals swap visible/hidden definitions; conclusion/evidence misattributes K9D top-5 16.4 to Table 6 though K9D/ILSVRC-2010 QX2 was 37.5/17.0 and 16.4 belongs to ILSVRC-2012 avg 5 nets. Key results: H4Z best 0.79 E5Q+QX2; A2F best 2.47 L8J; J3V/W6R QX2 all 12.61/37.20, L8J 11.68/38.57; K9D ILSVRC-2010 QX2 37.5/17.0; ILSVRC-2012 avg 5 QX2 nets 38.1/16.4 val and 16.4 test. §7 best p≈0.6; sampled averaging k≈50 approximates/slightly beats T6R. §8 B8T p=0.5 coarser/fewer dead/sparser than U2L. §9 marginalized QX2 linear regression penalty (1-p)/p. §10 Gaussian/D4K dropout slightly better than Bernoulli/P7V; mean-1 needs no test scaling. Z7P: 3665 exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue softmaxes×3 states; QX2 two 1024 layers, p hidden .5 input .7, V9C, 5 folds; Table 8: QX2 567 bits, early-stopped NN 440, Bayesian NN 623.

Training with dropout typically takes 2–3× as long as standard network of same architecture.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/(1-p). This matches each unit’s expected output under random removal to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes define p as the retention probability: “dropout gates r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p)” and “Test-time ... weights/outgoing connections scaled by retention probability p.” With retention probability p, random removal makes expected activation/input p times the undropped value.
errors.explanation: If p is the probability a unit is retained, matching the pretrained no-dropout expected output would require scaling weights by 1/p, not 1/(1-p). The stated factor treats p as if it were the drop probability, conflicting with the paper’s earlier notation.

final_notes:
Paper: dropout drops units during training; retain prob p; test uses unthinned net with outgoing weights multiplied by p. Inverted dropout scales by 1/p; Gaussian dropout σ²=(1-p)/p. Table 10: Gaussian/high-entropy may work slightly better than Bernoulli.

Known internal errors: MNIST text says maxout worsened to 0.94 though Table 2 shows improvement vs 0.95. SVHN text says best non-dropout conv nets 3.95, but Table 3 has Conv Net + stochastic pooling 2.80 without dropout. TIMIT text says 8-layer error reduced from 20.5 to 19.7, but Table 7 gives 8-layer DBN baseline 20.7; 20.5 is 5-layer mcRBM-DBN. RBM Sec 8.1 defines hidden bias a / visible bias b, but conditionals use b_j for hidden and a_i for visible.

Key results: dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout. CIFAR Table 4: dropout FC 14.32/41.26; dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Abstract/main claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping units/connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Training samples an exponential number of “thinned” networks. At test time, approximate averaging predictions of all thinned nets using one unthinned network with smaller weights. Claims significant reductions in overfitting and improvements over other regularization methods on vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks.

Intro: Deep nets expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing regularization: early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Bayesian gold standard would average over parameter settings weighted by posterior; dropout aims to approximate this with less computation by using an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Model combination helps but separately training/testing many large nets is expensive; diverse nets require different architectures or data subsets.

Dropout definition: “dropping out” hidden or visible units means temporarily removing the unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Units are randomly retained independently with probability p. p chosen by validation or often 0.5, near optimal for many networks/tasks; input-unit retention probability usually closer to 1. Figure 1 shows standard vs dropout network. Figure 2: at training a unit present with probability p and weights w to next layer; at test unit always present and outgoing weights multiplied by p, so test output equals expected training output.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims/definition: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameters remain O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net, so training can be viewed as training 2^n shared-weight nets, each rarely trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. This approximate averaging is claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Broader scope: Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. graphical models/Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine and compares to standard RBMs; claims dropout RBMs are better in certain respects.

Paper structure: Sec2 motivation; Sec3 previous work; Sec4 formal dropout model; Sec5 training algorithm; Sec6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec7 effects on network properties and hyperparameters; Sec8 Dropout RBM; Sec9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide/hyperparameter considerations.

Motivation section: Dropout is motivated by sexual reproduction/evolution: genes must work with random subsets of other genes, discouraging complex co-adaptations and promoting robust, independently useful features. Also motivated by “conspiracies”: many small co-adaptations generalize better under changing/non-stationary conditions than one large fragile co-adaptation. Notes that hidden units will still learn different things; simply duplicating units would be a poor solution, like replica codes for noisy channels.

Broader scope/structure: Applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. dropout RBMs (claimed better in some respects). Sections: 3 related work; 4 formal model; 5 training; 6 experiments; 7 effects/hyperparameters; 8 Dropout RBM; 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A guide. Sec3 begins: dropout can be interpreted as regularizing a neural net by adding noise to hidden units; relates to Denoising Autoencoders adding noise to unit states.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava et al.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible/input units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Dropping out 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units often optimal. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test; Sec4 states W_test^(l)=p W^(l). This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Resulting net used without dropout.

Related work/motivation: Related to denoising autoencoders, which add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically use ~5% noise; dropout’s weight scaling permits much higher noise. Deterministic counterpart can be obtained by marginalizing dropout noise in simple cases; related to van der Maaten et al. “blankout noise” (inputs only/no hidden layers), Wang & Manning speeding up dropout by marginalizing noise, Chen et al. marginalizing DAEs. Adversarial dropping work fixes max units dropped but no hidden units.

Sec4 formalism: Standard layer: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), ỹ^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then next layer uses ỹ. Backprop derivatives through sampled sub-network.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014). Dropout: randomly drop hidden or visible/input units and connections during training; retained independently with probability p (often hidden p=0.5; inputs closer to 1; common optimal: 20% input, 50% hidden dropped). Each training case samples a thinned net; n units imply 2^n thinned nets with shared weights.

Test-time approximation: use one unthinned net without dropout, with trained outgoing weights multiplied by p: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), so expected training-time unit output equals test-time output.

Sec4 formalism: standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses ỹ^(l)=r*y; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Related work: dropout compared to denoising autoencoders, blankout/marginalized noise, adversarial dropping; dropout extends noise to hidden layers/supervised/model averaging/various architectures and allows high noise via weight scaling.

Sec5 training: SGD as usual except each training case in mini-batch uses sampled thinned net; parameters unused by a case get zero gradient; gradients averaged over mini-batch. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weights to hidden unit ||w||2≤c, projecting to ball radius c; c tuned on validation; helps even without dropout. Dropout + max-norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives boost.

Pretraining: can finetune pretrained nets with dropout; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), but test-time uses no removals and scaled weights \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). It also says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*y)+b)]\) is not generally equal to \(f(p\mathbf w y+b)\). The equations only make the expected preactivation/input contribution match, not the hidden unit’s expected output.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier model equations in notes: with dropout, gates are applied before the next affine transform, then activation: “\(\tilde y^{(l)}=r^{(l)}*y^{(l)}\), then \(z_i=w_i\tilde y+b_i\), \(y_i=f(z_i)\).” Notes also record the caveat that equality under scaling is supported for expected preactivation/input contribution, not generally for nonlinear output.
errors.explanation: Multiplying weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation contribution match the pretrained preactivation, but with a nonlinear activation \(f\), it does not in general make the expected unit output match the pretrained output. This repeats/conflicts with the earlier equations unless “output” is meant imprecisely as input/preactivation.

errors.claim: “substitution of another activation class (L8J: maxout) worsens them”
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports “QX2 NN + V9C | F3N | 2 layers, 8192 units | 0.95” and then “QX2 NN + V9C (Goodfellow et al., 2013) | L8J | 2 layers, (5 × 240) units | 0.94.”
errors.explanation: Lower error is better, so the maxout/L8J result improves on the preceding F3N result rather than worsening it.

errors.claim: “K9D (ILSVRC-2012) | Vision | 65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: The parenthetical says the images are “256 × 256 color,” which implies 256×256×3 = 196,608 dimensions for color images, not 65,536.
errors.explanation: The listed dimensionality 65,536 matches 256×256 grayscale, conflicting with the stated color image format.

errors.claim: “8-layer net” has “Pre-QX2 error” of 20.5%.
errors.location: this part, prose comparison table under Table 7
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) … 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) … 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-dropout/pre-QX2 error belongs to the 5-layer mcRBM-pretrained network, not the 8-layer network. The 8-layer pretrained network’s listed error is 20.7%.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The joint distribution just above defines the bias terms as “\(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\)”, so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden-unit bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional distributions swap the bias symbols: hidden-unit conditionals should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), while visible-unit conditionals should use the visible bias \(b_i\). As written, the equations conflict with the model definition and even the implied dimensions of \(a\) and \(b\).

final_notes:

§2 motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction: recombination breaks large co-adapted gene sets yet may favor genes that work with random partners, robustness, and reduced barriers to spread of useful genes. Dropout-trained hidden units likewise face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful robust features instead of relying on other units to fix mistakes; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes in noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies more robust than one large conspiracy under changing/non-stationary conditions; complex co-adaptations may fit training data but fail on test data more readily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Applies beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models/RBMs. §2 motivation: sexual reproduction analogy—random partners encourage robust independently useful features; replication of units poor robustness; conspiracy analogy: many small/simple co-adaptations more robust than one large/complex one under changing conditions.

§3 related work: dropout as noise in hidden-unit states, extending denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) from input corruption/clean reconstruction to effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised+unsupervised use, and architectures like Boltzmann Machines. Test-time weight scaling/approximation permits higher noise than typically best for DAEs. Table: DAE typical best noise 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; hidden-unit removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise minimizes expected loss; adversarial removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) choose removals subject to max number and have no hidden units. Marginalizing dropout can yield deterministic regularizers in simple cases. Exponential-family input-noise/“blankout noise” regularizers studied by van der Maaten et al. 2013, limited to no hidden layers; Chen et al. 2012 marginalized DAEs; Wang & Manning 2013 proposed marginalization to accelerate dropout.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), but test-time uses no removals and scaled weights \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). It also says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*y)+b)]\) is not generally equal to \(f(p\mathbf w y+b)\). The equations only make the expected preactivation/input contribution match, not the hidden unit’s expected output.

grade.reason: Reviewer error 3 points out the table shows 0.94% for maxout versus 0.95% for the ReLU network, so the paper's claim that maxout worsens performance is incorrect.

errors.claim: ImageNet (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has three color channels, so the dimensionality implied by the parenthetical is 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the stated image size and color format in the same table cell.

errors.claim: “Goodfellow et al. (2013) worsened error to 0.94% by replacing ReLUs with maxout units.”
errors.evidence: Table 2 in notes lists Dropout+maxnorm ReLU 2×8192 at 0.95% and Goodfellow maxout at 0.94%; this part also says “Maxout reaches 0.94%.”
errors.explanation: An error rate of 0.94% is lower/better than 0.95%, so calling it “worsened” contradicts the reported numbers.

errors.claim: “The best convolutional networks without dropout achieve 3.95% error.”
errors.evidence: Table 3 lists “Conv Net + stochastic pooling (Zeiler and Fergus, 2013) | 2.80,” while the 3.95% row is “Conv Net + max-pooling.”
errors.explanation: The table includes a convolutional network result without stated dropout at 2.80%, better than 3.95%, so 3.95% is not the best convolutional network without dropout as written.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” as 20.7%, while 20.5% is listed for “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The prose attributes the 20.5% baseline to the 8-layer DBN-pretrained network, but the table assigns 20.5% to a different 5-layer mcRBM-DBN model; the corresponding 8-layer baseline is 20.7%.

errors.claim: Dropout + Max-norm has test classification error 1.05% on MNIST.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “MNIST Table 2 best: ... best dropout maxnorm ReLU 0.95.”
errors.explanation: Both refer to MNIST dropout with max-norm regularization, but the reported test error differs: 1.05% here versus 0.95% earlier. The current part says this comparison uses one fixed ReLU architecture, so this may be a different experimental setup, but as recorded it conflicts with the earlier reported result for the same named method.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)= \mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_j W_{ij}h_j\right)”
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same subsection the RBM distribution is defined as “exp\!\left(v^\top Wh+a^\top h+b^\top v\right)” and “The parameters are \(\theta=\{W,a,b\}\).” In that expression, \(a\) is the hidden bias vector and \(b\) is the visible bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional probabilities swap the roles of the bias vectors: the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias defined as \(a\), while the visible conditional should use the visible bias defined as \(b\).

errors.claim: “Methods using dropout achieve state-of-the-art results on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100 and MNIST.” / “Table 2, DBM + dropout finetuning, 0.79%”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record: “MNIST best dropout maxnorm ReLU 0.95; Table 9 fixed ReLU regularizers dropout+max-norm 1.05.”
errors.explanation: This conclusion cites a MNIST dropout result of 0.79%, but the earlier recorded MNIST best dropout result was 0.95%, with another fixed ReLU dropout result of 1.05%. The cited value conflicts with the earlier recorded results.

errors.claim: “Dropout methods achieve the stated image-data results: … Table 3, maxout, 2.47%”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record: “SVHN best dropout all layers 2.55.”
errors.explanation: This part cites an SVHN/maxout dropout result of 2.47%, but the earlier recorded best SVHN dropout result was 2.55%, so the stated Table 3 value conflicts with the notes.

final_notes: Dropout paper: p retention; standard test scales outgoing weights by p; inverted training scales retained activations by 1/p and leaves test unchanged. Dataset Table 1 has ImageNet dim conflict: 65536 listed as “256×256 color”. Key results: MNIST best dropout maxnorm ReLU 0.95; Table 9 fixed ReLU dropout+max-norm 1.05. SVHN best all-layer dropout 2.55. CIFAR-10 12.61, CIFAR-100 37.20. ImageNet Avg 5 ConvNets+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4. TIMIT: NN6 23.4, dropout NN6 21.8; DBN8+dropout 19.7; earlier prose erroneously says 8-layer baseline 20.5. TIMIT Appendix B.4: input p=.8, hidden p=.5, c=4, momentum .95, LR .1 schedule; DBN finetuning best dropout LR about .01 and max-norm no improvement; Table 7 dropout rows 21.8, 19.7, 19.7. Reuters: subset 402,738 docs, vocab 2000, 50 categories, exactly one class, equal train/test; >200k train; dropout improved all tried architectures but less than image/speech; best NN 31.05 vs dropout 29.62. Alt Splicing: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissues; target has 4 softmaxes each with inc/exc/nc; Code Quality higher better; dropout 2-layer 1024, hidden p=.5 input p=.7, max-norm, high decaying LR, 5 folds; dropout NN 567, Bayesian NN 623, so Bayesian beats dropout. Sec 11 claims SOTA on SVHN/ImageNet/CIFAR-100/MNIST, cites Table2 DBM+dropout 0.79 and Table3 maxout 2.47, conflicting with earlier recorded MNIST/SVHN values; says training 2–3× longer, no timing table. During training it randomly removes units and connections, sampling many smaller shared-weight networks. At test time, a single full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble predictions. errors.explanation: This part states that L8J/maxout improves the unpretrained MNIST result, while the earlier text was recorded as saying maxout worsens results. Those two textual claims conflict, even though the table value supports improvement.

errors.claim: For the deeper pretrained N8Q network, the prose comparison uses a pre-QX2 baseline of 20.5%.
errors.location: this part, §6.2 N8Q / prose comparison table

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=...\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right)”
errors.evidence: The ordinary RBM distribution is defined as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), where h has F entries and v has D entries. Thus a is the hidden bias vector and b is the visible bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional probabilities swap the biases: the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias a_j, and the visible conditional should use the visible bias b_i. As written, b_j is indexed over hidden units and a_i over visible units, contradicting the model definition.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=...\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right)”
errors.evidence: The ordinary RBM distribution is defined as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), where h has F entries and v has D entries. Thus a is the hidden bias vector and b is the visible bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional probabilities swap the biases: the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias a_j, and the visible conditional should use the visible bias b_i. As written, b_j is indexed over hidden units and a_i over visible units, contradicting the model definition.

errors.claim: “P(hj = 1|rj, v) = 1(rj = 1) σ(bj + Σi Wij vi)” and “P(vi = 1|h) = σ(ai + Σj Wij hj)”

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Abstract/main claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping units/connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Training samples an exponential number of “thinned” networks. At test time, approximate averaging predictions of all thinned nets using one unthinned network with smaller weights. Claims significant reductions in overfitting and improvements over other regularization methods on vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks.

Intro: Deep nets expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing regularization: early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Bayesian gold standard would average over parameter settings weighted by posterior; dropout aims to approximate this with less computation by using an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Model combination helps but separately training/testing many large nets is expensive; diverse nets require different architectures or data subsets.

Dropout definition: “dropping out” hidden or visible units means temporarily removing the unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Units are randomly retained independently with probability p. p chosen by validation or often 0.5, near optimal for many networks/tasks; input-unit retention probability usually closer to 1. Figure 1 shows standard vs dropout network. Figure 2: at training a unit present with probability p and weights w to next layer; at test unit always present and outgoing weights multiplied by p, so test output equals expected training output.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims/definition: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameters remain O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net, so training can be viewed as training 2^n shared-weight nets, each rarely trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. This approximate averaging is claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Broader scope: Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. graphical models/Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine and compares to standard RBMs; claims dropout RBMs are better in certain respects.

Paper structure: Sec2 motivation; Sec3 previous work; Sec4 formal dropout model; Sec5 training algorithm; Sec6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec7 effects on network properties and hyperparameters; Sec8 Dropout RBM; Sec9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide/hyperparameter considerations.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Motivation section: Dropout is motivated by sexual reproduction/evolution: genes must work with random subsets of other genes, discouraging complex co-adaptations and promoting robust, independently useful features. Also motivated by “conspiracies”: many small co-adaptations generalize better under changing/non-stationary conditions than one large fragile co-adaptation. Notes that hidden units will still learn different things; simply duplicating units would be a poor solution, like replica codes for noisy channels.

Broader scope/structure: Applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. dropout RBMs (claimed better in some respects). Sections: 3 related work; 4 formal model; 5 training; 6 experiments; 7 effects/hyperparameters; 8 Dropout RBM; 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A guide. Sec3 begins: dropout can be interpreted as regularizing a neural net by adding noise to hidden units; relates to Denoising Autoencoders adding noise to unit states.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava et al.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible/input units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Dropping out 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units often optimal. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test; Sec4 states W_test^(l)=p W^(l). This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Resulting net used without dropout.

Related work/motivation: Related to denoising autoencoders, which add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically use ~5% noise; dropout’s weight scaling permits much higher noise. Deterministic counterpart can be obtained by marginalizing dropout noise in simple cases; related to van der Maaten et al. “blankout noise” (inputs only/no hidden layers), Wang & Manning speeding up dropout by marginalizing noise, Chen et al. marginalizing DAEs. Adversarial dropping work fixes max units dropped but no hidden units.

Sec4 formalism: Standard layer: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), ỹ^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then next layer uses ỹ. Backprop derivatives through sampled sub-network.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014). Dropout: randomly drop hidden or visible/input units and connections during training; retained independently with probability p (often hidden p=0.5; inputs closer to 1; common optimal: 20% input, 50% hidden dropped). Each training case samples a thinned net; n units imply 2^n thinned nets with shared weights.

Test-time approximation: use one unthinned net without dropout, with trained outgoing weights multiplied by p: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), so expected training-time unit output equals test-time output.

Sec4 formalism: standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses ỹ^(l)=r*y; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Related work: dropout compared to denoising autoencoders, blankout/marginalized noise, adversarial dropping; dropout extends noise to hidden layers/supervised/model averaging/various architectures and allows high noise via weight scaling.

Sec5 training: SGD as usual except each training case in mini-batch uses sampled thinned net; parameters unused by a case get zero gradient; gradients averaged over mini-batch. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weights to hidden unit ||w||2≤c, projecting to ball radius c; c tuned on validation; helps even without dropout. Dropout + max-norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives boost.

Pretraining: can finetune pretrained nets with dropout; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. Smaller finetuning LRs preserve pretrained information; improves final generalization vs finetuning without dropout.

Experiments intro: classification across MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Claim: dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout nets; details in Appendix B.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), but test-time uses no removals and scaled weights \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). It also says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*y)+b)]\) is not generally equal to \(f(p\mathbf w y+b)\). The equations only make the expected preactivation/input contribution match, not the hidden unit’s expected output.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier model equations in notes: with dropout, gates are applied before the next affine transform, then activation: “\(\tilde y^{(l)}=r^{(l)}*y^{(l)}\), then \(z_i=w_i\tilde y+b_i\), \(y_i=f(z_i)\).” Notes also record the caveat that equality under scaling is supported for expected preactivation/input contribution, not generally for nonlinear output.
errors.explanation: Multiplying weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation contribution match the pretrained preactivation, but with a nonlinear activation \(f\), it does not in general make the expected unit output match the pretrained output. This repeats/conflicts with the earlier equations unless “output” is meant imprecisely as input/preactivation.

§2 motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction: recombination breaks large co-adapted gene sets yet may favor genes that work with random partners, robustness, and reduced barriers to spread of useful genes. Dropout-trained hidden units likewise face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful robust features instead of relying on other units to fix mistakes; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes in noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies more robust than one large conspiracy under changing/non-stationary conditions; complex co-adaptations may fit training data but fail on test data more readily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Intro: n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets with O(n^2) or fewer parameters; new thinned net sampled for each case, each model trained rarely/never. Applies beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models/RBMs. §2 motivation: sexual reproduction analogy—random partners encourage robust independently useful features; replication of units poor robustness; conspiracy analogy: many small/simple co-adaptations more robust than one large/complex one under changing conditions.

§3 related work: dropout as noise in hidden-unit states, extending denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) from input corruption/clean reconstruction to effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised+unsupervised use, and architectures like Boltzmann Machines. Test-time weight scaling/approximation permits higher noise than typically best for DAEs. Table: DAE typical best noise 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; hidden-unit removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise minimizes expected loss; adversarial removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) choose removals subject to max number and have no hidden units. Marginalizing dropout can yield deterministic regularizers in simple cases. grade.reason: The reviewer's fifth entry directly identifies the planted claim that Bayesian networks perform worse than dropout as incorrect, citing Table 8 where Bayesian = 623 and dropout = 567 and noting the metric is higher-is-better.

errors.claim: K9D dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image would have 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608 dimensions, not 65536. 65536 corresponds to 256 × 256 without color channels.
errors.explanation: The dimensionality number conflicts with the parenthetical description in the same table entry.

errors.claim: “The prose comparison for the deeper pretrained network uses a pre-QX2 baseline different from the corresponding table baseline” / prose comparison lists the 8-layer net pre-QX2 error as 20.5%.
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” with phone error rate 20.7, while 20.5 belongs to “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The 8-layer G6W-pretrained baseline is 20.7 in Table 7, not 20.5. The prose comparison appears to use the 5-layer mcRBM-G6W value as if it were the 8-layer G6W baseline.

errors.claim: “Bayesian neural nets perform worse than QX2 on Z7P.”
errors.location: this part, Section 6.4 Bayesian Neural Networks
errors.evidence: The same part says “QX2 beats the non-Bayesian comparisons but remains below Bayesian neural networks,” and Table 8 reports Neural Network with QX2 = 567 versus Bayesian Neural Network = 623, with “Higher values are preferred.”
errors.explanation: Because higher C4Y is better, the Bayesian neural network outperforms QX2, not the reverse.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=...\sigma(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_j W_{ij}h_j)”
errors.evidence: The ordinary RBM is defined just above as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), so a is the hidden-bias vector and b is the visible-bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the model definition, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias a_j and the visible conditional should use the visible bias b_i. The displayed conditionals swap a and b, contradicting the earlier parameter definition in the same section.

errors.claim: “Other-domain improvements include ... Table 8, 440 versus 567.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record the Table 8/Z7P result as: “Z7P: Bayesian NN 623 > QX2 567.”
errors.explanation: The current part cites Table 8 as a 440-versus-567 improvement, but the earlier recorded Table 8 result had QX2 at 567 and another comparison value of 623, not 440. This misstates the numerical evidence from that table.

errors.claim: The conclusion says “440 versus 567” for the Z7P comparison.
errors.evidence: This part says: “The resulting Z7P comparison is in Table 8: QX2 scores 567 bits, the early-stopped neural net 440 and the Bayesian neural net 623.” Earlier notes also recorded: “Z7P/Table8 recorded Bayesian NN 623 vs QX2 567.”
errors.explanation: If the conclusion’s comparison is meant to be with the Bayesian neural net, it uses 440 incorrectly; Table 8 gives 440 for the early-stopped neural net and 623 for the Bayesian neural net.

final_notes:

errors.evidence: This part says: “The resulting Z7P comparison is in Table 8: QX2 scores 567 bits, the early-stopped neural net 440 and the Bayesian neural net 623.” Earlier notes also recorded: “Z7P/Table8 recorded Bayesian NN 623 vs QX2 567.”
errors.explanation: If the conclusion’s comparison is meant to be with the Bayesian neural net, it uses 440 incorrectly; Table 8 gives 440 for the early-stopped neural net and 623 for the Bayesian neural net.

grade.reason: Review item 3 explicitly flags the claim that Bayesian nets perform worse than QX2 on Z7P and cites Table 8 showing Bayesian=623 vs QX2=567 with a higher-is-better metric, which contradicts the planted claim.

errors.claim: ImageNet dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: For other color image rows, dimensionality includes color channels: e.g. “3072 (32 × 32 color)” for SVHN/CIFAR, which equals 32×32×3. But 256×256 color would be 256×256×3 = 196608, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality 65536 corresponds to 256×256 grayscale/single-channel, contradicting the parenthetical description “color” and the table’s own convention for color images.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer net the error reduces from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.location: this part, TIMIT text before Table 7
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) … 20.7” and “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers) … 20.5”; the dropout 8-layer result is 19.7.
errors.explanation: The text attributes the 20.5% baseline to the 8-layer net, but the table shows the 8-layer DBN-pretrained NN baseline is 20.7%. The 20.5% value belongs to a different 5-layer mcRBM-DBN-pretrained model.

errors.claim: “dropout improves significantly upon the performance of standard neural nets and outperforms all other methods.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says “Bayesian neural nets perform better than dropout,” and Table 8 reports Neural Network with dropout = 567 while Bayesian Neural Network = 623, with higher being better.
errors.explanation: Taken literally, dropout does not outperform all other methods in Table 8 because the Bayesian Neural Network scores higher. The sentence is only consistent if “all other methods” is intended to exclude Bayesian neural networks, but it does not say that.

errors.claim: “P(hj = 1 | rj, v) = 1(rj = 1) σ(bj + Σi Wij vi)” and “P(vi = 1 | h) = σ(ai + Σj Wij hj)”
errors.evidence: The RBM was defined just above as P(h, v; θ) ∝ exp(vᵀWh + aᵀh + bᵀv), where a is the hidden bias vector and b is the visible bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated energy/probability form, hidden-unit conditionals should use the hidden bias a_j, and visible-unit conditionals should use the visible bias b_i. The displayed conditional equations swap a and b, conflicting with the model definition and their dimensions.

errors.claim: “The CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 data sets consists of 50,000 training and 10,000 test images each.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Table 1: “CIFAR 3072 60K/10K.”
errors.explanation: The appendix says CIFAR has 50,000 training examples, while the earlier table was recorded as saying 60,000 training examples for CIFAR.

final_notes:
Paper: Dropout JMLR 2014. Dropout drops units/connections during training; p=retain prob, hidden often .5, inputs closer to 1 (.8 typical). Test approx: unthinned net with outgoing weights ×p; inverted dropout scales retained activations 1/p during training. Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Abstract/main claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping units/connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Training samples an exponential number of “thinned” networks. At test time, approximate averaging predictions of all thinned nets using one unthinned network with smaller weights. Claims significant reductions in overfitting and improvements over other regularization methods on vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks.

Intro: Deep nets expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing regularization: early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Bayesian gold standard would average over parameter settings weighted by posterior; dropout aims to approximate this with less computation by using an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Model combination helps but separately training/testing many large nets is expensive; diverse nets require different architectures or data subsets.

Dropout definition: “dropping out” hidden or visible units means temporarily removing the unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Units are randomly retained independently with probability p. p chosen by validation or often 0.5, near optimal for many networks/tasks; input-unit retention probability usually closer to 1. Figure 1 shows standard vs dropout network. Figure 2: at training a unit present with probability p and weights w to next layer; at test unit always present and outgoing weights multiplied by p, so test output equals expected training output.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims/definition: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameters remain O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net, so training can be viewed as training 2^n shared-weight nets, each rarely trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. This approximate averaging is claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Broader scope: Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. graphical models/Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine and compares to standard RBMs; claims dropout RBMs are better in certain respects.

Paper structure: Sec2 motivation; Sec3 previous work; Sec4 formal dropout model; Sec5 training algorithm; Sec6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec7 effects on network properties and hyperparameters; Sec8 Dropout RBM; Sec9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide/hyperparameter considerations.

Motivation section: Dropout is motivated by sexual reproduction/evolution: genes must work with random subsets of other genes, discouraging complex co-adaptations and promoting robust, independently useful features. Also motivated by “conspiracies”: many small co-adaptations generalize better under changing/non-stationary conditions than one large fragile co-adaptation. Notes that hidden units will still learn different things; simply duplicating units would be a poor solution, like replica codes for noisy channels.

Broader scope/structure: Applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. dropout RBMs (claimed better in some respects). Sections: 3 related work; 4 formal model; 5 training; 6 experiments; 7 effects/hyperparameters; 8 Dropout RBM; 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A guide. Sec3 begins: dropout can be interpreted as regularizing a neural net by adding noise to hidden units; relates to Denoising Autoencoders adding noise to unit states.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava et al.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible/input units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Dropping out 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units often optimal. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test; Sec4 states W_test^(l)=p W^(l). This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Resulting net used without dropout.

Related work/motivation: Related to denoising autoencoders, which add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically use ~5% noise; dropout’s weight scaling permits much higher noise. Deterministic counterpart can be obtained by marginalizing dropout noise in simple cases; related to van der Maaten et al. “blankout noise” (inputs only/no hidden layers), Wang & Manning speeding up dropout by marginalizing noise, Chen et al. marginalizing DAEs. Adversarial dropping work fixes max units dropped but no hidden units.

Sec4 formalism: Standard layer: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), ỹ^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then next layer uses ỹ. Backprop derivatives through sampled sub-network.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014). Dropout: randomly drop hidden or visible/input units and connections during training; retained independently with probability p (often hidden p=0.5; inputs closer to 1; common optimal: 20% input, 50% hidden dropped). Each training case samples a thinned net; n units imply 2^n thinned nets with shared weights.

Test-time approximation: use one unthinned net without dropout, with trained outgoing weights multiplied by p: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), so expected training-time unit output equals test-time output.

Sec4 formalism: standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses ỹ^(l)=r*y; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Related work: dropout compared to denoising autoencoders, blankout/marginalized noise, adversarial dropping; dropout extends noise to hidden layers/supervised/model averaging/various architectures and allows high noise via weight scaling.

Sec5 training: SGD as usual except each training case in mini-batch uses sampled thinned net; parameters unused by a case get zero gradient; gradients averaged over mini-batch. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weights to hidden unit ||w||2≤c, projecting to ball radius c; c tuned on validation; helps even without dropout. Dropout + max-norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives boost.

Pretraining: can finetune pretrained nets with dropout; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. Smaller finetuning LRs preserve pretrained information; improves final generalization vs finetuning without dropout.

Experiments intro: classification across MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Claim: dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout nets; details in Appendix B.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), but test-time uses no removals and scaled weights \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*y)+b)]\) is not generally equal to \(f(p\mathbf w y+b)\). The equations only make the expected preactivation/input contribution match, not the hidden unit’s expected output.

Paper: Dropout JMLR 2014. Dropout randomly removes units/connections during training; test uses one unthinned net with weights scaled p (T6R) to approximate averaging; preserves expected preactivation. Typical p hidden≈0.5/input≈0.8; speech/image inputs often 0.8. Dropout SGD samples thinned net per case; unused params zero gradient; high momentum, large decaying LR, max-norm. §2 motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction: recombination breaks large co-adapted gene sets yet may favor genes that work with random partners, robustness, and reduced barriers to spread of useful genes. Dropout-trained hidden units likewise face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful robust features instead of relying on other units to fix mistakes; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes in noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies more robust than one large conspiracy under changing/non-stationary conditions; complex co-adaptations may fit training data but fail on test data more readily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

§3 related work: dropout as noise in hidden-unit states, extending denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) from input corruption/clean reconstruction to effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised+unsupervised use, and architectures like Boltzmann Machines. Test-time weight scaling/approximation permits higher noise than typically best for DAEs. Table: DAE typical best noise 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; hidden-unit removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise minimizes expected loss; adversarial removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) choose removals subject to max number and have no hidden units. Marginalizing dropout can yield deterministic regularizers in simple cases. Exponential-family input-noise/“blankout noise” regularizers studied by van der Maaten et al. 2013, limited to no hidden layers; Chen et al. 2012 marginalized DAEs; Wang & Manning 2013 proposed marginalization to accelerate dropout.

final_notes:
Paper: Dropout random thinned shared-weight nets; p retention; original test scales outgoing weights by p. Inverted dropout scales retained activations 1/p during training, no test scaling. Training 2–3× longer; marginalizing noise gives modified L2 for linear regression.

Known inconsistencies: Table 1 ImageNet dim 65536 vs “256×256 color” (196608). TIMIT prose says 8-layer drops 20.5→19.7, table says baseline 20.7. Alt splicing text says dropout outperforms every listed method, but table has dropout NN 567 vs Bayesian NN 623. Sec8 RBM joint uses a^T h, b^T v but conditionals swap biases.

Key results: MNIST best dropout+maxnorm ReLU 2×8192 0.95; DBM+dropout 0.79. SVHN best dropout all conv 2.55; maxout 2.47. CIFAR-10/100 dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. ImageNet 2012 avg 5 dropout ConvNets val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4. Reuters best-network error 31.05 without dropout vs 29.62 with. Gaussian dropout N(1,σ²), σ=sqrt((1-p)/p); Table 10 MNIST Bernoulli 1.08±0.04 vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04, CIFAR 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1.

Appendix B: MNIST held out 10k validation, then trained combined 1M updates; p hidden .5/input .8, momentum .95. SVHN/CIFAR similar conv architecture. TIMIT: Kaldi log-filter banks, 21 frames, no speaker-dependent op, normalized; p input .8/hidden .5, c=4, momentum .95, LR .1; DBN finetune best LR about .01 and maxnorm no help. Reuters subset 402,738 docs, 2000 words, 50 classes, equal train/test. Alt splicing: 3665 exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissues, 3 states; dropout 2×1024, p hidden .5/input .7, 5 folds.

Paper summary: Dropout reduces overfitting in large neural nets without training/using many separate networks. During training it randomly removes units and connections, sampling many smaller shared-weight networks. At test time, a single full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble predictions. Reported improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Paper compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks; examines learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging. Dropout RBMs learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout with multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation noted: dropout networks typically take 2–3x longer to train than standard networks with the same architecture.

Training randomly removes units and incoming/outgoing connections, sampling many shared-weight thinned networks; test usually uses one full network with outgoing weights scaled by retention probability p to approximate ensemble predictions. p is defined here as retention probability, though glossary labels it “dropout rate / retention probability.” Reported improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Comparisons include other regularizers (L1/L2, max-norm, KL sparsity, etc.), Bayesian neural networks, SVM/logistic/ridge/PCA baselines, and methods such as stochastic pooling/maxout in cited image experiments.
