Dropout RBMs use binary variables retaining hidden units and are trained with CD-1; they learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression/Tikhonov-style objective in expectation; logistic regression approximate marginalization is also mentioned. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout with multiplicative Gaussian noise matched by mean/variance/entropy. Alternative-splicing task uses RNA features and Code Quality, described as negative KL divergence where higher is better; target can be softmax with three states. Image terms: conv nets with convolutional/max-pooling/fully connected layers; preprocessing includes global contrast normalization and ZCA whitening; metrics include ImageNet top-1/top-5. Limitation noted: dropout networks typically take 2–3x longer to train than standard networks with same architecture.

final_notes: Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. QX2/dropout gates units during training; test uses full net with outgoing weights scaled by retention p. Claims lower generalization error across varied classification problems; improves over no-dropout on every tested dataset; usually 2–3× training time. Conclusion claims QX2 methods attain SOTA on A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z and improve other domains. Definitions: O3U=L1, Y5F=L2, V9C=max-norm, U2L=RBM, B8T=Dropout RBM, E5Q=DBM, F3N=ReLU, L8J=maxout, G6W=DBN/stacked RBM init, X9M=sampled averaging, T6R=weight scaling approximation, P7V=Bernoulli dropout, D4K=Gaussian dropout. Pretraining with QX2: multiply pretrained weights by 1/p. Known internal errors: Table 1 K9D row says 65536 = “256×256 color” though color would be ×3; N8Q prose uses 20.5% as deeper pretrained baseline but Table 7’s 8-layer G6W baseline is 20.7%; §6 summary says “Table 2, 1.60 versus 1.35” evidences QX2, but table has 1.35 as V9C without QX2; §8.1 RBM energy biases swapped in conditionals. Key results: H4Z best E5Q+QX2 0.79; A2F L8J 2.47, QX2 all conv 2.55; J3V QX2 all 12.61, L8J 11.68; W6R QX2 all 37.20, L8J 38.57; K9D Avg 5 ConvNets+QX2 38.1 val top-1, 16.4 top-5. N8Q Table7: NN 23.4→21.8; G6W 4-layer 22.7→19.7; 8-layer 20.7→19.7. M5X 31.05→29.62. Z7P/C4Y: early-stopped NN 440, QX2 567, Bayesian NN 623 bits; same 5 folds as Xiong et al.; QX2 two 1024 layers vs Bayesian “few tens.”

grade.reason: None of the reported errors address the planted dropout/CIFAR-10 claim or the contradictory Table 4 evidence showing CIFAR-10 improves with all-layer dropout.

errors.claim: “These data sets include different image types and training set sizes, with SVHN smaller than MNIST.”
errors.location: this part, Section 6.1 Results on Image Data Sets
errors.evidence: Table 1 lists MNIST training/test sets as 60K/10K and SVHN as 600K/26K.
errors.explanation: The table shows SVHN has both a larger training set and a larger test set than MNIST, so the claim that SVHN is smaller than MNIST conflicts with the paper’s own dataset overview.

errors.claim: ImageNet dimensionality is listed as “65536 (256 × 256 color).”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image would have 256×256 pixels with multiple color channels, whereas 65536 equals only 256×256.
errors.explanation: Within the same table entry, the stated dimensionality corresponds to a single-channel 256×256 image, not a color image as described.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer net the error reduces from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.location: this part, Sec. 6.2 Results on TIMIT
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” as 20.7, and “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) + dropout” as 19.7. The 20.5 value belongs to “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers)” in Table 7.
errors.explanation: The prose says the 8-layer net without dropout has 20.5% error, but the table gives 20.7% for the 8-layer baseline; 20.5% is a different 5-layer model.

errors.claim: “P(hj = 1|rj, v) = 1(rj = 1) σ(bj + Σi Wij vi)” and “P(vi = 1|h) = σ(ai + Σj Wij hj)”
errors.evidence: The model was just defined as “P(h, v; θ) = 1/Z(θ) exp(vᵀWh + aᵀh + bᵀv),” where θ = {W, a, b}. Thus a is the hidden-unit bias and b is the visible-unit bias.
errors.explanation: The conditional distributions swap the roles of a and b. Given the stated joint distribution, P(hj=1|v) should use the hidden bias aj, and P(vi=1|h) should use the visible bias bi.

errors.claim: “The CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 data sets consists of 50,000 training and 10,000 test images each.”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 1 notes: “CIFAR-10/100 3072 60K/10K.”
errors.explanation: This appendix states CIFAR-10/100 have 50,000 training images, while the earlier data table recorded 60,000 training images for the same datasets.

final_notes:
Paper: Dropout JMLR 2014. Dropout drops units during training; retain prob p; test uses full net with outgoing weights ×p. Equivalent inverted dropout: retained activations ×1/p at train and no test scaling. Max-norm useful; pretrained weights scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning.

Data Table 1: MNIST 784 60K/10K; SVHN 3072 600K/26K; CIFAR-10/100 3072 60K/10K; ImageNet 65536, 1.2M/150K; TIMIT 2520 1.1M/58K; Reuters 2000 200K/200K; Alt Splicing 1014 2932/733. Prior inconsistencies: SVHN called smaller than MNIST despite table; ImageNet dimensionality conflicts with “color”; Appendix B.3 says CIFAR-10/100 have 50K train/10K test, conflicting with Table 1’s 60K/10K.

Key results: MNIST best DBM+dropout 0.79. SVHN dropout all 2.55, maxout 2.47. CIFAR-10 dropout all 12.61, maxout 11.68. CIFAR-100 dropout all 37.20, maxout 38.57. ImageNet Avg 5 ConvNets+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top-5 16.4. TIMIT Table 7: 8-layer DBN-pretrained 20.7, +dropout 19.7; prose inconsistency says 20.5 to 19.7. Reuters no-dropout 31.05%, dropout 29.62%. Alt Splicing bits higher better: dropout NN 567, Bayesian NN 623.

Sec7: MNIST p≈0.4–0.8 good; no gains tiny data. Sec7.5: MC sampled nets reaches weight-scaling around k=50; weight scaling good approximation. Sec8 prior inconsistency swapped RBM biases in conditionals. Sec9–10: marginalizing dropout gives deterministic regularization; Gaussian noise σ²=(1−p)/p comparable.

Appendix: MNIST validation/recombine; SVHN p=(.9,.75,.75,.5,.5,.5), c=4; TIMIT input p=.8 hidden .5, c=4, DBN dropout finetune LR .01; Reuters subset 402,738 equal split; Alt Splicing p hidden .5/input .7.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Abstract/main claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping units/connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Training samples an exponential number of “thinned” networks. At test time, approximate averaging predictions of all thinned nets using one unthinned network with smaller weights. Claims significant reductions in overfitting and improvements over other regularization methods on vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks.

Intro: Deep nets expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing regularization: early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Bayesian gold standard would average over parameter settings weighted by posterior; dropout aims to approximate this with less computation by using an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Model combination helps but separately training/testing many large nets is expensive; diverse nets require different architectures or data subsets.

Dropout definition: “dropping out” hidden or visible units means temporarily removing the unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Units are randomly retained independently with probability p. p chosen by validation or often 0.5, near optimal for many networks/tasks; input-unit retention probability usually closer to 1. Figure 1 shows standard vs dropout network. Figure 2: at training a unit present with probability p and weights w to next layer; at test unit always present and outgoing weights multiplied by p, so test output equals expected training output.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims/definition: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameters remain O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net, so training can be viewed as training 2^n shared-weight nets, each rarely trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. This approximate averaging is claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Broader scope: Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. graphical models/Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine and compares to standard RBMs; claims dropout RBMs are better in certain respects.

Paper structure: Sec2 motivation; Sec3 previous work; Sec4 formal dropout model; Sec5 training algorithm; Sec6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec7 effects on network properties and hyperparameters; Sec8 Dropout RBM; Sec9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide/hyperparameter considerations.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Motivation section: Dropout is motivated by sexual reproduction/evolution: genes must work with random subsets of other genes, discouraging complex co-adaptations and promoting robust, independently useful features. Also motivated by “conspiracies”: many small co-adaptations generalize better under changing/non-stationary conditions than one large fragile co-adaptation. Notes that hidden units will still learn different things; simply duplicating units would be a poor solution, like replica codes for noisy channels.

Broader scope/structure: Applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. dropout RBMs (claimed better in some respects). Sections: 3 related work; 4 formal model; 5 training; 6 experiments; 7 effects/hyperparameters; 8 Dropout RBM; 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A guide. Sec3 begins: dropout can be interpreted as regularizing a neural net by adding noise to hidden units; relates to Denoising Autoencoders adding noise to unit states.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava et al.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible/input units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Dropping out 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units often optimal. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test; Sec4 states W_test^(l)=p W^(l). This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Resulting net used without dropout.

Related work/motivation: Related to denoising autoencoders, which add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically use ~5% noise; dropout’s weight scaling permits much higher noise. Deterministic counterpart can be obtained by marginalizing dropout noise in simple cases; related to van der Maaten et al. “blankout noise” (inputs only/no hidden layers), Wang & Manning speeding up dropout by marginalizing noise, Chen et al. marginalizing DAEs. Adversarial dropping work fixes max units dropped but no hidden units.

Sec4 formalism: Standard layer: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), ỹ^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then next layer uses ỹ. Backprop derivatives through sampled sub-network.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014). Dropout: randomly drop hidden or visible/input units and connections during training; retained independently with probability p (often hidden p=0.5; inputs closer to 1; common optimal: 20% input, 50% hidden dropped). Each training case samples a thinned net; n units imply 2^n thinned nets with shared weights.

Test-time approximation: use one unthinned net without dropout, with trained outgoing weights multiplied by p: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), so expected training-time unit output equals test-time output.

Sec4 formalism: standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses ỹ^(l)=r*y; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Related work: dropout compared to denoising autoencoders, blankout/marginalized noise, adversarial dropping; dropout extends noise to hidden layers/supervised/model averaging/various architectures and allows high noise via weight scaling.

Sec5 training: SGD as usual except each training case in mini-batch uses sampled thinned net; parameters unused by a case get zero gradient; gradients averaged over mini-batch. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weights to hidden unit ||w||2≤c, projecting to ball radius c; c tuned on validation; helps even without dropout. Dropout + max-norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives boost.

Pretraining: can finetune pretrained nets with dropout; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. Smaller finetuning LRs preserve pretrained information; improves final generalization vs finetuning without dropout.

Experiments intro: classification across MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Claim: dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout nets; details in Appendix B.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), but test-time uses no removals and scaled weights \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). It also says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*y)+b)]\) is not generally equal to \(f(p\mathbf w y+b)\). The equations only make the expected preactivation/input contribution match, not the hidden unit’s expected output.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier model equations in notes: with dropout, gates are applied before the next affine transform, then activation: “\(\tilde y^{(l)}=r^{(l)}*y^{(l)}\), then \(z_i=w_i\tilde y+b_i\), \(y_i=f(z_i)\).” Notes also record the caveat that equality under scaling is supported for expected preactivation/input contribution, not generally for nonlinear output.
errors.explanation: Multiplying weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation contribution match the pretrained preactivation, but with a nonlinear activation \(f\), it does not in general make the expected unit output match the pretrained output. This repeats/conflicts with the earlier equations unless “output” is meant imprecisely as input/preactivation.

§2 motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction: recombination breaks large co-adapted gene sets yet may favor genes that work with random partners, robustness, and reduced barriers to spread of useful genes. Dropout-trained hidden units likewise face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful robust features instead of relying on other units to fix mistakes; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes in noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies more robust than one large conspiracy under changing/non-stationary conditions; complex co-adaptations may fit training data but fail on test data more readily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958; authors Srivastava et al. Core claims: dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned nets; at test time one unthinned net with reduced/scaled weights approximates averaged predictions/geometric mean. Claims reduced overfitting, improvements vs other regularizers, SOTA on many benchmarks. Intro: n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets with O(n^2) or fewer parameters; new thinned net sampled for each case, each model trained rarely/never. Applies beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models/RBMs. §2 motivation: sexual reproduction analogy—random partners encourage robust independently useful features; replication of units poor robustness; conspiracy analogy: many small/simple co-adaptations more robust than one large/complex one under changing conditions.

§3 related work: dropout as noise in hidden-unit states, extending denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) from input corruption/clean reconstruction to effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised+unsupervised use, and architectures like Boltzmann Machines. Test-time weight scaling/approximation permits higher noise than typically best for DAEs. Table: DAE typical best noise 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; hidden-unit removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise minimizes expected loss; adversarial removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) choose removals subject to max number and have no hidden units. Marginalizing dropout can yield deterministic regularizers in simple cases. Exponential-family input-noise/“blankout noise” regularizers studied by van der Maaten et al. 2013, limited to no hidden layers; Chen et al. 2012 marginalized DAEs; Wang & Manning 2013 proposed marginalization to accelerate dropout.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), but test-time uses no removals and scaled weights \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). It also says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*y)+b)]\) is not generally equal to \(f(p\mathbf w y+b)\). The equations only make the expected preactivation/input contribution match, not the hidden unit’s expected output.

grade.reason: Review item 3 correctly identifies that the paper's claim 'A2F smaller than H4Z' contradicts Table 1 which shows A2F (~600K) is larger than H4Z (~60K).

errors.claim: “with SVHN smaller than MNIST”
errors.evidence: Table 1 lists MNIST training/test sets as 60K/10K and SVHN as 600K/26K.
errors.explanation: By the table’s own dataset sizes, SVHN is larger than MNIST, not smaller.

errors.claim: ImageNet dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: The same cell describes the input as “256 × 256 color.” For color images, the dimensionality implied by 256 × 256 × 3 is 196,608, not 65,536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the parenthetical description if color means three channels, as it does elsewhere in the same table for 32 × 32 color = 3072.

errors.claim: “The best convolutional networks without dropout achieve 3.95% error.”
errors.evidence: Table 3 lists “Conv Net + stochastic pooling (Zeiler and Fergus, 2013) | 2.80” and does not describe it as using dropout.
errors.explanation: Within the same table, a convolutional network without any stated dropout has 2.80% error, which is better than 3.95%. Therefore 3.95% cannot be the best convolutional result without dropout as stated.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” as 20.7 and “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) + dropout” as 19.7. The 20.5 value belongs to “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The prose uses 20.5% as the non-dropout baseline for the 8-layer pretrained network, but the table gives the 8-layer baseline as 20.7%; 20.5% is a different 5-layer mcRBM-DBN model.

errors.claim: “dropout ... outperforms every other method listed.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 lists “Bayesian Neural Network” with 623 bits and “Neural Network with dropout” with 567 bits; the same paragraph also says “Bayesian networks perform better than dropout.”
errors.explanation: Since higher Code Quality is better, dropout does not outperform every other listed method; it is worse than the Bayesian Neural Network row.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)= 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j+∑_i W_{ij}v_i)” and “P(v_i=1\mid h)=σ(a_i+∑_j W_{ij}h_j)”
errors.evidence: The RBM distribution was defined just above as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), with parameters θ={W,a,b}. Thus a is the hidden-bias vector and b is the visible-bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional distributions swap the biases: the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias a_j, and the visible conditional should use the visible bias b_i. As written, the conditionals conflict with the model definition and even the implied dimensions of a and b.

errors.claim: “This form essentially scales the cost on weight \(w_i\) by the standard deviation of data dimension \(i\).”
errors.evidence: The penalty is defined using \(\Gamma=\left(\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X)\right)^{1/2}\), so the cost on \(w_i\) is based on \(\sqrt{\sum_n X_{ni}^2}\), not on the centered standard deviation of dimension \(i\).
errors.explanation: The displayed formula uses the uncentered L2 norm/root sum of squares of each feature column. That is not the standard deviation unless additional centering/scaling assumptions are made, which are not stated here.

errors.claim: “Dropout improved classification accuracy across all the many architectures tried.”
errors.evidence: The same subsection’s claims/evidence says: “The best-network comparison is 31.05% without dropout and 29.62% with dropout.”
errors.explanation: If these percentages are accuracies, dropout’s value is lower, not improved. The statement would only be consistent if the percentages were error rates, but this part calls the metric classification accuracy.

ImageNet Table 1 listed 65536 “256×256 color” dimension inconsistency. SVHN text claimed best convnets without dropout 3.95, but Table 3 has stochastic pooling convnet 2.80. TIMIT prose says 8-layer pretrained 20.5→19.7, but Table 7 gives 20.7→19.7. Alt-splicing prose says dropout outperforms every other listed method, but Table 8 Bayesian NN 623 bits beats dropout 567. Section 8.1 RBM conditionals swap biases. Section 9.1 says penalty scales by standard deviation, but Gamma=(diag X^T X)^1/2 is uncentered column norm. Reuters B.5 says dropout improved classification accuracy, but associated best-network figures are 31.05% without vs 29.62% with dropout, which is inconsistent if they are accuracies.

errors.claim: “Dropout improved classification accuracy across all the many architectures tried.”
errors.evidence: The same subsection’s claims/evidence says: “The best-network comparison is 31.05% without dropout and 29.62% with dropout.”
errors.explanation: If these percentages are accuracies, dropout’s value is lower, not improved. The statement would only be consistent if the percentages were error rates, but this part calls the metric classification accuracy.

grade.reason: The first reported error directly contradicts the planted claim by citing Table 1 which shows SVHN (~600K) is larger than MNIST (~60K).

errors.claim: “The five vision collections differ in image type and training-set size, with A2F smaller than H4Z.”
errors.evidence: Table 1 lists H4Z training set = 60K and test set = 10K, while A2F training set = 600K and test set = 26K.
errors.explanation: According to the paper’s own table, A2F is larger than H4Z in both training and test set size, not smaller.

errors.claim: “K9D (ILSVRC-2012) | Vision | 65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: The table describes K9D as “256 × 256 color” but gives dimensionality 65536.
errors.explanation: A 256 × 256 color image has 256×256×3 = 196608 values if represented with three color channels; 65536 corresponds only to 256×256 single-channel data. The dimensionality conflicts with the parenthetical description.

errors.claim: K9D contains over 15 million labeled high-resolution images in roughly 22,000 categories.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from §6/Table 1: “K9D ImageNet 65536 ‘256×256 color’ 1.2M/150K.” This part also says ILSVRC “uses a subset with roughly 1000 images in each of 1000 categories.”
errors.explanation: The paper’s earlier dataset table treated K9D as the evaluated ImageNet/ILSVRC dataset with about 1.2M training and 150K test examples, not the full 15M-image, 22K-category ImageNet collection. If K9D is the same dataset identifier, the size/category description is inconsistent.

errors.claim: For the 8-layer pretrained network, the pre-QX2 error is 20.5%.
errors.evidence: Table 7 in this part lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) … 20.7” and separately lists “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) … 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The prose uses 20.5% as the baseline for the 8-layer pretrained network, but the table’s 8-layer G6W baseline is 20.7%; 20.5% belongs to a different 5-layer mcRBM-G6W model.

errors.claim: “The QX2 gain is absent for the smallest sets”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record the paper’s claim: “QX2 improves over no-dropout on every tested dataset.”
errors.explanation: If the QX2 gain is absent for the smallest data sets, then QX2 does not improve over no-dropout on every tested data set. This contradicts the earlier global claim unless the paper later qualifies one of the statements.

errors.claim: Hidden conditional: “P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + ∑_i W_ij v_i)” and visible conditional: “P(v_i=1 | h)=σ(a_i+∑_j W_ij h_j).”
errors.evidence: The RBM joint distribution in the same section is defined as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), so a is the hidden bias vector and b is the visible bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias a_j, and the visible conditional should use the visible bias b_i. The formulas swap a and b, conflicting with the model definition.

errors.claim: “Each collection contains 50,000 training and 10,000 test images.”
errors.location: this part, B.3 J3V and W6R
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Dataset Table 1: “J3V/W6R CIFAR 3072 60K/10K.”
errors.explanation: This part says the CIFAR collections have 50,000 training images, but the recorded dataset table gave 60,000 training images for J3V/W6R.

errors.claim: “The resulting Z7P comparison is in Table 8: QX2 scores 567 bits, the early-stopped neural net 440 and the Bayesian neural net 623.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record the Z7P result as “Z7P 567→440,” i.e. the reported improvement goes from 567 to 440, with QX2/dropout corresponding to the improved 440-bit result rather than 567.
errors.explanation: This part appears to reverse the QX2/dropout and early-stopped neural-net Z7P scores. The earlier recorded result indicates QX2/dropout achieved 440 bits, improving over 567, not that QX2 scored 567.

final_notes:
Paper JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. QX2/dropout gates units; n units => 2^n subnetworks. Test T6R/weight scaling: full net outgoing weights scaled by retention p; X9M/MC averaging samples k thinned nets, matches T6R around k=50 then slightly better within 1 SD; k→∞ true average. Training usually 2–3× standard net. Defaults: O3U=L1, Y5F=L2, U2L=RBM, B8T=Dropout RBM, E5Q/DBM, G6W=DBN, F3N=ReLU, L8J=maxout, V9C=max-norm incoming weights ≤c. Appendix A heuristics: width ≥n/p; LR 10–100×; momentum .95–.99; V9C c 3–4; hidden p .5–.8; real inputs p≈.8; pretrained weights ×1/p before dropout finetuning.

Dataset Table1: H4Z MNIST 784 60K/10K; A2F SVHN 3072 600K/26K; J3V/W6R CIFAR 3072 60K/10K; K9D ImageNet 65536 “256×256 color” 1.2M/150K; N8Q TIMIT 2520 1.1M/58K; M5X Reuters 2000 200K/200K; Z7P splicing 1014 2932/733. Prior conflicts: A2F called smaller than H4Z; K9D dimension inconsistent with 256×256 color and later 15M/22K; N8Q prose 20.5 vs table 19.7; B.3 says J3V/W6R 50K train vs Table1 60K.

Results: H4Z best .79; A2F 2.47; K9D top-5 16.4; J3V 11.68, W6R 37.20; Table7 23.4 vs 21.8; M5X 31.05→29.62; Z7P 567→440, so current part’s claim QX2=567/early-stopped=440 appears reversed. Table9 H4Z regularizers: QX2+V9C 1.05 best.

Appendix: B.1 H4Z validation 10K, final combined-data. B.2 A2F validation 6000, conv 96/128/256 + two FC 2048, p=(.9,.75,.75,.5,.5,.5), c=4. B.3 CIFAR validation 5K, contrast norm+ZCA, A2F architecture. B.4 N8Q 21 frames, p input .8/hidden .5, c=4, momentum .95, high LR .1, pretrained finetune LR ~.01, V9C no improvement. B.5 M5X subset 402,738 docs, 50 disjoint classes, single-label. B.6 Z7P 3665 exons, 1014 features, four tissue softmaxes ×3 states, two 1024 layers, p hidden .5/input .7, 5 folds.

Intro: Deep nets expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing regularization: early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Bayesian gold standard would average over parameter settings weighted by posterior; dropout aims to approximate this with less computation by using an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Model combination helps but separately training/testing many large nets is expensive; diverse nets require different architectures or data subsets.

Dropout definition: “dropping out” hidden or visible units means temporarily removing the unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Units are randomly retained independently with probability p. p chosen by validation or often 0.5, near optimal for many networks/tasks; input-unit retention probability usually closer to 1. Figure 1 shows standard vs dropout network. Figure 2: at training a unit present with probability p and weights w to next layer; at test unit always present and outgoing weights multiplied by p, so test output equals expected training output.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims/definition: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameters remain O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net, so training can be viewed as training 2^n shared-weight nets, each rarely trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. This approximate averaging is claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Broader scope: Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. graphical models/Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine and compares to standard RBMs; claims dropout RBMs are better in certain respects.

Motivation section: Dropout is motivated by sexual reproduction/evolution: genes must work with random subsets of other genes, discouraging complex co-adaptations and promoting robust, independently useful features. Also motivated by “conspiracies”: many small co-adaptations generalize better under changing/non-stationary conditions than one large fragile co-adaptation. Notes that hidden units will still learn different things; simply duplicating units would be a poor solution, like replica codes for noisy channels.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava et al.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible/input units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Dropping out 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units often optimal. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test; Sec4 states W_test^(l)=p W^(l). This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Resulting net used without dropout.

Related work/motivation: Related to denoising autoencoders, which add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically use ~5% noise; dropout’s weight scaling permits much higher noise. Deterministic counterpart can be obtained by marginalizing dropout noise in simple cases; related to van der Maaten et al. “blankout noise” (inputs only/no hidden layers), Wang & Manning speeding up dropout by marginalizing noise, Chen et al. marginalizing DAEs. Adversarial dropping work fixes max units dropped but no hidden units.

Sec4 formalism: Standard layer: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), ỹ^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then next layer uses ỹ. Backprop derivatives through sampled sub-network.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014). Dropout: randomly drop hidden or visible/input units and connections during training; retained independently with probability p (often hidden p=0.5; inputs closer to 1; common optimal: 20% input, 50% hidden dropped). Each training case samples a thinned net; n units imply 2^n thinned nets with shared weights.

Test-time approximation: use one unthinned net without dropout, with trained outgoing weights multiplied by p: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), so expected training-time unit output equals test-time output.

Sec4 formalism: standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses ỹ^(l)=r*y; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Related work: dropout compared to denoising autoencoders, blankout/marginalized noise, adversarial dropping; dropout extends noise to hidden layers/supervised/model averaging/various architectures and allows high noise via weight scaling.

Sec5 training: SGD as usual except each training case in mini-batch uses sampled thinned net; parameters unused by a case get zero gradient; gradients averaged over mini-batch. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weights to hidden unit ||w||2≤c, projecting to ball radius c; c tuned on validation; helps even without dropout. Dropout + max-norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives boost.

Pretraining: can finetune pretrained nets with dropout; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. Smaller finetuning LRs preserve pretrained information; improves final generalization vs finetuning without dropout.

Experiments intro: classification across MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Claim: dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout nets; details in Appendix B.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), but test-time uses no removals and scaled weights \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). It also says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*y)+b)]\) is not generally equal to \(f(p\mathbf w y+b)\). The equations only make the expected preactivation/input contribution match, not the hidden unit’s expected output.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”

errors.explanation: Multiplying weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation contribution match the pretrained preactivation, but with a nonlinear activation \(f\), it does not in general make the expected unit output match the pretrained output. final_notes:
Paper: Dropout/QX2 randomly thins units during training; test uses unthinned net with weights scaled by p. Scaling preserves expected preactivation/input contributions, not generally nonlinear activations. Typical p hidden≈0.5 (Appendix: hidden 0.5–0.8; default 0.5), input≈0.8 for real-valued/image/speech; input optimum generally closer to 1 than 0.5. If standard optimal layer has n units, QX2 layer should have at least n/p units; QX2 LR often 10–100× standard, momentum 0.95–0.99; max-norm/V9C typically c=3–4. Pretraining finetuning multiplies by 1/p before dropout. Overall claim: dropout improves vs non-dropout NNs on every tested dataset; SOTA on five vision collections.

H4Z/MNIST: best reported DBM+dropout 0.79; Table 9 QX2+V9C 1.05 lowest. Appendix H4Z: c=2, p hidden .5 input .8; two smallest data sets show no QX2 improvement; gain rises then falls. SVHN/A2F: best +maxout 2.47; appendix c=4, p=(.9,.75,.75,.5,.5,.5). J3V/W6R: dropout all 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. ImageNet: 2010 conv+dropout 37.5/17.0; 2012 avg 5 conv+dropout 38.1 top1 val, 16.4 top5 val/test. Speech Table 7: pretrained+QX2 4- and 8-layer both 19.7; prose wrongly assigns 20.5 to 8-layer pre-QX2. Speech appendix: 21 frames, input p=.8 hidden p=.5, V9C c=4, momentum .95, high LR .1 decay, G6W pretraining U2L CD-1, Gaussian-U2L variance fixed 1, best QX2 finetune LR about .01; adding V9C during G6W finetuning no improvement. Practical inference: weight scaling uses one unthinned net instead of explicit exponential averaging; Monte Carlo model averaging is more expensive. §2 motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction: recombination breaks large co-adapted gene sets yet may favor genes that work with random partners, robustness, and reduced barriers to spread of useful genes. Dropout-trained hidden units likewise face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful robust features instead of relying on other units to fix mistakes; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes in noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies more robust than one large conspiracy under changing/non-stationary conditions; complex co-adaptations may fit training data but fail on test data more readily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Claims reduced overfitting, improvements vs other regularizers, SOTA on many benchmarks. Intro: n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets with O(n^2) or fewer parameters; new thinned net sampled for each case, each model trained rarely/never. Applies beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models/RBMs. §2 motivation: sexual reproduction analogy—random partners encourage robust independently useful features; replication of units poor robustness; conspiracy analogy: many small/simple co-adaptations more robust than one large/complex one under changing conditions.

§3 related work: dropout as noise in hidden-unit states, extending denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) from input corruption/clean reconstruction to effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised+unsupervised use, and architectures like Boltzmann Machines. Test-time weight scaling/approximation permits higher noise than typically best for DAEs. Table: DAE typical best noise 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; hidden-unit removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise minimizes expected loss; adversarial removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) choose removals subject to max number and have no hidden units. Marginalizing dropout can yield deterministic regularizers in simple cases. Exponential-family input-noise/“blankout noise” regularizers studied by van der Maaten et al. 2013, limited to no hidden layers; Chen et al. 2012 marginalized DAEs; Wang & Manning 2013 proposed marginalization to accelerate dropout.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), but test-time uses no removals and scaled weights \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). It also says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*y)+b)]\) is not generally equal to \(f(p\mathbf w y+b)\). The equations only make the expected preactivation/input contribution match, not the hidden unit’s expected output.

grade.reason: The reviewer’s sixth reported error points out the paper itself earlier reports M5X error 31.05% without QX2 and 29.62% with QX2, contradicting the claim that nets perform better without dropout.

sol_grade.reason: The sixth reported error identifies the planted claim and contradicts it using the reported error decrease from 31.05% without dropout to 29.62% with dropout.

errors.claim: ImageNet (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has three color channels, so the dimensionality implied by the parenthetical is 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the stated image size and color format in the same table cell.

errors.claim: “The best convolutional networks without dropout achieve 3.95% error.”
errors.location: this part, SVHN discussion after Table 3
errors.evidence: Table 3 lists “Conv Net + stochastic pooling (Zeiler and Fergus, 2013) | 2.80,” which is a convolutional network entry not described as using dropout, and has lower error than 3.95%.
errors.explanation: The text’s claim that the best convolutional networks without dropout achieve 3.95% conflicts with the table’s lower non-dropout convolutional result of 2.80%, unless the claim was meant only for the authors’ max-pooling architecture, which it does not say.

errors.claim: “Dropout improves the max-pooling network: Table 3, ‘Conv Net + max-pooling,’ 3.95%; dropout in fully connected layers, 3.02%; dropout in all layers, 2.55%.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes for Table 3: “Conv Net + max-pooling 3.95; +dropout FC 3.02; Conv Net + stochastic pooling 2.80; +dropout all layers 2.55; maxout 2.47.”
errors.explanation: The 2.55% all-layer dropout result was recorded as following the stochastic-pooling convolutional net, not the max-pooling network. This part characterizes it as a max-pooling-network result, conflicting with the earlier Table 3 notes.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” as 20.7%, and “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) + dropout” as 19.7%. The 20.5% value belongs to “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The prose assigns the 20.5% baseline to the 8-layer pretrained network, but the table assigns 20.7% to that model and 20.5% to a different 5-layer mcRBM-DBN model.

errors.claim: “dropout substantially improves standard neural networks and outperforms every other method listed.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says “Bayesian networks perform better than dropout,” and Table 8 shows Bayesian Neural Network = 623 bits versus Neural Network with dropout = 567 bits.
errors.explanation: Since higher Code Quality is better, dropout does not outperform the Bayesian Neural Network listed in the table. The claim is only true if “other” is meant to exclude the Bayesian method, but as written it conflicts with the table and preceding sentence.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)=1(r_j=1) σ(b_j+∑_i W_{ij}v_i)” and “P(v_i=1\mid h)=σ(a_i+∑_j W_{ij}h_j)”
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same subsection the RBM distribution is defined as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), so a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the hidden conditional should use hidden bias a_j and the visible conditional should use visible bias b_i. The displayed conditional equations swap a and b.

errors.claim: On Reuters, standard networks perform better without dropout than with it.
errors.evidence: This part’s own Claims and evidence says: “Reuters error 31.05% versus 29.62%.” Earlier notes also record: “Reuters: NN 31.05, dropout 29.62.”
errors.explanation: Lower error is better, so the reported Reuters numbers show dropout performs better than the standard network, not worse.

errors.claim: “Dropout improved classification accuracy across all the many architectures tried.”
errors.evidence: The same subsection’s claims/evidence says: “The best-network comparison is 31.05% without dropout and 29.62% with dropout.”
errors.explanation: If these percentages are classification accuracies, 29.62% with dropout is lower than 31.05% without dropout, so it does not show improved accuracy. This repeats the earlier Reuters inconsistency in the notes.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=...\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same model definition, the RBM exponent is “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+ \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\)”, so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden-bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible-bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional distributions swap the biases: hidden-unit probabilities should use the hidden bias indexed by j, while visible-unit probabilities should use the visible bias indexed by i. As written, the equations use \(b_j\) for hidden units and \(a_i\) for visible units, contradicting the preceding definition of the joint distribution.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Abstract/main claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping units/connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Training samples an exponential number of “thinned” networks. At test time, approximate averaging predictions of all thinned nets using one unthinned network with smaller weights. Intro: Deep nets expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing regularization: early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Bayesian gold standard would average over parameter settings weighted by posterior; dropout aims to approximate this with less computation by using an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Model combination helps but separately training/testing many large nets is expensive; diverse nets require different architectures or data subsets.

Dropout definition: “dropping out” hidden or visible units means temporarily removing the unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Units are randomly retained independently with probability p. p chosen by validation or often 0.5, near optimal for many networks/tasks; input-unit retention probability usually closer to 1. Figure 1 shows standard vs dropout network. Figure 2: at training a unit present with probability p and weights w to next layer; at test unit always present and outgoing weights multiplied by p, so test output equals expected training output.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims/definition: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameters remain O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net, so training can be viewed as training 2^n shared-weight nets, each rarely trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. This approximate averaging is claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Broader scope: Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. graphical models/Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine and compares to standard RBMs; claims dropout RBMs are better in certain respects.

Paper structure: Sec2 motivation; Sec3 previous work; Sec4 formal dropout model; Sec5 training algorithm; Sec6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec7 effects on network properties and hyperparameters; Sec8 Dropout RBM; Sec9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide/hyperparameter considerations.

Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Motivation section: Dropout is motivated by sexual reproduction/evolution: genes must work with random subsets of other genes, discouraging complex co-adaptations and promoting robust, independently useful features. Also motivated by “conspiracies”: many small co-adaptations generalize better under changing/non-stationary conditions than one large fragile co-adaptation. Notes that hidden units will still learn different things; simply duplicating units would be a poor solution, like replica codes for noisy channels.

Broader scope/structure: Applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. dropout RBMs (claimed better in some respects). Sections: 3 related work; 4 formal model; 5 training; 6 experiments; 7 effects/hyperparameters; 8 Dropout RBM; 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A guide. Sec3 begins: dropout can be interpreted as regularizing a neural net by adding noise to hidden units; relates to Denoising Autoencoders adding noise to unit states.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava et al.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible/input units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Dropping out 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units often optimal. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test; Sec4 states W_test^(l)=p W^(l). This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Resulting net used without dropout.

Related work/motivation: Related to denoising autoencoders, which add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically use ~5% noise; dropout’s weight scaling permits much higher noise. Deterministic counterpart can be obtained by marginalizing dropout noise in simple cases; related to van der Maaten et al. “blankout noise” (inputs only/no hidden layers), Wang & Manning speeding up dropout by marginalizing noise, Chen et al. marginalizing DAEs. Adversarial dropping work fixes max units dropped but no hidden units.

Sec4 formalism: Standard layer: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), ỹ^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then next layer uses ỹ. Backprop derivatives through sampled sub-network.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014). Dropout: randomly drop hidden or visible/input units and connections during training; retained independently with probability p (often hidden p=0.5; inputs closer to 1; common optimal: 20% input, 50% hidden dropped). Each training case samples a thinned net; n units imply 2^n thinned nets with shared weights.

Test-time approximation: use one unthinned net without dropout, with trained outgoing weights multiplied by p: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), so expected training-time unit output equals test-time output.

Sec4 formalism: standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses ỹ^(l)=r*y; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Related work: dropout compared to denoising autoencoders, blankout/marginalized noise, adversarial dropping; dropout extends noise to hidden layers/supervised/model averaging/various architectures and allows high noise via weight scaling.

Sec5 training: SGD as usual except each training case in mini-batch uses sampled thinned net; parameters unused by a case get zero gradient; gradients averaged over mini-batch. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weights to hidden unit ||w||2≤c, projecting to ball radius c; c tuned on validation; helps even without dropout. Dropout + max-norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives boost.

Pretraining: can finetune pretrained nets with dropout; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. Smaller finetuning LRs preserve pretrained information; improves final generalization vs finetuning without dropout.

Experiments intro: classification across MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Claim: dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout nets; details in Appendix B.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), but test-time uses no removals and scaled weights \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). It also says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*y)+b)]\) is not generally equal to \(f(p\mathbf w y+b)\). The equations only make the expected preactivation/input contribution match, not the hidden unit’s expected output.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”

errors.explanation: Multiplying weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation contribution match the pretrained preactivation, but with a nonlinear activation \(f\), it does not in general make the expected unit output match the pretrained output. This repeats/conflicts with the earlier equations unless “output” is meant imprecisely as input/preactivation.

§2 motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction: recombination breaks large co-adapted gene sets yet may favor genes that work with random partners, robustness, and reduced barriers to spread of useful genes. Dropout-trained hidden units likewise face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful robust features instead of relying on other units to fix mistakes; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes in noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies more robust than one large conspiracy under changing/non-stationary conditions; complex co-adaptations may fit training data but fail on test data more readily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Test-time weight scaling/approximation permits higher noise than typically best for DAEs. Table: DAE typical best noise 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; hidden-unit removal 50%. Exponential-family input-noise/“blankout noise” regularizers studied by van der Maaten et al. 2013, limited to no hidden layers; Chen et al. 2012 marginalized DAEs; Wang & Manning 2013 proposed marginalization to accelerate dropout.

Dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned nets; test uses one unthinned net with reduced/scaled weights to approximate averaged predictions/geometric mean. §3: related to denoising AEs/noise/model averaging; typical optimal dropout: hidden removal 50% (retention p≈0.5), input removal 20% (retention p≈0.8), DAE noise 5%; marginalization/noise regularizer related work.

§4 model: L hidden layers; ordinary feed-forward \(z_i^{l+1}=w_i^{l+1}y^l+b_i^{l+1}\), \(y_i=f(z_i)\); any activation, example sigmoid. Dropout/QX2 operation: independent Bernoulli gates \(r_j^{(l)}\sim Bernoulli(p)\), thinned outputs \(	ilde y^{(l)}=r^{(l)}*y^{(l)}\), then \(z_i=w_i	ilde y+b_i\), backprop through sampled subnetwork; hidden and visible/input units can both be removed. Test/inference: no units removed; scale weights \(W_{test}^{(l)}=pW^{(l)}\); figures describe unit present with prob p in training, always present at test with outgoing weights pw. Potential inconsistency noted: §4 opening claims expected hidden-unit output under deletion equals test-time output under reduced weights, but with nonlinear f equations only support equality of expected preactivation/input contribution, not output.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier model equations in notes: with dropout, gates are applied before the next affine transform, then activation: “\(\tilde y^{(l)}=r^{(l)}*y^{(l)}\), then \(z_i=w_i\tilde y+b_i\), \(y_i=f(z_i)\).” Notes also record the caveat that equality under scaling is supported for expected preactivation/input contribution, not generally for nonlinear output.
errors.explanation: Multiplying weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation contribution match the pretrained preactivation, but with a nonlinear activation \(f\), it does not in general make the expected unit output match the pretrained output. This repeats/conflicts with the earlier equations unless “output” is meant imprecisely as input/preactivation.

steps.notes_before:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958; Srivastava et al. Dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned nets; test uses one unthinned net with scaled weights pW to approximate averaged predictions/geometric mean. §3: related to denoising AEs/noise/model averaging; typical optimal dropout: hidden removal 50% (p≈0.5), input removal 20% (p≈0.8), DAE noise 5%.

§4 model: independent Bernoulli gates r~Bernoulli(p), thinned outputs r*y, affine z=w(r*y)+b, activation y=f(z); hidden and visible/input units can both be removed. Test: no units removed; scale weights W_test=pW. Internal issue noted: claims that scaling preserves expected “output” are only generally true for preactivation/input contribution, not nonlinear activations.

§5 learning: dropout SGD differs by sampling a thinned net per training case; gradients averaged, unused parameter gets zero gradient for that case. Combining dropout with high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and max-norm regularization improves results. Max-norm/incoming-weight constraint: hidden-unit incoming vector ||w||₂≤c; project to radius-c ball if exceeded; c tuned on validation. §5.2: unsupervised pretraining unchanged; before dropout finetuning pretrained weights multiplied by 1/p to match expected random-removal output to pretraining output—same potential output-vs-preactivation inconsistency. Smaller finetuning learning rates preserve pretrained info; large random-init-style rates erased it. Pretraining methods include stacked RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs.

errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the parenthetical description if “color” means three channels, as it does elsewhere in the same table for 32×32 color images listed as 3072.

grade.reason: None of the reported errors point to the paper's specific false claim that the approximate marginalization results apply directly to arbitrary-depth networks or note that assumptions weaken with added layers as Section 9.2 states.

errors.claim: ImageNet (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has three color channels, so the dimensionality implied by the parenthetical is 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the stated image size and color format in the same table cell.

errors.claim: “The best convolutional networks without dropout achieve 3.95% error.”

errors.explanation: The text’s claim that the best convolutional networks without dropout achieve 3.95% conflicts with the table’s lower non-dropout convolutional result of 2.80%, unless the claim was meant only for the authors’ max-pooling architecture, which it does not say.

final_notes:
Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. QX2/dropout gates units during training; standard test scales weights by retention p; inverted scales retained activations by 1/p/no test scaling. Claims lowers generalization error across varied classification problems, improves over no-dropout on every tested dataset; usually 2–3× training time. Key defs: O3U=L1, Y5F=L2, U2L=RBM, B8T=Dropout RBM, E5Q/DBM, F3N=ReLU, L8J=maxout, G6W=DBN/stacked RBM init, V9C=max-norm, X9M=sampled averaging, T6R=weight-scaling approximation, P7V=Bernoulli, D4K=Gaussian.
Results: H4Z best E5Q+QX2 0.79; regularizers max-norm 1.35, QX2+max-norm 1.05. A2F maxout 2.47 vs QX2 all 2.55. J3V/W6R QX2 all 12.61/37.20, maxout 11.68/38.57. K9D 2010 ConvNet+QX2 37.5/17.0; 2012 single 40.7/18.2 val; avg 5 38.1/16.4 val/test top-5. TIMIT/N8Q QX2 DBNs 19.7. Docs/M5X 31.05% to 29.62%. C4Y/Z7P Table8 early-stop NN 440, NN+QX2 567, Bayesian NN 623. Z7P: QX2 uses many more hidden units than Bayesian comparison; settings table says “1000s” vs “few tens,” trained QX2 has 2 layers of 1024. Results averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al. (2011).
Appendix settings: H4Z val 10k, endpoint 1M updates, p hidden .5/input .8, momentum .95, c=2; architecture sweep. A2F val 6000, conv 96/128/256, FC 2048×2, p=(.9,.75,.75,.5,.5,.5), c=4. J3V/W6R: 50k/10k, val 5k, contrast norm+ZCA, A2F arch. N8Q: 21 frames, p input .8 hidden .5, c=4, LR .1 decay, pretrained finetune LR ~.01, no V9C improvement. Z7P: 3665 exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissues×3 states, QX2 p hidden .5/input .7, 5 folds.
Internal errors noted: K9D 65536=color; TIMIT 20.5 vs Table7 20.7; §8.1 RBM biases swapped; §9.2 arbitrary-depth applicability conflict.

Test-time T6R/weight scaling uses full network, no units removed, with weights/outgoing connections scaled by retention probability p (part 4: W_test^(l)=pW^(l) in fixed-p construction; Fig. 2 outgoing weights pw), approximating geometric mean/model averaging. Part 4 notation: L hidden layers; y^(0)=x; feedforward z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i, y=f(z); dropout gates r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), ytilde^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), backprop through sampled subnetwork; hidden and visible units can be removed. Default hidden retention near optimal; input retention usually closer to complete retention; p can be validation-selected.
Motivation: QX2 discourages co-adaptations; replication poor.

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. QX2/dropout randomly gates unit outputs/inputs during training, sampling thinned shared-parameter subnetworks; n units => 2^n nets. Test-time T6R/weight scaling uses full net with outgoing weights scaled by retention p (W_test^(l)=pW^(l)), approximating geometric mean/model averaging; MC averaging samples k thinned nets/test case and §7.5 later says ~50 samples before as good as T6R. Claims QX2 lowers generalization error vs other regularizers across varied classification problems and improves over no-dropout on every tested dataset; usually 2–3× training time. Table 9 comparison: Y5F/L2 1.62, V9C/max-norm 1.35, QX2+Y5F 1.25, QX2+V9C 1.05.
Definitions: O3U=L1, Y5F=L2, U2L=RBM, B8T=Dropout RBM, E5Q/DBM mentioned as pretraining methods. Max-norm/V9C constrains each hidden unit incoming-weight vector norm ||w||2≤c; if outside radius-c ball, project to surface; c tuned by validation. Width heuristic n/p for expected retained width pn. Default hidden retention near optimal; input retention usually closer to complete retention; p validation-selected.
Training: backprop through sampled subnetworks; each case has its own sampled net; unused parameter contributes zero gradient. Momentum, annealed/large learning rates, Y5F useful. High LR/momentum and max-norm said to boost QX2; Appendix A.2: LR often 10–100× standard-net optimum, momentum ~0.95–0.99. Weight-space exploration account proposed, not numerically established here.
Pretraining: unchanged; QX2 finetuning with smaller LR preserves pretrained info. Before QX2 finetuning, multiply pretrained weights by 1/p to match expected output under random removal. Table 2 claims pretrained H4Z: G6W finetune 1.18 no QX2 vs 0.92 QX2; E5Q 0.96 vs 0.79. Appendix B.4: best QX2 G6W finetune LR ~0.01 vs high LR 0.1.

errors.claim: ImageNet dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: For other color image rows, dimensionality includes color channels: e.g. “3072 (32 × 32 color)” for SVHN/CIFAR, which equals 32×32×3. But 256×256 color would be 256×256×3 = 196608, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality 65536 corresponds to 256×256 grayscale/single-channel, contradicting the parenthetical description “color” and the table’s own convention for color images.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer net the error reduces from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.location: this part, Section 6.2 Results on TIMIT

errors.explanation: The text says the 8-layer net’s non-dropout error is 20.5%, but Table 7 gives 20.7% for the 8-layer DBN-pretrained NN. The 20.5% value belongs to a different 5-layer mcRBM-DBN-pretrained model.

errors.claim: "dropout ... outperforms all other methods"
errors.location: this part, Section 6.4 text after Table 8
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports Neural Network with dropout = 567 code-quality bits, while Bayesian Neural Network = 623, and the text itself says "Bayesian neural nets perform better than dropout."
errors.explanation: Since higher code quality is better, dropout does not outperform all other methods; it is worse than the Bayesian neural network reported in the same table.

errors.evidence: Earlier notes: MNIST Table 2 reported "+max-norm ReLU" with dropout at 0.95% test error.

errors.claim: “Thereafter, the Monte-Carlo method is slightly better than the approximate method ... This shows that weight scaling always matches or outperforms Monte-Carlo averaging for the tested model.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says: “Thereafter, the Monte-Carlo method is slightly better than the approximate method...”
errors.explanation: If Monte-Carlo averaging is slightly better after about k=50, then weight scaling does not always match or outperform it. The conclusion contradicts the preceding result description.

errors.claim: In the RBM definition, θ={W,a,b} with energy term “vᵀWh + aᵀh + bᵀv”, but the conditional hidden probability is given as “P(hj=1|rj,v)=1(rj=1)σ(bj + Σi Wij vi)” and visible probability as “P(vi=1|h)=σ(ai + Σj Wij hj)”.
errors.evidence: The joint distribution defines “aᵀh” as the hidden bias term and “bᵀv” as the visible bias term.
errors.explanation: Given the model definition, hidden unit conditionals should use hidden bias a_j, and visible unit conditionals should use visible bias b_i. The displayed conditionals swap a and b, contradicting the earlier parameter definition.

final_notes:
Paper: Dropout JMLR 2014. Dropout trains sampled thinned nets; retain prob p; test uses full net with outgoing weights scaled by p. Inverted dropout scales retained activations by 1/p during training and no test scaling. Hidden p often .5; input ~.8/closer to 1. Max-norm incoming hidden weights ||w||≤c, typical c=3-4. Pretrained weights scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetune. Appendix heuristics: if n units optimal without dropout, use at least n/p hidden units; dropout nets often need 10-100x learning rate and momentum .95-.99; training 2-3x longer.

Dataset details: Table1 MNIST 784 60K/10K; SVHN 3072 color 600K/26K; CIFAR-10/100 3072 color Table1 60K/10K but App B.3 50K/10K; ImageNet 65536, 1.2M/150K (possible dimensional conflict with 256×256 color=196608); TIMIT 2520 1.1M/58K; Reuters 2000 200K/200K; Alt Splicing 1014 2932/733.

Internal errors found: TIMIT text wrongly says 8-layer reduces from 20.5; Table7 DBN8+dropout 19.7. Alt splicing main text wrongly says dropout outperforms all; Table8 dropout 567, BNN 623. Sec7.5/Fig11 text contradicts itself by concluding weight scaling always matches/outperforms MC though after k>50 MC slightly better within 1 SD. Sec8 RBM conditional equations swap biases. Appendix B.3 says CIFAR 50K/10K vs Table1 60K/10K.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Abstract/main claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping units/connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Training samples an exponential number of “thinned” networks. Intro: Deep nets expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing regularization: early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Bayesian gold standard would average over parameter settings weighted by posterior; dropout aims to approximate this with less computation by using an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Model combination helps but separately training/testing many large nets is expensive; diverse nets require different architectures or data subsets.

Dropout definition: “dropping out” hidden or visible units means temporarily removing the unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Units are randomly retained independently with probability p. p chosen by validation or often 0.5, near optimal for many networks/tasks; input-unit retention probability usually closer to 1. Figure 1 shows standard vs dropout network. Figure 2: at training a unit present with probability p and weights w to next layer; at test unit always present and outgoing weights multiplied by p, so test output equals expected training output.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims/definition: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameters remain O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net, so training can be viewed as training 2^n shared-weight nets, each rarely trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. This approximate averaging is claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Broader scope: Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. graphical models/Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine and compares to standard RBMs; claims dropout RBMs are better in certain respects.

Paper structure: Sec2 motivation; Sec3 previous work; Sec4 formal dropout model; Sec5 training algorithm; Sec6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec7 effects on network properties and hyperparameters; Sec8 Dropout RBM; Sec9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide/hyperparameter considerations.

Motivation section: Dropout is motivated by sexual reproduction/evolution: genes must work with random subsets of other genes, discouraging complex co-adaptations and promoting robust, independently useful features. Also motivated by “conspiracies”: many small co-adaptations generalize better under changing/non-stationary conditions than one large fragile co-adaptation. Notes that hidden units will still learn different things; simply duplicating units would be a poor solution, like replica codes for noisy channels.
