Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava et al.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible/input units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Dropping out 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units often optimal. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test; Sec4 states W_test^(l)=p W^(l). This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Resulting net used without dropout.

Related work/motivation: Related to denoising autoencoders, which add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically use ~5% noise; dropout’s weight scaling permits much higher noise. Deterministic counterpart can be obtained by marginalizing dropout noise in simple cases; related to van der Maaten et al. “blankout noise” (inputs only/no hidden layers), Wang & Manning speeding up dropout by marginalizing noise, Chen et al. marginalizing DAEs. Adversarial dropping work fixes max units dropped but no hidden units.

Sec4 formalism: Standard layer: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), ỹ^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then next layer uses ỹ. Backprop derivatives through sampled sub-network.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014). Dropout: randomly drop hidden or visible/input units and connections during training; retained independently with probability p (often hidden p=0.5; inputs closer to 1; common optimal: 20% input, 50% hidden dropped). Each training case samples a thinned net; n units imply 2^n thinned nets with shared weights.

Test-time approximation: use one unthinned net without dropout, with trained outgoing weights multiplied by p: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), so expected training-time unit output equals test-time output.

Sec4 formalism: standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses ỹ^(l)=r*y; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Related work: dropout compared to denoising autoencoders, blankout/marginalized noise, adversarial dropping; dropout extends noise to hidden layers/supervised/model averaging/various architectures and allows high noise via weight scaling.

Sec5 training: SGD as usual except each training case in mini-batch uses sampled thinned net; parameters unused by a case get zero gradient; gradients averaged over mini-batch. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weights to hidden unit ||w||2≤c, projecting to ball radius c; c tuned on validation; helps even without dropout. Dropout + max-norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives boost.

Pretraining: can finetune pretrained nets with dropout; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. Smaller finetuning LRs preserve pretrained information; improves final generalization vs finetuning without dropout.

Experiments intro: classification across MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Claim: dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout nets; details in Appendix B.

§2 motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction: recombination breaks large co-adapted gene sets yet may favor genes that work with random partners, robustness, and reduced barriers to spread of useful genes. Dropout-trained hidden units likewise face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful robust features instead of relying on other units to fix mistakes; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes in noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies more robust than one large conspiracy under changing/non-stationary conditions; complex co-adaptations may fit training data but fail on test data more readily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

grade.reason: Reviewer item 5 points out the direct contradiction that the paper both claims T6R always matches/outperforms X9M and that X9M performs slightly better after enough samples, which matches the planted error.

errors.claim: ImageNet (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has three color channels, so the dimensionality implied by the parenthetical is 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the stated image size and color format in the same table cell.

errors.claim: “The best convolutional networks without dropout achieve 3.95% error.”
errors.location: this part, SVHN discussion after Table 3
errors.evidence: Table 3 lists “Conv Net + stochastic pooling (Zeiler and Fergus, 2013) | 2.80,” which is a convolutional network entry not described as using dropout, and has lower error than 3.95%.
errors.explanation: The text’s claim that the best convolutional networks without dropout achieve 3.95% conflicts with the table’s lower non-dropout convolutional result of 2.80%, unless the claim was meant only for the authors’ max-pooling architecture, which it does not say.

errors.claim: “Dropout improves the max-pooling network: Table 3, ‘Conv Net + max-pooling,’ 3.95%; dropout in fully connected layers, 3.02%; dropout in all layers, 2.55%.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes for Table 3: “Conv Net + max-pooling 3.95; +dropout FC 3.02; Conv Net + stochastic pooling 2.80; +dropout all layers 2.55; maxout 2.47.”
errors.explanation: The 2.55% all-layer dropout result was recorded as following the stochastic-pooling convolutional net, not the max-pooling network. This part characterizes it as a max-pooling-network result, conflicting with the earlier Table 3 notes.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” as 20.7%, and “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) + dropout” as 19.7%. The 20.5% value belongs to “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The prose assigns the 20.5% baseline to the 8-layer pretrained network, but the table assigns 20.7% to that model and 20.5% to a different 5-layer mcRBM-DBN model.

errors.claim: “dropout substantially improves standard neural networks and outperforms every other method listed.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says “Bayesian networks perform better than dropout,” and Table 8 shows Bayesian Neural Network = 623 bits versus Neural Network with dropout = 567 bits.
errors.explanation: Since higher Code Quality is better, dropout does not outperform the Bayesian Neural Network listed in the table. The claim is only true if “other” is meant to exclude the Bayesian method, but as written it conflicts with the table and preceding sentence.

errors.claim: “This shows that weight scaling always matches or outperforms Monte-Carlo averaging for the tested model.”
errors.evidence: The immediately preceding sentence says: “Beyond that, it is slightly better, but well within one standard deviation,” referring to Monte-Carlo averaging beyond about k=50.
errors.explanation: If Monte-Carlo averaging is slightly better beyond k=50, then weight scaling does not always match or outperform it, even if the difference is within one standard deviation.

errors.claim: The hidden conditional is \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i)\), and the visible conditional is \(P(v_i=1\mid h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_j W_{ij}h_j)\).
errors.evidence: The RBM distribution is defined earlier in the same subsection as \(\exp(v^\top Wh+a^\top h+b^\top v)\), with parameters \(\theta=\{W,a,b\}\). Thus \(a\) is the hidden bias vector and \(b\) is the visible bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated energy/probability expression, hidden-unit conditionals should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), and visible-unit conditionals should use the visible bias \(b_i\). The displayed conditionals swap \(a\) and \(b\), and even index \(b_j\) as if it were a hidden bias.

errors.claim: “CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 each contain 50,000 training and 10,000 test images”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 1 recorded in notes: “CIFAR 3072 60K/10K.”
errors.explanation: The paper’s earlier dataset table gave CIFAR as having 60K training cases and 10K test cases, while this appendix says each CIFAR dataset has 50K training and 10K test images.

final_notes:
Paper: Dropout = random thinned shared-weight nets; p retention; standard test scales outgoing weights by p. Inverted dropout: retained activations ×1/p during training, no test scaling.

Dataset issues: Table 1 says CIFAR 60K/10K, but App B.3 says CIFAR-10/100 each 50K train/10K test. ImageNet Table dim 65536 conflicts with “256×256 color” (should be 196608). Reuters subset 402,738 equally split (~201,369 train/test), Table rounds to 200K/200K. Alt splicing 3665 exons = 2932/733 split.

Reported internal inconsistencies: SVHN prose misstates best no-dropout conv net as 3.95 despite stochastic pooling 2.80, and calls 2.55 all-layer dropout a max-pooling result. TIMIT prose says 8-layer falls from 20.5, table says 20.7. Alt splicing prose says dropout beats every listed method, but Bayesian NN 623 > dropout 567. Section 7 MC averaging: k≈50 matches weight scaling; beyond k MC slightly better within 1 SD, contradicting claim weight scaling always matches/outperforms. Section 8 Dropout RBM: energy says a hidden bias, b visible bias, but conditionals swap them.

Key results: MNIST best dropout+maxnorm ReLU 2×8192 0.95; DBN+dropout 0.92; DBM+dropout 0.79. SVHN best maxout 2.47, all-layer dropout 2.55. CIFAR all-layer dropout 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. ImageNet avg 5 dropout conv nets top-5 16.4. TIMIT dropout 23.4→21.8; DBN-pretrained 4-layer 22.7→19.7; 8-layer 20.7→19.7. Reuters NN 31.05, dropout 29.62. Alt splicing dropout CQ 567, Bayesian NN 623.

Appendix B: MNIST held out 10K validation, then reunited. SVHN/CIFAR use similar conv architecture. TIMIT dropout p input .8 hidden .5, c=4, LR .1; DBN finetune best LR .01, max-norm no improvement. Alt splicing dropout 2×1024, input p=.7 hidden p=.5, max-norm, 5 folds.

Paper summary: Dropout reduces overfitting in large neural nets without training/using many separate networks. During training it randomly removes units and connections, sampling many smaller shared-weight networks. At test time, a single full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble predictions. Reported improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Paper compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks; examines learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging. Dropout RBMs learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout with multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation noted: dropout networks typically take 2–3x longer to train than standard networks with the same architecture.

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. QX2/dropout randomly gates units during training; usual test-time scales weights by retention p. Claims QX2 lowers generalization error across varied classification problems and improves over no-dropout on every tested dataset; usually 2–3× training time. Definitions: O3U=L1, Y5F=L2, U2L=RBM, B8T=Dropout RBM, E5Q/DBM; F3N=ReLU; L8J=maxout; G6W=DBN/stacked RBM init; V9C=max-norm.
Key results: H4Z best E5Q+QX2 0.79; A2F maxout/QX2 2.47 vs QX2 all 2.55; J3V/W6R QX2 all 12.61/37.20, maxout 11.68/38.57. K9D Conv Net+QX2 37.5/17.0 (2010); 2012 single 40.7/18.2 val, avg 5 38.1/16.4 val and 16.4 top-5 test. Docs: 31.05% to 29.62%. Genetics Table8 C4Y/Z7P: early-stop NN 440, NN+QX2 567, Bayesian NN 623; results averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al.; QX2 used much larger net, two layers of 1024 hidden units vs Bayesian “few tens.” Table9 H4Z: max-norm 1.35, QX2+max-norm 1.05. Gaussian dropout Table10: H4Z D4K 1.08±0.04 vs Bernoulli 0.95±0.04; J3V 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1; inverted scaling variance (1-p)/p.
Known errors: Table1 K9D 65536 as “256×256 color”; TIMIT prose 8-layer baseline 20.5 vs Table7 G6W8 20.7; §7.5 X9M/T6R inconsistency and Appendix B.1 k≈50 “to match” despite X9M slightly better; §8 RBM joint swaps visible/hidden bias notation.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Abstract/main claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping units/connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Training samples an exponential number of “thinned” networks. At test time, approximate averaging predictions of all thinned nets using one unthinned network with smaller weights. Claims significant reductions in overfitting and improvements over other regularization methods on vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmarks.

Intro: Deep nets expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing regularization: early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Bayesian gold standard would average over parameter settings weighted by posterior; dropout aims to approximate this with less computation by using an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned models sharing parameters. Model combination helps but separately training/testing many large nets is expensive; diverse nets require different architectures or data subsets.

Dropout definition: “dropping out” hidden or visible units means temporarily removing the unit and all incoming/outgoing connections. Units are randomly retained independently with probability p. p chosen by validation or often 0.5, near optimal for many networks/tasks; input-unit retention probability usually closer to 1. Figure 1 shows standard vs dropout network. Figure 2: at training a unit present with probability p and weights w to next layer; at test unit always present and outgoing weights multiplied by p, so test output equals expected training output.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims/definition: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; network with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameters remain O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net, so training can be viewed as training 2^n shared-weight nets, each rarely trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. This approximate averaging is claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Broader scope: Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. graphical models/Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout Restricted Boltzmann Machine and compares to standard RBMs; claims dropout RBMs are better in certain respects.

Paper structure: Sec2 motivation; Sec3 previous work; Sec4 formal dropout model; Sec5 training algorithm; Sec6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec7 effects on network properties and hyperparameters; Sec8 Dropout RBM; Sec9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide/hyperparameter considerations.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test. This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Claimed to significantly reduce generalization error versus other regularization methods across many classification problems.

Motivation section: Dropout is motivated by sexual reproduction/evolution: genes must work with random subsets of other genes, discouraging complex co-adaptations and promoting robust, independently useful features. Also motivated by “conspiracies”: many small co-adaptations generalize better under changing/non-stationary conditions than one large fragile co-adaptation. Notes that hidden units will still learn different things; simply duplicating units would be a poor solution, like replica codes for noisy channels.

Broader scope/structure: Applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. dropout RBMs (claimed better in some respects). Sections: 3 related work; 4 formal model; 5 training; 6 experiments; 7 effects/hyperparameters; 8 Dropout RBM; 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A guide. Sec3 begins: dropout can be interpreted as regularizing a neural net by adding noise to hidden units; relates to Denoising Autoencoders adding noise to unit states.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp.1929–1958). Authors: Srivastava et al.

Core definition/claims: Dropout combats overfitting by randomly dropping hidden or visible/input units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Units retained independently with probability p; p often 0.5 for hidden units, input p usually closer to 1. Dropping out 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units often optimal. Applying dropout samples a “thinned” network; n units imply 2^n possible thinned networks, with shared weights so parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. Each training case presentation samples a new thinned net.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging over exponentially many thinned nets infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit is retained with probability p at training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test; Sec4 states W_test^(l)=p W^(l). This makes each hidden unit’s expected training-time output equal its actual test-time output. Resulting net used without dropout.

Related work/motivation: Related to denoising autoencoders, which add noise to inputs and reconstruct clean input; dropout extends noise to hidden layers, supervised learning, model averaging, and architectures such as Boltzmann Machines. DAEs typically use ~5% noise; dropout’s weight scaling permits much higher noise. Deterministic counterpart can be obtained by marginalizing dropout noise in simple cases; related to van der Maaten et al. “blankout noise” (inputs only/no hidden layers), Wang & Manning speeding up dropout by marginalizing noise, Chen et al. marginalizing DAEs. Adversarial dropping work fixes max units dropped but no hidden units.

Sec4 formalism: Standard layer: z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), ỹ^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then next layer uses ỹ. Backprop derivatives through sampled sub-network.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014). Dropout: randomly drop hidden or visible/input units and connections during training; retained independently with probability p (often hidden p=0.5; inputs closer to 1; common optimal: 20% input, 50% hidden dropped). Each training case samples a thinned net; n units imply 2^n thinned nets with shared weights.

Test-time approximation: use one unthinned net without dropout, with trained outgoing weights multiplied by p: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), so expected training-time unit output equals test-time output.

Sec4 formalism: standard z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses ỹ^(l)=r*y; backprop through sampled subnetwork.

Related work: dropout compared to denoising autoencoders, blankout/marginalized noise, adversarial dropping; dropout extends noise to hidden layers/supervised/model averaging/various architectures and allows high noise via weight scaling.

Sec5 training: SGD as usual except each training case in mini-batch uses sampled thinned net; parameters unused by a case get zero gradient; gradients averaged over mini-batch. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weights to hidden unit ||w||2≤c, projecting to ball radius c; c tuned on validation; helps even without dropout. Dropout + max-norm + large decaying LR + high momentum gives boost.

Pretraining: can finetune pretrained nets with dropout; pretraining unchanged. Pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/p before dropout finetuning so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. Smaller finetuning LRs preserve pretrained information; improves final generalization vs finetuning without dropout.

Experiments intro: classification across MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Claim: dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout nets; details in Appendix B.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), but test-time uses no removals and scaled weights \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). It also says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*y)+b)]\) is not generally equal to \(f(p\mathbf w y+b)\). The equations only make the expected preactivation/input contribution match, not the hidden unit’s expected output.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier model equations in notes: with dropout, gates are applied before the next affine transform, then activation: “\(\tilde y^{(l)}=r^{(l)}*y^{(l)}\), then \(z_i=w_i\tilde y+b_i\), \(y_i=f(z_i)\).” Notes also record the caveat that equality under scaling is supported for expected preactivation/input contribution, not generally for nonlinear output.
errors.explanation: Multiplying weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation contribution match the pretrained preactivation, but with a nonlinear activation \(f\), it does not in general make the expected unit output match the pretrained output. This repeats/conflicts with the earlier equations unless “output” is meant imprecisely as input/preactivation.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout,” JMLR 2014. Dropout/QX2 randomly removes units/connections during training; test uses unthinned net with weights scaled pW. Caveat §§4–5: expected “output” preservation really applies to preactivations, not nonlinear activations. Typical optimal p: hidden around 0.5/default, input around 0.8/closer to 1; appendix hidden range 0.5–0.8, real-valued inputs 0.8. Appendix heuristics: dropout layer at least n/p units if standard layer has n; dropout LR 10–100× standard; momentum 0.95–0.99 vs standard 0.9; max-norm/V9C c typically 3–4. Training often 2–3× standard net; acceleration future work.

Experiments claim dropout improves generalization on every tested dataset, but §7.4 says two smallest MNIST/H4Z training sizes show no QX2 improvement. Domains: H4Z, A2F, J3V, W6R, K9D, N8Q, M5X, Z7P. Possible K9D dimensionality inconsistency: Table 1 says 65536 “256×256 color.” A2F: 6000 validation; conv filters 96/128/256; p=(.9,.75,.75,.5,.5,.5), c=4, momentum .95. J3V/W6R: 50k train/10k test, 5k validation, same architecture/retention as A2F.

TIMIT/N8Q Table 7: NN 23.4→21.8; G6W 4-layer 22.7→19.7; G6W 8-layer 20.7→19.7; mcRBM-G6W 20.5. Internal error: prose says 8-layer pre-QX2 20.5. N8Q appendix: 21-frame window; input p=.8, hidden p=.5, V9C c=4, momentum .95, high LR .1, decay eps0(1+t/T)^-1, G6W pretraining U2L CD-1, Gaussian variance fixed 1, best QX2 finetune LR about .01; adding V9C during G6W finetune gave no improvement.

M5X 31.05→29.62; subset 402,738 docs, 2000-word vocab, 50 categories, equal train/test. Z7P: NN+QX2 567, Bayesian NN 623; error if QX2 said to exceed every other method. Z7P appendix: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue-type softmaxes with inc/exc/nc; QX2 net 2×1024, hidden p=.5, input p=.7, V9C/high decaying LR, same 5 folds as Xiong. §8.1 conditionals swap RBM biases vs joint.

Intro claims: with unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is best regularization; dropout cheaply approximates equally weighted geometric mean of predictions from exponentially many learned parameter-sharing models. Practical inference: weight scaling uses one unthinned net instead of explicit exponential averaging; Monte Carlo model averaging is more expensive. Dropout said to extend beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models incl. RBMs / Dropout RBM. Figure 1: standard net with two hidden layers vs dropout thinned net removing crossed units and incoming/outgoing connections. Intro: Bayesian/model averaging ideal but expensive; dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean over exponentially many learned thinned nets. §2 motivation: analogy to sexual reproduction: recombination breaks large co-adapted gene sets yet may favor genes that work with random partners, robustness, and reduced barriers to spread of useful genes. Dropout-trained hidden units likewise face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful robust features instead of relying on other units to fix mistakes; units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is poor robustness, analogous to replica codes in noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies more robust than one large conspiracy under changing/non-stationary conditions; complex co-adaptations may fit training data but fail on test data more readily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958; authors Srivastava et al. Core claims: dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, inhibits co-adaptation, samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned nets; at test time one unthinned net with reduced/scaled weights approximates averaged predictions/geometric mean. Claims reduced overfitting, improvements vs other regularizers, SOTA on many benchmarks. Intro: n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets with O(n^2) or fewer parameters; new thinned net sampled for each case, each model trained rarely/never. Applies beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models/RBMs. §2 motivation: sexual reproduction analogy—random partners encourage robust independently useful features; replication of units poor robustness; conspiracy analogy: many small/simple co-adaptations more robust than one large/complex one under changing conditions.

§3 related work: dropout as noise in hidden-unit states, extending denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010) from input corruption/clean reconstruction to effective hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised+unsupervised use, and architectures like Boltzmann Machines. Test-time weight scaling/approximation permits higher noise than typically best for DAEs. Table: DAE typical best noise 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; hidden-unit removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise minimizes expected loss; adversarial removal alternatives (Globerson & Roweis 2006; Dekel et al. 2010) choose removals subject to max number and have no hidden units. Marginalizing dropout can yield deterministic regularizers in simple cases. Exponential-family input-noise/“blankout noise” regularizers studied by van der Maaten et al. 2013, limited to no hidden layers; Chen et al. 2012 marginalized DAEs; Wang & Manning 2013 proposed marginalization to accelerate dropout.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines training output as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), but test-time uses no removals and scaled weights \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\), giving \(f(p\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\mathbf y^{(l)}+b_i^{(l+1)})\). It also says any activation is admissible, including the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid, \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*y)+b)]\) is not generally equal to \(f(p\mathbf w y+b)\). The equations only make the expected preactivation/input contribution match, not the hidden unit’s expected output.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”

grade.reason: Reviewer item about W6R vs L8J (Table 4 showing maxout/L8J error 38.57% > 37.20% for QX2) directly identifies the planted overbroad claim that maxout/L8J gives further gains on every image benchmark as false.

errors.claim: ImageNet (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has three color channels, so the dimensionality implied by the parenthetical is 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608, not 65536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the stated image size and color format in the same table cell.

errors.claim: “The best convolutional networks without dropout achieve 3.95% error.”
errors.location: this part, SVHN discussion after Table 3
errors.evidence: Table 3 lists “Conv Net + stochastic pooling (Zeiler and Fergus, 2013) | 2.80” and does not identify it as using dropout, while “Conv Net + max-pooling | 3.95” is only one non-dropout conv net row.
errors.explanation: As written, the claim says the best convolutional networks without dropout are at 3.95%, but the same table reports a convolutional network without any dropout label at 2.80%, which is better.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer network, error falls from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” as 20.7%, while 20.5% belongs to “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).” The dropout 8-layer row is 19.7%.
errors.explanation: The prose uses the 20.5% error rate for the 8-layer pretrained baseline, but the table assigns that number to a different 5-layer mcRBM-DBN model. The matching 8-layer baseline in the table is 20.7%, not 20.5%.

errors.claim: “dropout ... outperforms every other method listed.”
errors.location: this part, Section 6.4 prose after Table 8
errors.evidence: Table 8 lists “Neural Network with dropout” at 567 bits and “Bayesian Neural Network” at 623 bits; the same paragraph says “Bayesian networks perform better than dropout.”
errors.explanation: Since higher Code Quality is better, dropout does not outperform every listed method. It outperforms the non-Bayesian baselines but not the Bayesian Neural Network.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,v)= 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j+∑_i W_{ij}v_i)” and “P(v_i=1\mid h)=σ(a_i+∑_j W_{ij}h_j)”
errors.evidence: The same subsection defines the RBM energy/probability term as “exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v)”, so a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional distributions swap the biases: hidden conditionals should use the hidden bias a_j, and visible conditionals should use the visible bias b_i, given the model definition immediately above.

final_notes: Dropout definition: retention p; test scales outgoing weights by p. Inverted dropout multiplier 1/p if retained; mean 1 var (1-p)/p. Table 1 ImageNet dim 65536 “256×256 color” conflicts with color dim 196608. Sec 6 claims dropout improves NN comparisons on every dataset. Vision: MNIST Table 2 dropout improves; best DBM+dropout 0.79. Appendix B.1 MNIST uses 10k validation then reunited, 1M updates, hidden p=.5 input p=.8, momentum .95, c=2; 4096/8192 2-layer improve, 3-layer worse. SVHN best dropout/maxout 2.47; conv+pool+dropout 2.55; human 2.0. CIFAR-10/100 dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. ImageNet: ILSVRC-2010 Conv+dropout 37.5/17.0; ILSVRC-2012 avg 5 Conv+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top-5 16.4. Conclusion claims SOTA on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST. TIMIT Table 7: NN 23.4→21.8 dropout; DBN 4-layer 22.7→19.7; DBN 8-layer 20.7→19.7. Internal error: prose says 8-layer falls 20.5→19.7, but 20.5 is mcRBM 5-layer. Appendix B.4 TIMIT: p=.8 input/.5 hidden, c=4, momentum .95, LR .1; DBN finetune best LR about .01; max-norm no improvement. Reuters: RCV1 subset 402,738 docs, 2000 vocab, 50 cats, one class/doc, equal train/test; dropout improved all tried architectures but less; best comparison 31.05% no dropout vs 29.62% dropout. Alt splicing Table 8: dropout NN 567 bits, Bayesian NN 623; internal error: prose says dropout outperforms every other listed method. Appendix B.6: 3665 exons, 1014 features, 4 tissues; 2-layer 1024 dropout p=.5 hidden/.7 input; 5 folds.

Paper summary: Dropout reduces overfitting in large neural nets without training/using many separate networks. During training it randomly removes units and connections, sampling many smaller shared-weight networks. At test time, a single full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble predictions. Reported improvements on image, speech, text, and alternative-splicing tasks. Paper compares dropout with other regularizers and Bayesian neural networks; examines learned features, sparsity, dropout rates, network size, training-set size, and test-time averaging. Dropout RBMs learn qualitatively different features and sparser representations. For linear regression, marginalizing dropout yields a modified ridge-regression objective. Preliminary experiments compare Bernoulli dropout with multiplicative Gaussian noise. Limitation noted: dropout networks typically take 2–3x longer to train than standard networks with the same architecture.

Comparisons include other regularizers (L1/L2, max-norm, KL sparsity, etc.), Bayesian neural networks, SVM/logistic/ridge/PCA baselines, and methods such as stochastic pooling/maxout in cited image experiments. grade.reason: None of the reported errors mention Maxout or the CIFAR-100 counterexample in Table 4, so the planted claim about Maxout beating all benchmarks was not identified.

errors.claim: K9D dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image would have 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608 dimensions, not 65536. 65536 corresponds to 256 × 256 without color channels.
errors.explanation: The dimensionality number conflicts with the parenthetical description in the same table entry.

errors.claim: Across all image benchmarks, L8J permits another gain.
errors.evidence: Table 4 shows W6R error is 37.20 for “Conv Net + max pooling + QX2 in all layers” but 38.57 for “Conv Net + L8J (Goodfellow et al., 2013).”
errors.explanation: If W6R is one of the image benchmarks, L8J does not give another gain over the all-layer QX2 result there; its listed error is higher.

errors.claim: The prose comparison for the deeper pretrained network uses 20.5% as the pre-QX2 error for the 8-layer net.
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) ... 20.7” and lists “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) ... 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% value belongs to a 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained model, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained model. The corresponding 8-layer baseline in Table 7 is 20.7%.

errors.claim: “An ordinary U2L defines … exp( v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v )” together with later conditionals “P(h_j=1 | r_j,v)=…σ(b_j+∑_i W_ij v_i)” and “P(v_i=1 | h)=σ(a_i+∑_j W_ij h_j).”
errors.evidence: The joint distribution assigns \(\mathbf a\) to hidden units via \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h\) and \(\mathbf b\) to visible units via \(\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\). But the conditional equations use \(b_j\) as the hidden bias and \(a_i\) as the visible bias.
errors.explanation: Within the same model description, the roles of \(a\) and \(b\) are reversed between the joint distribution and the conditional distributions.

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. QX2=dropout; test weights scaled by retention p; pretrained weights multiplied by 1/p before QX2. Claims lower gen error across varied classification, improves no-dropout on every tested dataset; usually 2–3× training. Codes: O3U=L1, Y5F=L2, U2L=RBM, B8T=Dropout RBM, E5Q=DBM, F3N=ReLU, L8J=maxout, G6W=DBN/stacked RBM init, V9C=max-norm, X9M=sampled averaging, T6R=weight scaling, P7V=Bernoulli dropout, D4K=Gaussian dropout.
Known inconsistencies: Table1 K9D 65536 listed as 256×256 color though color would be ×3. Image summary “Across all image benchmarks, L8J permits another gain” conflicts with W6R Table4 where QX2 all layers 37.20 beats L8J 38.57. N8Q/Table7 prose uses 20.5 as 8-layer pre-QX2 baseline, but table’s 8-layer baseline is 20.7; QX2 example 23.4 vs 21.8. Sec8.1 RBM joint uses a^T h + b^T v, but conditionals use b_j for hidden bias and a_i for visible bias.
Key results: H4Z best 0.79; A2F best L8J 2.47; J3V/W6R QX2 12.61/37.20; K9D 5-net QX2 38.1/16.4 val/test; Z7P QX2 NN 567 vs early NN 440, Bayesian 623. Gaussian multiplicative noise as good/slightly better; D4K no test scaling.

Dropout randomly removes selected units and connections during training, effectively training many smaller parameter-sharing networks; at test time uses one complete network with reduced weights to approximate averaged predictions. Training with dropout typically takes 2–3× as long as standard network of same architecture.

Conclusion: QX2 trains sampled submodels; U2L/RBM fits, B8T has desirable feature/sparsity properties; QX2 methods attain SOTA on A2F,K9D,W6R,H4Z; stochasticity likely prevents overfitting but increases training time; noise marginalization gives modified Y5F for linear regression, harder for complex models.
Codes: O3U=L1, Y5F=L2, U2L=RBM, B8T=Dropout RBM, E5Q=DBM, F3N=ReLU, L8J=maxout, G6W=DBN/stacked RBM init, V9C=max-norm, X9M=sampled averaging, T6R=weight scaling, P7V=Bernoulli dropout, D4K=Gaussian dropout.
Known inconsistencies: Table1 K9D 65536 listed as 256×256 color though color would be ×3. Image summary “Across all image benchmarks, L8J permits another gain” conflicts with W6R Table4 where QX2 all layers 37.20 beats L8J 38.57. N8Q/Table7 prose uses 20.5 as 8-layer pre-QX2 baseline, but table’s 8-layer baseline is 20.7; QX2 example 23.4 vs 21.8. Sec8.1 RBM joint uses a^T h + b^T v, but conditionals use b_j for hidden bias and a_i for visible bias.
